# Agent Guide

Rust + Godot multi PTY emulator with a tiling grid GUI.

## Guides

This file holds the rules every change needs. The detailed rules live in one page per topic; read the ones your change touches before editing.

| Guide | Read it when |
|---|---|
| [Quick reference](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/quick-reference.md) | Invariable rules cheat sheet for Rust, GDScript, PTY, security and CI |
| [Testing](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/testing.md) | Writing or running tests, the gate commands, the UI/UX assessment method |
| [Defect classes](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/defect-classes.md) | Writing a bug fix, triaging a defect, or running the per-release defect review |
| [Rust conventions](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/rust.md) | Touching anything under `crates/` |
| [GDScript conventions](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/gdscript.md) | Touching anything under `godot/` |
| [GDScript performance](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/gdscript-performance.md) | Auditing a GDScript hot path, or deciding whether work belongs in Rust |
| [Concept capture](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/concept-capture.md) | Concepts, triggers, stop conditions, routing |
| [Inspector, Reasoning, and OMP](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/inspector-reasoning-omp.md) | The agent-observability panes |
| [Plugin manifest](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/plugins.md) | Plugin manifests, catalog, install and trust |
| [Security rules](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/security.md) | Any change near IPC, PTY, the filesystem, plugins, networking, or secrets (read before editing) |
| [Pitfalls and tool notes](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/pitfalls.md) | Before debugging, and before touching an FFI or CLI boundary: the known traps |
| [Pitfalls: GDScript](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/pitfalls-gdscript.md) | Godot UI, nodes, theme tokens, styling, signals, and viewport traps |
| [Pitfalls: Rust & FFI](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/pitfalls-rust.md) | gdext, Variant packing, thread boundaries, stores, and FFI rules |
| [Pitfalls: Terminal & PTY](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/pitfalls-terminal.md) | ANSI/VTE parsing, SGR, escape codes, alt screen, and ConPTY traps |
| [Pitfalls: Platform & CI](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/pitfalls-platform-ci.md) | Windows paths/DACL, macOS Mach-O, namespaces, and cache traps |

## Project Structure

- Stack: Rust (edition 2024, `crates/`) backend + Godot (4.7, `godot/`) GDScript frontend via `gdext` (0.5); entry point `godot/scenes/main.tscn` → `workspace.gd` (root `Control` node).
- Crates: `gpty-core` (PTY spawn, vte parser, alacritty grid, capture, history, vault), `gpty-ai` (Inspector backends: mock, private OMP RPC, CLI NDJSON bridge; no tools), `gpty-ipc` (JSON-RPC transport, client, server), `gpty-gdext` (the GDExtension: `GptyTerminal`, `GptyAi`, `GptyCliView`, `GptyMarkdown`, `GptyMedia`), `gpty` (in `crates/gpty-cli`: CLI + MCP), `gpty-media` (pinned FFmpeg backend), `gpty-plugin` (installed-plugin store the CLI and GDExtension share).
- Godot: `godot/scenes/autoloads/` (managers + persistence base), `terminal/` (workspace, pane rendering and input, IPC dispatch, tile lifecycle), `ui/` (chrome, overlays, theme, graph canvas), `panes/` (one body per pane type); tests in `godot/tests/{unit,integration}`, the capture harness in `godot/tests/bench/`.
- The file-by-file map with one-line roles is [Repository map](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/repo-map.md) - read it to find which module owns a behaviour.

## Commands

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](gpty-doc:CONTRIBUTING.md) for all development, build, test, and CLI commands.

### Data Flow

```
Shell → PTY I/O thread → vte parser → alacritty_terminal grid → Arc<Mutex<TermGrid>> → GptyTerminal (gdext) → GDScript _draw()
```

```
CLI → Unix socket (gpty.sock) → IpcServer (tokio) → PENDING_IPC queue → GDScript _poll_ipc_requests() → workspace methods → IPC_RESPONDERS → CLI response
```

```
OMP TUI (user-launched in a terminal) → @gpty/omp-events extension → gpty-events.sock (ompEvent) → omp_events.rs translates to the generic vocabulary (session.bound, agent.started, turn.started, tool.call, thinking.delta, …) → GptyTerminal.drain_agent_events() → Reasoning pane + Tier 1 agent-state badges

Any pane program → `gpty state <value>` → gpty-events.sock (ompEvent, the pane's own capability) → `state.declared` → Tier 1 agent-state badge (the declaration path on Windows, where ConPTY consumes the `gpty_state` OSC)
```

```
Inspector prompt → GptyAi.session_open/session_prompt → private omp --mode rpc --no-tools --no-session process → session_poll envelopes
```

```
cli_view pane config (command + shell_args) → GptyCliView.start(argv) → CliProcess (piped child, merged stdout/stderr) → line queue → GptyCliView.poll_lines → CliViewPane body
```

```
media pane → GptyMedia.open(JSON) → gpty-media MediaSession worker thread (pinned FFmpeg demux/decode) → bounded RGBA/PCM queues → GptyMedia.poll_video/poll_audio → pane
```

## MCP Integration

gPTY ships an MCP server (`gpty mcp`) that exposes 27 tools for AI agent integration.
AI agents and coding harnesses can discover these via the `mcp.json` that's at the root of the repository.

```json
// mcp.json - Coding harnesses should discover this automatically
{"mcpServers": {"gpty": {"command": "gpty", "args": ["mcp"]}}}
```

Tools: `new-pane`, `list-panes`, `workspace-list`, `kill-pane`, `focus-pane`, `move-pane`, `inject`, `profile-save`, `profile-load`, `profile-list`, `daemon-start`, `daemon-stop`, `daemon-status`, `concept-list`, `concept-toggle`, `pane-read`, `pane-status`, `pane-view`, `pane-set`, `pane-settings`, `pane-run`, `pane-wait`, `broadcast`, `vault-search`, `vault-read`, `vault-weight`, `version`.

`tools/call` validates the requested name against `schema::mcp_tool_names()` before dispatch: the kebab→camel mapping turns any string into an IPC method, so without the gate a client reaches methods that were never published as tools (e.g. `shutdown`).

A tool's arguments travel under the ids clap gives them (`pane_type`), while the handler reads the CLI's wire key (`type`). `commands/wire.rs` is the one translation: it derives each argument's JSON type from the clap definition (an `Append` list, a boolean flag, an integer field), renames the handful of ids that differ (`RENAMES`), and refuses an unknown key (naming the nearest valid one), a value of the wrong JSON type, or a contradictory pair with `-32602`. A new argument needs no second list; a *renamed* wire key needs an entry in that table, and `wire_keys_are_the_keys_the_handlers_read` fails if a translated key is one no handler reads.

The MCP tool schemas are auto-generated from clap command definitions in `crates/gpty-cli/src/commands/schema.rs`. Nested subcommands (`daemon`, `profile`) are flattened into prefixed tools. Self-referential tools (`mcp`, `schema`) are excluded.

A tool call the handler refuses is a *successful* `tools/call` response with `isError: true`, the handler's own sentence in the text content, and its code in `structuredContent`; JSON-RPC errors are reserved for a malformed call (the argument translation's `-32602`, an unknown tool or method) and a dead endpoint. Refusals travel flat end to end: the GUI's drain loop answers the handler's `{code, message}` error object itself, and the Rust edge builds the JSON-RPC error from it, so a CLI or MCP caller reads the sentence instead of a stringified envelope.

See `skill://gpty-omp-integration` (body at `.omp/skills/gpty-omp-integration/SKILL.md`) for usage patterns.

## Roadmap workflow

`ROADMAP.md` is an index, and the roadmap itself is a **prioritized queue** split into one page per release chain under `docs/content/docs/roadmap/` (`v0.1.md` … `v1.0.md`, then `future.md`; the Hugo site renders them as children of the Roadmap section, and `docs/content/docs/roadmap/_index.md` renders `ROADMAP.md` as the section's front page).

- **Execution guide & gates:** Read [Roadmap workflow](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/roadmap-workflow.md) and load `skill://gpty-roadmap-task` (body at `.omp/skills/gpty-roadmap-task/SKILL.md`) before working a row: they carry the execution order, per-area gates, row format (`| ✅ or ⬜ | AREA | **Title** - evidence, fix, tests |`), priority rules, screenshot conventions, and close-out contract.
- **Picking the next task:** The next task is always the first unchecked row (⬜) in the *earliest unfinished release*. Row order *is* priority.
- **Priority ordering:** Data-loss and correctness first, then reachable security, headline features, robustness and tests, low-reachability hardening, polish, and release-time work.
- **Defects & follow-ups:** A defect or follow-up discovered mid-task gets its own row in priority position with actionable evidence rather than being fixed silently or folded into unrelated commits.

## ADE Architecture Boundary

gPTY is evolving from a multi-terminal emulator into an ADE - a graphical PTY foundation with a public, agent-facing API:

| Layer | Owner | Content |
|---|---|---|
| L4 | ecosystem | Agent CLIs & apps: claude code, codex, opencode, OMP, vim, btop |
| L3 | ecosystem (open market) | Orchestration: agent waits, pane states, plugin workflows (herdr-class) |
| L2 | gPTY | Control surface: JSON-RPC socket, CLI, MCP, event socket |
| L1 | gPTY | PTY foundation: PTY lifecycle, grid, capture, history, security |
| L0 | OS | /dev/ptmx, ConPTY, sockets |

- **gPTY owns L0–L2; L3 is an open market.** gPTY ships a thin built-in L3 (concept routing, Inspector sessions, profile restore) but never absorbs an orchestrator's state machine into core. Herdr-class tools are guests (they run in panes today) and substrate consumers (they drive the public API), not competitors to clone.
- **Observe/display, never orchestrate.** Core observes and displays agent state (badges, status); it never manages or orchestrates it (no agent runtime, no wait/block state machine). Primitives only: `paneStatus`, `waitForOutput`, events.
- **Non-goals** (do not re-propose without new evidence):
  - `pane-pipe` MCP tool - the concept engine already routes pane output; a generic pipe is a broad-trigger concept.
  - `layout-apply-preset` workflow automation - plugin territory (events + actions).
  - First-party `gpty herdr *` subcommands - couples gPTY core to a foreign, versioned socket protocol with an auth model gPTY does not control (L3 creep).
  - Native third-party GDScript/Rust pane plugins in v1 - `PaneTypes.ALL` is the layout-trust anchor; a plugin-registered registry lets profile files instantiate arbitrary code at restore time. `cli_view` (stdout streaming) is the v1 plugin UI; a native pane SDK needs its own trust design.
  - `ToolRunning` state via exit codes - foreground-command exits are not reliably attributable in a PTY.
  - Webview/WebSocket panes - a new trust boundary; not v1.
- **Positioning & naming:** the wedge is GUI + public-API PTY foundation + concept engine + Windows + hardening. Keep the `gpty` name (2026-09 decision): rebranding is positioning, not renaming. Two-tier naming convention: the display name is `gPTY` (UI, docs, prose); machine-facing identifiers stay lowercase/actual - `gpty` binary, crates, repo, and socket paths; `GPTY_*` env vars; `GptyTerminal`; `@gpty/omp-events`.

## Logging

- **A program's output is not log material.** Pane output, a captured buffer, injected or pasted text, environment values and an agent backend's stderr are never logged above `debug`, and never written to a file by default. Ids, paths, counts, PIDs, error discriminants and mode bits are fine.
- **The rule is enforced, not remembered.** `scripts/check-log-hygiene` (run by `ci-check`) fails a `log::*!` whose format string or arguments name program content (`text`, `data`, `output`, `payload`, `stdout`, `stderr`, `line`, `input`, `capture`, `content`, `body`, `prompt`, `command`, `argv`, `env`) unless the call carries a `// log-ok: <why it is safe>` marker, and the marker is a claim a reviewer checks.
- **Backend stderr has one path.** `gpty_ai::logtext::spawn_drain` strips escape sequences and control characters, bounds each line to `MAX_LINE_BYTES`, logs at `debug` and fills the bounded `StderrTail` that rides the failure message a user sees. A failed `omp` start-up appends that tail to its error; the `cli` backend answers a non-zero exit with it. Do not add a second drain and do not raise the level.
- **No log file by default.** `project.godot` leaves Godot's file logging off; a launch that turns it on (`--log-file`) inside the user directory has that directory repaired to 0700 and its `*.log` files to 0600 at start-up (`BasePersistenceManager.secure_user_root`, through the same `owner_only` primitive the stores use).

## Licensing

- Core is **GPL-3.0-or-later** ([LICENSE](LICENSE)); [LICENSE-EXCEPTIONS.md](gpty-doc:LICENSE-EXCEPTIONS.md) holds the two section 7 additional permissions. Plugins, extensions, adapters, and pane types are **not** required to be GPLv3, which is why the bundled `extensions/gpty-omp-events` ships MIT and `godot/addons/gut` stays MIT. Do NOT "correct" a bundled permissive license into GPLv3, and never add license headers to JSON.
- Data files (profiles, workspaces, layouts, concepts, settings) carry no copyleft: user-authored ones are the user's own, and the shipped `godot/*.json` defaults are Apache-2.0. The engine and pane code that reads them stays GPLv3.
- First-party code is GPLv3 everywhere it is declared: `license = "GPL-3.0-or-later"` in every `crates/*/Cargo.toml`, `license=('GPL-3.0-or-later')` in `dist/aur/PKGBUILD`. Keep them in sync when adding a crate or package.
- Release artifacts must carry `LICENSE` and `LICENSE-EXCEPTIONS.md` next to the binaries (GPLv3 §4/§6 requires giving recipients a copy of the license). `.github/workflows/release-build.yml`'s `export` job stages both copies into all three archives and publishes a `SHA256SUMS` covering every asset (`release.yml` calls that shared build workflow from the tag) - keep both when editing that job. Every uploaded asset is also build-provenance attested (`actions/attest-build-provenance`, needing `id-token: write` + `attestations: write`), so `gh attestation verify` binds a download to the workflow run that produced it. Supply-chain rules for the workflows: every third-party action is pinned to a full commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment, and every CI download (Godot editor, Godot export templates, Hugo) is checksum-verified against the vendor's published sums before use - the tag is mutable, the hash is the pin.

## Commits

- Format: [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) - `feat(scope):`, `fix(scope):`, `chore(scope):`, `docs(scope):`
- DCO: every commit carries a `Signed-off-by` trailer (`git commit -s`); `githooks/commit-msg` refuses a commit without one.
- Scopes: `settings`, `terminal`, `layout`, `workspace`, `sidebar`, `ui`, `gdext`, `core`, `cli`, `ipc`, `profiles`, `concepts`, `icons`, `ci`, `ai`, `inspector`, `media`, `plugin`, `wiki`, `deps`, `docs`, `build`, `sec`, `project` (aligned with core crates, subsystems, and roadmap areas).
- Every `fix` commit carries a `Cause: <class>` trailer naming one value from [Defect classes](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/defect-classes.md) (`scripts/fix-forensics --classes` prints them); `githooks/commit-msg` refuses one without. `external` covers dependency advisories, upstream API changes and retired runners. If a fix honestly fits no class the taxonomy is missing one - add it to the guide and to `scripts/fix-forensics` in the same commit.
- Workflow: use the commit skill (`skill://commit`, body at `.omp/skills/commit/SKILL.md`) to discover changes, group them logically and write the message. The hooks are the enforcement layer: `pre-commit` runs `./scripts/ci-check --fast` (fmt, workflow lint, clippy), `pre-push` runs the full `./scripts/ci-check`; install them with `./scripts/install-hooks` once per clone.
- Skills protocol compatibility: Skills are stored at `.omp/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. OMP routes them natively via `skill://<name>`. Non-OMP agent harnesses (Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot) can navigate directly to `.omp/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
- Never commit without the full suite passing. `cargo fmt`/`cargo clippy` also run in pre-commit - run them explicitly before staging to avoid amend churn.
- A failing test: fix the source, not the test. Update a test only when the behaviour change is intentional and documented in the commit body; a test-only commit without a source change is a red flag.
- `git commit -n` / `git push --no-verify` bypass the hooks: emergencies only, and say why in the commit body.

# Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

## Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

* Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
* Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
* Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
* Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
* Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

* The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
* Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
* Public or private harassment
* Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
* Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

## Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

## Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

## Enforcement

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the maintainer at [@1nv1n](https://github.com/1nv1n). If you need confidentiality, open a private advisory at https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty/security/advisories/new with `Code of Conduct` in the title; only the maintainer can see it. Please do not open a public issue for a report.

All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly. The maintainer is obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

## Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

**Consequence**: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

**Consequence**: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

### 3. Temporary Ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

**Consequence**: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

### 4. Permanent Ban

**Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

**Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

## Attribution

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant][homepage], version 2.1, available at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html][v2.1].

Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by [Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder][Mozilla CoC].

For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq][FAQ]. Translations are available at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations][translations].

# Contributing

## Prerequisites

- Rust >= 1.85 (tested with 1.96)
- Godot 4.4+ (tested with 4.7.2) with GDExtension support
- Linux (primary target), macOS, or Windows 11 (all continuously verified in CI; native Windows ConPTY, process DACL security tests, and macOS multi-arch release builds).
- FFmpeg build dependencies for `./scripts/media-deps`: `curl`, a C toolchain, `make`, and
  `nasm` on x86 Linux (without nasm the script warns and disables hand-written SIMD). Windows
  uses vcpkg (`VCPKG_ROOT`). The script builds the pinned FFmpeg the GDExtension links.
- Python 3 (for `scripts/docs-check` and `scripts/build-wiki`).

## Setup

### Clone the repository

```bash
# Clone
git clone https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty.git gpty
cd gpty
```

### Install `git` hooks (one-time per clone)

```bash
./scripts/install-hooks
```

This installs:

- `pre-commit` (fast checks: `fmt`, `lint`, `clippy`)
- `commit-msg` (Conventional Commits enforcement)
- `pre-push` (full CI suite).

Run `./scripts/ci-check` directly to validate changes before committing.

### Build media dependencies (once per checkout)

The GDExtension links a pinned FFmpeg; build it before the first `cargo build`:

```bash
./scripts/media-deps
source dist/ffmpeg/<platform>-<arch>/env.sh   # in every new shell
```

`ci-check` builds or sources this prefix automatically. The library must be beside the extension
for a bundled run; `$ORIGIN`/`@loader_path` is baked into the GDExtension, so a dev build falls
back to the system FFmpeg when the pinned one is not on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`/`DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH`.

### Build

**Editor / day-to-day** (`res://bin/*.so` should symlink to `target/debug/`):

```bash
ln -sfn ../../target/debug/libgpty_gdext.so godot/bin/libgpty_gdext.linux.x86_64.so
cargo build -p gpty-gdext && cd godot && godot -e
```

Restart the editor after a rebuild so it remaps the `.so`.

One-shot standalone build (detects the host platform, builds gpty-gdext in release mode, stages it into `godot/bin/`, and exports into `dist/`):

```bash
./scripts/build
```

Requires Godot on PATH with export templates for **exactly** that version: a `4.7.2.stable` editor needs `4.7.2.stable` templates, and a symlinked older directory silently exports with the other engine build. The script fails early with the download command when they are missing. It also calls `scripts/bundle-media` after the export, so the host bundle carries the pinned FFmpeg runtime beside the GDExtension (run `./scripts/media-deps` first).
The manual steps below are what the script does internally.


```bash
# Build the GDExtension library (required before running Godot)
cargo build -p gpty-gdext

# Release build + stage into godot/bin for export
cargo build -p gpty-gdext --release
cp target/release/libgpty_gdext.so godot/bin/libgpty_gdext.linux.x86_64.so

godot --headless --path godot --import
godot --headless --path godot --export-release "Linux/X11" ../dist/gpty
```

### Clean

Remove build/test artifacts for a clean slate - stale IPC sockets, Godot import caches, and standalone `dist/` outputs:

```bash
./scripts/clean             # default: transient artifacts
./scripts/clean --dry-run   # list what would be removed
./scripts/clean --all       # also remove target/ and built gdext libraries
```

Sockets with a live listener (a running GUI or an in-flight test run) are never touched, and user data (`user://` settings, profiles, layouts, history.db) is preserved. Tracked files such as `dist/aur/` and `godot/.gutconfig.json` are left alone.


### MCP

Generate the current tools manifest: `cargo run --bin gpty -- schema --format mcp`

### Run

```bash
# Open in Godot editor
cd godot && godot -e

# Launch the GUI (backgrounded; add --headless for headless)
godot --path godot &
```

The GUI starts an IPC server on `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/gpty.sock` (or `GPTY_SOCKET` env var if set).
Once running, control it with the CLI:

```bash
cargo run --bin gpty -- version
cargo run --bin gpty -- new-pane -t terminal
cargo run --bin gpty -- list-panes
cargo run --bin gpty -- inject T1 -t "echo hello"
cargo run --bin gpty -- daemon stop
```

`cargo run` always builds the CLI from this checkout, and a `gpty` earlier on
`PATH` (a `cargo install`ed copy, the AUR package, or an old release bundle)
shadows it. The stale binary fails opaquely - a subcommand it lacks dies in clap
before any IPC, which is why the CLI warns once when it reads a running GUI
whose version or IPC protocol differs. Reinstall a `cargo install`ed copy after a
version bump (`cargo install --path crates/gpty-cli --force`), or install a
release bundle as below and drop the cargo copy.

To run a release CLI instead, install it once into a stable layout and rotate
behind it:

```bash
scripts/install-cli ~/Downloads/gpty-v0.8.3-linux-x86_64.tar.gz   # or an extracted bundle dir
scripts/install-cli --check                                       # diagnose install + PATH
```

It copies the bundle to `~/.local/opt/gpty/<version>`, points `current` at it,
and links `~/.local/bin/gpty` and `gpty-gui` through that link - so an upgrade
is the same command with the newer bundle, `--keep N` bounds how many old
versions stay (default 2), and `--force` replaces a regular file or a
same-version bundle from somewhere else. Nothing links a download directory, so
cleaning `Downloads` cannot leave a dangling `gpty` behind. `--check` names every
`gpty` on `PATH` in order - dangling, shadowing, or behind - and answers an MCP
`initialize` through the CLI an MCP client would launch, exiting 1 when the
lookup does not reach this install. `GPTY_INSTALL_ROOT` and `GPTY_BIN_DIR`
override the two directories.

Standalone commands (no GUI needed):

```bash
cargo run --bin gpty -- schema                    # JSON Schema
cargo run --bin gpty -- schema --format mcp       # MCP tools manifest
echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize"}' | cargo run --bin gpty -- mcp
```

### Test

- **Automated**: `./scripts/ci-check` runs the full suite (Rust + GUT + audit). CI runs on pushes to `main` and `0.*` and on pull requests targeting either; a release PR to `main` also runs CodeQL and Secret scan. The `docs` and `commit-lint` jobs are required checks on `main`.
- **Manual pre-release**: [docs/content/docs/overview/testing.md](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/overview/testing.md) - smoke tests for CLI bridge, daemon lifecycle, UI shortcuts, and error paths that require a running GUI.
- Test format: `Given / When / Then` with expected output. See the manual checklist for examples.

```bash
# Rust tests only
cargo test --workspace    # Tests across core, gdext, cli
cargo test -p gpty-core   # Core library only

# Rust type-check (fast, no codegen)
cargo check

# Godot (GUT) tests only
godot --headless --path godot --import # Required before first run
./scripts/gut-check                       # runs full GUT suite under sandbox
./scripts/gut-check test_test_paths.gd    # runs matching test script under sandbox
./scripts/gut-check -s <script> -t <test> # runs specific test method

# OMP extension unit tests (no omp install required)
(cd extensions/gpty-omp-events && node --test)

# Explicitly link the OMP observability plugin (user action; gpty never auto-installs)
omp plugin link "$(pwd)/extensions/gpty-omp-events"

# Workflow lint (YAML, permissions, SHA-pinned actions, checkout credentials,
# dangerous triggers, job timeouts and concurrency groups)
./scripts/lint-workflows

# Run all CI checks locally (fmt, workflow lint, clippy, tests, GUT, audit)
./scripts/ci-check

# Fast checks only (fmt, workflow lint, clippy)
./scripts/ci-check --fast

# Terminal renderer cost (needs a display; see the script header)
godot --path godot --disable-vsync -s res://tests/bench/draw_bench.gd

# UI captures (need a display): list the committed states, save one, or prove
# two runs are pixel-identical and a perturbation is local
./scripts/ui-capture --list
./scripts/ui-capture palette /tmp/ui-captures
./scripts/ui-capture-check

# Markdown preview cost: Rust render + parse + the label's shape pass
godot --headless --path godot -s res://tests/bench/markdown_bench.gd
```

The render benchmark fills a pane with a deterministic ANSI-rich screen, prints
the cost of a forced full repaint against an idle frame, and saves the rendered
frame to `/tmp/gpty_draw_<BENCH_TAG>.png`. Two revisions must render
byte-identical pixels, so diff the two PNGs before trusting a timing delta.

The Markdown benchmark prints `render_ms` / `parse_ms` / `shape_ms` /
`total_ms` per size for a repeated block; `shape_ms` is the frame after the
text lands, which is the pass a document's markup can make superlinear (see
`GptyMarkdown`'s docs) and the number a change to the renderer's output has to
be argued against. Run it against a release GDExtension
(`cargo build --release -p gpty-gdext`, then point the platform's
`godot/bin/libgpty_gdext.*` symlink at `target/release/`) for the numbers a
user would see, and restore the debug symlink afterwards.

## Dependencies

- Rust crates come from crates.io only. `deny.toml` denies unknown registries and git sources.
- The licence allow-list lives in `deny.toml`: MIT, Apache-2.0 (and its LLVM exception), BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC, MPL-2.0, Unicode-3.0, Unlicense, Zlib and GPL-3.0-or-later, with named WTFPL exceptions for the two FFmpeg binding crates. A dependency outside the policy fails `cargo deny check` with the crate named; the fix is a decision - allow the licence, add a named exception with its reason, or drop the dependency - not a config edit.
- Dependabot opens one grouped pull request per ecosystem per week: Cargo, the fuzz workspace's own lockfile, and GitHub Actions. Every third-party action is pinned to a full commit SHA.
- `./scripts/ci-check` runs `cargo audit --deny warnings` for advisories over both committed lockfiles, the workspace's `Cargo.lock` and the fuzz workspace's `fuzz/Cargo.lock`, each behind a `cargo metadata --locked` drift check because GitHub's dependency graph reads both - and `cargo deny check` for licences, sources, yanked crates and duplicate versions; CI runs the same gates.
- A release publishes the three archives, `SHA256SUMS` and build-provenance attestations. The tag must be a signed annotated tag reachable from `main`; the read-only gate verifies the tag, version, defect-class and docs checks before building, and the write/OIDC `publish` job waits on the `release` environment's required reviewer. The release process is [RELEASING.md](gpty-doc:RELEASING.md); the agent execution checklist is `.omp/skills/release/SKILL.md`; the tag path is `.github/workflows/release.yml` (gate, shared build, publish) and the platform builds and export live in `.github/workflows/release-build.yml`, which a `workflow_dispatch` on `main` also runs to fill the caches a tag restores. The read-only `scripts/check-github-settings` reads the rulesets, `release` environment and Actions flags back from the API.

## Branches

`main` is the release branch. Every commit on it arrives through a release pull request from the active integration branch: `0.8.x` for the 0.8 line, `0.9.x` for 0.9. The maintainer approves the release PR and tags the release from `main`.

Day-to-day changes land on the integration branch. Branch from it, open pull requests against it, and do not open feature pull requests against `main`. The `gpty-bot` GitHub App pushes the integration branch and opens the release PR; the bot never approves or merges. Dependency updates target the active integration branch; bump `.github/dependabot.yml`'s three `target-branch` entries when the line rolls (`0.8.x` → `0.9.x`). A push does not change commit authorship: the application token is only the push credential, so the branch history remains the maintainer's signed commits while the pull request is authored by `app/gpty-bot`.

## Pull Request Process

1. Fork the repository.
2. Create your feature branch.
3. Make your changes.
4. Test your changes (functionally).
5. Run `./scripts/ci-check` - ensure all checks pass
6. Add or update test cases as applicable.
7. Sign off every commit with `git commit -s` (DCO); the `commit-msg` hook refuses a commit without the trailer, and the `commit-lint` CI job runs the same check over human commits on a pull request (it exempts `[bot]`-authored commits).
8. See [AGENTS.md](gpty-doc:AGENTS.md) for commit information.
9. Submit a pull request against the active integration branch (`0.8.x` for the 0.8 line), not `main`.

[gPTY](https://gpty.dev/) - a desktop workspace built on Rust and Godot. It provides a tiling grid for panes (terminals, code viewers, file trees, wikis, media, and more), a concept capture engine, and a JSON-RPC/MCP control surface so AI agents and automation tools can spawn panes, inject text, and observe output on terminals without scraping a TUI. Every pane can be driven from a shell, a script, or an agent over one public API.

It is a side project in active development and a vast majority of this codebase, including most of the Godot UI layout and the Rust (`gpty-core`) GDExtension bridge, was generated using various LLMs under human review; and as such, the underlying code may contain unidiomatic patterns and/or bugs. It *does not* follow the core UNIX philosophy very well, as in, it does aim to do several things; though it does also intend to do them all well.

The chosen stack also brings with it more costs, much more than terminal emulators. A TUI can just draw into cells the terminal already owns, while gPTY runs a Godot renderer - an idle window can hold around 669 MB of resident memory, all of it owned by the renderer (multiple panes/terminals themselves are cheap in the GUI's own memory ([RSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resident_set_size)), under 1 MB each, but each one runs a shell in its own process at about 6 MB, up to the 96-pane ceiling). A first Forward+ launch (the implicit default, since `project.godot` names no renderer) holds about 1 GB because the graphics driver compiles its pipelines into that process; about 440 MB of it stays resident for the run, and later launches drop the number back to ~669 MB. Another drawback of a game engine is that it draws a frame every frame whether or not anything changed, whereas a terminal emulator composites only when its cells change (output, a blinking cursor, a resize). A GPU window that repaints even while idle draws power that a standard PTY simply would not. Memory usage and power draw remain areas that the project aims to continually refine and reduce, rather than have them be fixed prices to pay. Refer to the [Trade-offs](gpty-doc:README.md#Trade-offs) section for up-to-date statistics.

### Features

**Panes**

- **Tiling grid** - split, resize, and rearrange independent shell sessions; save and reload workspaces (tab sets) and named profiles.
- **Emulation** - `alacritty_terminal` grid with `16`/`256`/`true color`, scrollback with regex search, and wrapped text selection.

| Component | Choice | Rationale |
|----------|--------|-----------|
| PTY library | `portable-pty` | Cross-platform (Linux `/dev/ptmx` + Windows ConPTY) with a single API |
| ANSI parsing | `vte` crate | Fast Rust ANSI state machine |
| Async runtime | `tokio` | Per-terminal tasks; channel-driven capture state machine |
| I/O threading | Dedicated `std::thread` per PTY | Predictable blocking reads; bridges to tokio via `mpsc` |
| Concept capture | Rust `regex` over parsed `LineParser` output | Linear-time matching (ReDoS-safe); captures buffer raw bytes for grid-faithful replay |
| Grid rendering | `alacritty_terminal` | Full DEC STD 070 grid state machine; pass arrays to Godot `_draw()` |
| Godot bridge | `gdext 0.5` | Native GDExtension for Godot 4.7+ |
| Rust edition | 2024 | Requires Rust >= 1.85 |

### Trade-offs

Hosting a terminal inside a game engine is expensive, in terms of RAM & power usage. The following are measured on the shipped v0.8.5 Linux build (captured on CachyOS with Godot 4.7.2, the NVIDIA 620.70.06 driver and Vulkan 1.4.363 loader, `VmRSS` from `/proc` in a private sandbox, five readings per row after the app answers on its control socket):

| Configuration | Resident Memory |
|---|---|
| One pane, idle (Forward+, the default) | 669 MB |
| Zero panes, renderer still up | 669 MB - the cost is the renderer, not the terminals |
| First launch, cold pipeline cache | 1108 MB, back to ~669 MB on every later run |
| Same build, `--rendering-driver opengl3`, warm | 366 MB |
| 30,000 lines through one pane, past the 10,000-row scrollback cap | +50 MB, then flat |

![Memory cost by release: an idle one-pane window on Forward+ and on OpenGL3, and the first launch of a release with a cold pipeline cache](docs/static/images/cost-history.svg)

The chart is that table's history: every release from v0.1.0 was measured from its own shipped Linux archive on one machine (`scripts/backfill-cost-history` for the ones that shipped before the harness existed, `scripts/measure-cost --record` from now on), `docs/data/cost-history.json` holds the ledger, and `scripts/render-cost-chart` draws it - so the line is the project's own record, not a hand-drawn impression. Each point is what that build cost as shipped, its Godot engine included; a run is one launch sampled five times, so neighbours within a percent of each other are run-to-run noise rather than a change. v0.1.0 and v0.2.0 predate the control socket, so they are measured as they open (one terminal) rather than driven to a known pane count.

The above is Electron-level memory for what a TUI does inside a terminal window, and power follows from it: the window is GPU-composited and repaints while idle, so an idle gPTY is not "free" the way an idle shell (basically) is. Both of these issues are acknowledged, and are treated as debts with a plan, rather than leaving them as a permanent tax.

- **The renderer is the lever.** Compatibility (OpenGL3) is 1.8x lighter than Forward+ on the same build - a renderer ratio, not a release cost: a v0.8.1 build measures the same 366 MB on this driver stack, and the 290 MB this table carried before 2026-11-13 reproduces with neither build on it; the per-platform choice is an open item in the [v0.8 roadmap](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/roadmap/v0.8.md), and will be decided by running both through `scripts/ui-capture` (both themes, the visual-effect shaders, an 8-pane layout) rather than by preference.
- **Repaint is already bounded.** The `max_fps` setting and the terminal flood back-off limit how often a pane redraws; what is missing is an idle-frame measurement to hold it to.
- **Cost becomes a number in v0.9.** The [v0.9.0 instrumentation release](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/roadmap/v0.9.md) adds an in-app frame-time, CPU, memory and power readout (read from the OS, "unavailable" where the OS exposes nothing) and a gated performance budget, so later reductions are measured instead of claimed.

## Installation & Usage

Standalone binaries (no Godot install required) are published on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty/releases) for Linux, macOS, and Windows.

| Platform | Package |
|---|---|
| Linux | `gpty-v<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz` - extract; `./gpty-gui.sh` starts the GUI, `./gpty` is the CLI |
| macOS | `gpty-v<version>-macos.zip` - unzip, right-click the `.app` → Open; `gpty` beside it is the CLI |
| Windows | `gpty-v<version>-windows-x86_64.zip` - unzip; `gpty-gui.exe` starts the GUI, `gpty.exe` is the CLI |

Every release also bundles the gPTY knowledge base; the **Knowledge Base** profile in the sidebar opens the bundled wiki from your user data.

In the file names, `<version>` is the release tag you downloaded (for example `v0.7.0`).

### Verifying releases

Each release publishes a `SHA256SUMS` listing every asset. Check the file you downloaded before running it:

```bash
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS            # Linux
shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS        # macOS
certutil -hashfile <asset> SHA256  # Windows
```

Checksums catch a corrupted or tampered download in transit. Each asset also carries a build-provenance attestation binding it to the workflow run that built it:

```bash
gh attestation verify <asset> --repo godot-pty/gpty
```

The binaries are not code-signed (see [SECURITY.md](gpty-doc:SECURITY.md)).

### CLI

The `gpty` binary controls a running GUI over JSON-RPC IPC, and every release bundle ships it next to the GUI. It is also on crates.io - `cargo install gpty` puts the same binary on `PATH` (a Rust toolchain and a C compiler are required, for its bundled SQLite), and that copy is what an MCP client launches for `gpty mcp`. A downloaded bundle installs the same way from a checkout: `scripts/install-cli <bundle-or-tarball>` links it at `~/.local/bin/gpty` through a versioned directory, so upgrading is one command (see `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s CLI section). The CLI starts one on demand only for commands a fresh workspace can satisfy - `new-pane` and `profile load` - while `gpty daemon start` starts one explicitly and `--no-daemon` never starts one. Every other command needs a workspace that already exists, so it fails with `no gpty GUI is running (start one with \`gpty daemon start\`)` instead of opening a window it cannot use. Building from source (`cargo build -p gpty`, or `cargo build --workspace`) is only needed when working on the CLI itself; if you install it that way, **reinstall it after a version bump** (`cargo install --path crates/gpty-cli --force`). A stale `gpty` earlier on `PATH` shadows the release's CLI and fails opaquely (a subcommand it lacks dies in clap before any IPC), which is why the CLI warns once, on stderr, when it sees that the running GUI's version or IPC protocol differs from its own - the warning names both sides, but the reinstall is the fix.

Once the GUI is running (launched from Godot or a release binary), the CLI connects over a Unix socket (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/gpty.sock` on Linux, or `GPTY_SOCKET` env var):

```bash
# Check if the GUI is running (exit 1 when it is not)
gpty daemon status

# Print the bundled agent skill (for coding agents running inside a pane)
gpty --skill

# Declare this pane's agent state, from inside the pane (display only)
gpty state working

# Spawn a new terminal pane
gpty new-pane --pane-type terminal

# List all active panes
gpty list-panes

# Target a pane by id (what list-panes reports) or by a label that is unique
# across workspaces; a label two workspaces share is refused, not guessed
gpty inject T1 --text "echo hello"

# Read a pane's screen and scrollback; run a command in a new pane and wait for its output
gpty pane-read T1 --lines 200
gpty pane-run --command "cargo test"
gpty pane-wait T1 --pattern "tests passed" --timeout-ms 30000

# Change what a pane shows without taking the keyboard: a wiki pane's link
# graph, a note by vault-relative path, or the note view mode
gpty pane-view W1 --graph
gpty pane-view W1 --note index.md --mode split

# Configure a pane's own settings - the same closed per-type table the pane
# settings panel writes (gpty pane-settings lists every key)
gpty new-pane --pane-type media --setting file_path=/clip.mp4
gpty pane-set W1 --setting vault_path=/notes --setting font_size=16

# Search and read a wiki vault
gpty vault search <vault> <pattern>
gpty vault read <vault> <path>

# Close a pane
gpty kill-pane T1

# Save, load, and activate profiles
gpty profile save my-setup
gpty profile load my-setup
gpty profile list

# Install a plugin (reviewed in the GUI - its actions run as you)
gpty plugin install godot-pty/gpty-omp
gpty plugin list

# Manage the GUI daemon
gpty daemon start
gpty daemon status
gpty daemon stop

# Generate AI tool manifests (no GUI needed)
gpty schema
gpty schema --format mcp

# Run as MCP server over stdio (no GUI needed)
echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize"}' | gpty mcp
```

See `gpty --help` for all subcommands and flags.

### MCP integration

gpty ships an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server so AI agents and coding harnesses can control the workspace. The repo-root [`mcp.json`](mcp.json) declares it for auto-discovery:

```json
{"mcpServers": {"gpty": {"command": "gpty", "args": ["mcp"]}}}
```

- **Direct**: run `gpty mcp` over stdio - exposes a tool per CLI subcommand (`new-pane`, `list-panes`, `workspace-list`, `kill-pane`, `focus-pane`, `move-pane`, `inject`, `pane-read`, `pane-status`, `pane-view`, `pane-set`, `pane-settings`, `pane-run`, `pane-wait`, `broadcast`, `vault-search`, `vault-read`, `vault-weight`, `profile-*`, `daemon-*`, `concept-*`, `version`).
- **Manifest**: `gpty schema --format mcp` prints the MCP tool manifest (JSON Schema, works without a running GUI) for hand-off to agent configurations.

Tool schemas are generated from the same clap definitions as the CLI (`crates/gpty-cli/src/commands/schema.rs`), so they cannot drift from `gpty --help`.

# Releasing gPTY

This is the canonical release process. It is written for the maintainer and for
anyone preparing a release under their direction. The agent execution checklist
is `.omp/skills/release/SKILL.md`; it follows this page and records only the
agent-specific checkpoints, not a second runbook. Release authority is in
[MAINTAINERS.md](gpty-doc:MAINTAINERS.md).

A release is a pull request from the active integration branch (`X.Y.x` for the
line under development) to `main`, the maintainer's approval, a merge commit,
and a signed annotated `vX.Y.Z` tag on `main`. `main` is release-only: feature
pull requests land on the integration branch.

## Branches

Every release line `X.Y` has a long-lived integration branch named `X.Y.x`.
Exactly one is active - the line under development receives the feature pull
requests - and the others stay on `origin` at the last release their line
shipped. A closed line's branch is the tree that shipped: it is kept, the
`integration protection` ruleset covers every `0.*` branch, and it is where a
defect is reproduced against the release the user reported it on before the fix
is prepared as a pull request against the active line. Releases are cut from
`main`, never from an archive branch.

The remote is the inventory; nothing needs to list the branches by hand:

```bash
git branch -r --list 'origin/*.x'
git describe --tags --abbrev=0 origin/0.7.x   # the line's last release
```

A branch for a line that closed before the branch existed is created at that
line's last release tag, so it contains the release's changelog page, version
bump and blog entry - not the commit before them:

```bash
git branch 0.7.x v0.7.2
git push origin 0.7.x
```

Do not type the branch into a command; derive it from the tag being cut. The
rest of this page uses `$BRANCH`:

```bash
RELEASE=vX.Y.Z
BRANCH="${RELEASE#v}"; BRANCH="${BRANCH%.*}.x"   # vX.Y.Z -> X.Y.x
```

The first release of a new line creates its branch before step 1 - from the
previous line's last release commit - and pushes it.

## Preconditions

- A configured signing key (`git tag -v` must work) and the public key on
  GitHub. The tag ruleset has no bypass: every tag must be a signed annotated
  tag, and a bad tag cannot be moved or deleted. Cut the next patch instead.
- The `gpty-bot` app installed on `godot-pty/gpty` and
  `GPTY_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY` set; `./scripts/bot-token --check` passes. The bot
  pushes the integration branch and opens the release PR; it never approves or
  merges.
- A clean tree, the current integration branch, and the release's roadmap rows
  closed. Anything unshipped moves to the next chain in priority position with
  `(Deferred from vX.Y.Z.)`.
- `./scripts/check-github-settings` passes. It is read-only and needs a
  maintainer-authenticated `gh`: it reads back the rulesets, classic protection,
  `release` environment, SHA-pinning and sign-off flags instead of trusting the
  settings to stay put.
- `./scripts/ci-check` passes. Its Windows step cross-compiles only; the
  runtime legs (`windows-smoke`, GUT on Windows) exist only in CI and must be
  green on the release PR's head. Also run the
  [manual pre-release checklist](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/overview/testing.md#Manual pre-release checklist)
  against a real GUI; it covers the renderer, input and live-session paths that
  headless tests cannot.
- A graphical session for the home screenshot and, on Linux with a GPU, the
  cost-table measurement. Both have documented fallbacks.

## 1. Analyze the commit range

Release notes come from the commit history, never from memory. Set the tag
being cut, derive its branch, and inspect the range:

```bash
RELEASE=vX.Y.Z
BRANCH="${RELEASE#v}"; BRANCH="${BRANCH%.*}.x"   # vX.Y.Z -> X.Y.x
PREV=$(git describe --tags --abbrev=0 --match 'v*' HEAD^)
git log "$PREV"..HEAD --oneline
./scripts/fix-forensics --check --since "$PREV"
```

Classify every commit once into a single table: changelog bucket (`Added`,
`Changed`, `Fixed`), roadmap feature bullet (blank for non-features), and skip
marks. That one pass feeds the changelog, the roadmap and the blog. Skip
debug-logging churn, revert commits, lockfile/gitignore chores, and
agent-facing `AGENTS.md` edits. A fix saga gets one bullet describing the net
user-visible result. Note which commits produced user-visible UI changes; that
list is the feature-screenshot queue.

`fix-forensics` must exit 0. It checks every `fix` commit carries exactly one
`Cause:` trailer naming a class from the defect-class guide. The release
workflow runs the same check, so a missed trailer also stops the tag.

For the very first release, use `./scripts/fix-forensics --check`; there is no
previous tag.

## 2. Write the changelog

The release notes live on one page, `docs/content/docs/changelog/vX.Y.Z.md`,
with front matter (`title: "vX.Y.Z - YYYY-MM-DD"`, `weight`) and the compare
link `[Release on GitHub](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty/compare/vPREV...vX.Y.Z)`.
`CHANGELOG.md` is an index only; prepend the link
`- [X.Y.Z - YYYY-MM-DD](docs/content/docs/changelog/vX.Y.Z.md)` in the same
commit.

Use the Keep a Changelog buckets and write from step 1's classification. If the
release's roadmap DOCS row names the user-facing summary, use it as a
checklist: every item it names must appear, and the commit range catches the
ones it forgot.

`weight` is a ladder with one slot per release, newest smallest, in steps of
10. The smallest slot is 10; `weight: 0` is unset to Hugo. If the next page
would land on 10, or the ladder already holds a duplicate, shift every existing
page up one step (`10` → `20`, …) in one descending `sed -si` pass. Check:

```bash
grep -H '^weight' docs/content/docs/changelog/v0.*.md \
  | sed 's/.*weight: //' | sort -n | uniq -d
```

It must print nothing. `scripts/docs-check` holds the index and the page
directory in bijection: an unlinked page and a link with no page both fail.

## 3. Update the README and docs

The install table uses a `<version>` placeholder, so it needs no version edit.
Update any count, name or implementation-phase checklist item the release
changed; grep rather than assuming.

The cost paragraph, the Trade-offs table and the chart are a published claim
stamped with a build:

```bash
./scripts/build
./scripts/measure-cost --check
./scripts/measure-cost --record
```

`--check` re-measures the five published rows from a release build and fails
past 10% on a row, past the run-to-run noise on the scrollback delta, or when
the Forward+/OpenGL3 ratio falls below the prose's claim. Update the table, every
figure the paragraph repeats, the "Nx lighter" ratio, and the stamp line's
version. `--record` appends or replaces the release in
`docs/data/cost-history.json` and redraws `docs/static/images/cost-history.svg`.
`--check` needs Linux with a GPU; `scripts/ci-check` runs `--stamp` (no GPU) and
fails when the crate version moves and the table still names the old build.

The site's home page carries exactly one image: the current release's
`vX.Y.Z_1.png`. Feature screenshots belong only in the blog entry.

Check the docs mirrors and links before committing:

```bash
python3 scripts/docs-check
./scripts/check-capabilities
python3 scripts/build-wiki --check
```

## 4. Close the roadmap

`ROADMAP.md` is the index; `docs/content/docs/roadmap/vX.Y.md` holds the chain.
A shipped row is closed when the work lands, with its evidence, tests and
measured numbers. Verify no `⬜` remains in the release's section. Anything
unshipped moves to the next chain's page in priority position, keeps its
wording, and is tagged `(Deferred from vX.Y.Z.)`. A chain stays `in progress`
until its last planned release ships.

The release's DOCS row (the changelog page) is release-time work and is checked
off after the page exists. A row whose work closes on its own tag (the asset-set
row) is closed in a post-release commit with the published list measured.

## 5. Bump the versions

`gpty version` reports `env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")`, so every workspace crate and
the GUI's project version must match the tag:

- Every crate under `crates/*` (`gpty-ai`, `gpty-cli`, `gpty-core`,
  `gpty-gdext`, `gpty-ipc`, `gpty-media`, `gpty-plugin`).
- `server.json`: both `version` and `packages[0].version` are the published
  crate version, not the tag. `scripts/mcp-registry check` fails on drift with
  `crates/gpty-cli`.
- `godot/project.godot`'s `config/version`. `ci-check`'s crate-versions step
  fails when it is stale.
- Both lockfiles: `Cargo.lock` and `fuzz/Cargo.lock`. The fuzz workspace is not
  a repository member, so `cargo check --workspace` does not touch it;
  `cargo metadata --format-version 1 --manifest-path fuzz/Cargo.toml` rewrites
  its version lines.

The bump is a per-file edit. `sed -i` with multiple files treats them as one
stream without GNU sed's `-s`; use `sed -si` or loop per file. Then:

```bash
cargo check --workspace
cargo build -p gpty-gdext
cargo package -p gpty-core
```

`cargo package` runs the packaged tarball's verify build, which is the only
local check that catches a crate embedding a file from outside its own
directory. The other crates cannot verify locally before their path dependency
is on the index; check their tarball file lists with
`cargo package -p <crate> --no-verify --list`.

## 6. Screenshots and blog entry

Capture the home screen:

```bash
scripts/screenshot-gpty docs/static/images/vX.Y.Z_1.png godot --path godot
```

The script creates a private user-data/runtime sandbox, waits for first frames,
captures and tears down. It needs XWayland for Godot's window; on a pure-Wayland
session it cannot find the window. Report that and ask the user for the image;
that is the fallback, not a routine gate.

Run a vision sanity pass on the capture: giant overlays, clipped controls,
overlapping sections. Fix anything real; note cosmetic issues for the user.

For feature screenshots, ask the user which features deserve one. Stage each
with `--state <name>` and re-capture with the same script, naming the file
`vX.Y.Z_<n>.png`. `scripts/ui-capture --list` prints the available states. Do
not stage through GUT: a non-headless GUT run captures the runner panel rather
than the app. Size the window to a physical screen; a multi-monitor desktop
size can produce a clipped off-screen window. Check every referenced image
exists under `docs/static/images/` before committing.

Create `docs/content/blog/vX.Y.Z/index.md` using the established front matter
and body shape (see an earlier `vX.Y.Z/index.md`), with the home screenshot
first and feature screenshots next to the features they show. A patch release
with no visual changes may reuse the previous home screenshot, but a fresh
capture is preferred.

## 7. Final review pause

All preparation ends here. Do **not** commit or tag yet. Present to the user:

- the changelog summary;
- the blog draft path and text;
- the captured screenshots;
- `/tmp/gpty-release-body.md`, the release PR body (one paragraph on the
  release's user-facing story plus the changelog link).

Wait for an explicit OK. The user may rewrite the blog, replace images, or ask
for more screenshots. Iterate, then proceed only on their go-ahead.

## 8. Commit, open the release PR, and tag

Run the full local gate once more:

```bash
./scripts/ci-check
git switch "$BRANCH"
git pull --ff-only
```

Stage the release commit and sign it:

```bash
git add CHANGELOG.md README.md ROADMAP.md server.json godot/project.godot \
  crates/*/Cargo.toml Cargo.lock fuzz/Cargo.lock \
  docs/content/docs/changelog/vX.Y.Z.md \
  docs/content/blog/vX.Y.Z \
  docs/static/images/vX.Y.Z_*.png
git commit -s -m "docs: finalize vX.Y.Z release"
```

Push the integration branch and open the release PR as `gpty-bot`:

```bash
./scripts/bot-push "$BRANCH"
./scripts/bot-pr --base main --title "vX.Y.Z" --body-file /tmp/gpty-release-body.md
```

Wait until all required checks on the release PR are green: the CI jobs
(including both Windows legs), `docs`, `commit-lint`, CodeQL and secret-scan.
Do not merge a partially green PR. Approve it as the maintainer, then merge with
a merge commit so the integration branch remains ancestral to `main`:

```bash
gh pr review --approve <number>
gh pr merge --merge <number>
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
```

Tag from `main` and verify the signature before pushing:

```bash
git tag -s vX.Y.Z -m "vX.Y.Z"
git tag -v vX.Y.Z
git push origin vX.Y.Z
```

The tag push runs the `pre-push` hook's full `ci-check`, so it can take a couple
of minutes. Confirm the tag reached the remote with
`git ls-remote --tags origin vX.Y.Z` rather than assuming. Tags are immutable:
do not force-move one to include a late fix.

After the merge, bring the integration branch to the release commit:

```bash
git switch "$BRANCH"
git merge --ff-only main
git push origin "$BRANCH"
```

## 9. Understand the release workflow

The tag starts `.github/workflows/release.yml`, split so no write or OIDC
privilege is present while project code runs:

- **`release-gate`** is read-only. It validates the tag format (`vX.Y.Z`, no
  pre-release suffix), verifies the tag is a signed annotated tag through the
  GitHub API, checks it is an ancestor of `main`, compares the crate and
  `server.json` versions with the tag, runs `mcp-registry check`, checks both
  lockfiles with `cargo metadata --locked`, checks the defect-class trailers,
  and runs the docs, capability and knowledge-bundle gates.
- **`build`** calls `.github/workflows/release-build.yml`, the same definition a
  `workflow_dispatch` on `main` runs. It carries the platform jobs
  (`build-linux`, both `build-macos` arches, `build-windows`, `bundle-macos`,
  `export`) and restores the caches a run on `main` wrote: the FFmpeg prefix
  (Windows under `ci.yml`'s key; Linux under an image-scoped
  `Linux-ubuntu22-ffmpeg-*` key, because the release builds on 22.04 for the
  bundle's glibc floor while `ci.yml` builds on 24.04 and a 24.04-built
  `libav*.so` needs GLIBC_2.38), the Windows vcpkg tree only when that prefix
  missed, and the release-profile `target` under a
  `cargo-release-<os>-<arch>-<lock>` key kept apart from the debug caches. A
  tag run only restores: an entry it saves is tag-scoped, unreadable by the
  next tag, and would evict CI's caches from the 10 GB budget. `export` stamps
  `godot/project.godot` with the version input, installs Godot and the export
  templates, asserts the four GDExtension files exist, exports Linux, Windows
  and macOS, writes `SHA256SUMS`, and uploads the three archives plus the sums
  as `gpty-release-dist`.

  `workflow_dispatch` on that file is how the caches are filled and how the
  build definition is proved before it is used by a tag:

  ```bash
  gh workflow run release-build.yml --ref main -f version=vX.Y.Z
  ```

  Run it once on the release commit; it publishes nothing and writes
  `gpty-release-dist` as a run artifact. A dispatch on a cold key is the cold
  measurement; the next one (or the tag run after it) is the warm one. Read the
  step timings with `gh run view <id> --json jobs`.
- **`publish`** is the only write/OIDC job. It downloads the staged artifact,
  attests the four assets, and creates the GitHub release. It does not check
  out the repository and runs no project code. It waits on the `release`
  environment's required reviewer.

Review the `gpty-release-dist` artifact (three archives plus `SHA256SUMS`)
before approving the environment. The same environment protects the
`mcp-registry` publish job.

## 10. Verify the published release

A tag is not a finished release. Download and verify the assets:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/gpty-release
gh release download vX.Y.Z --pattern 'SHA256SUMS' --dir /tmp/gpty-release
gh release download vX.Y.Z --pattern 'gpty-vX.Y.Z-*' --dir /tmp/gpty-release
cd /tmp/gpty-release
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
```

Each archive must carry `LICENSE` and `LICENSE-EXCEPTIONS.md` next to the
binaries (GPLv3 §4/§6). Check with `tar -tzf` for the tarball and `unzip -l`
for the zips. Verify the build-provenance attestation by its **subject digest**,
not by the exit code: `gh attestation verify <asset> --repo godot-pty/gpty
--format json` can print nothing and exit 0 for a file with no matching
attestation; confirm the statement's subject digest equals the downloaded
file's SHA-256.

For the macOS archive, verify the new deployment floor and the dylib layout:

```bash
scripts/check-macos-minos --x86_64 10.13 --arm64 11.0 \
  <unpacked>/gPTY.app/Contents/Frameworks/*.dylib
```

Every FFmpeg dylib and GDExtension slice must report at most macOS 10.13 on
x86_64 and 11.0 on arm64. `zipinfo -l` must show one real
`libavcodec.63.1.102.dylib` (and its siblings) with the `.63` and unversioned
aliases as symlinks, not three real copies per library. The v0.8.3 asset did
not meet this floor; the first release after the fix is the proof.

## 11. Release tail

- **AUR.** Update `dist/aur/PKGBUILD` (`pkgver`/`pkgrel`, the tarball's
  `sha256sums`, and the bundle layout: the CLI as `gpty`, the GUI as `gpty-gui`
  with `gpty-gui.pck` and `libgpty_gdext.linux.x86_64.so`, both on `PATH`).
  Validate in a temp directory with `makepkg --noconfirm` (building in the tree
  leaves untracked `src/`, `pkg/` and package files), then publish to the AUR
  when the account can.
- **crates.io.** From the release commit with a clean tree, publish in
  dependency order: `gpty-core`, wait for the index, then `gpty-ipc`,
  `gpty-plugin`, `gpty`. `cargo publish` runs the packaged verify build; the
  later crates cannot verify locally because their path dependency is not on
  the index until the earlier one publishes.
- **MCP registry.** After the four crates are live, dispatch
  `gh workflow run mcp-registry.yml` on `main`. It validates `server.json`
  against the CLI crate, refuses a version crates.io does not have, verifies
  the publisher tarball, and publishes over OIDC. It uses the same `release`
  environment.
- **Record.** Close the release's asset-set roadmap row in a post-release
  commit with the published list measured. The changelog page and the release
  assets are the release record; do not rewrite a released page.

## Failure handling

- A red required check blocks the release. Fix the source or the release prep
  and push again; do not merge around it.
- A transient failure in the release workflow may be re-run. A workflow bug in
  the tagged tree cannot be fixed by changing `main`; cut the next patch so the
  fixed workflow is in the tagged tree.
- A bad tag is permanent. The tag ruleset blocks moving and deleting tags, and
  there is no bypass. Do not disable the ruleset to rescue a release; cut the
  next patch version and say what happened in its notes.
- If `publish` creates a partial or incorrect release, correct the assets or
  notes if GitHub allows it, but do not move the tag. Fix forward with a patch.

## Gotchas

- **`cargo package --no-verify` hides the packaging bug that matters.** The
  verify step compiles the tarball cargo would upload. Anything `include_str!`d
  into a published crate must live inside that crate's directory; a path
  reaching above it compiles in the workspace and fails at publish. This is why
  the agent skill lives at `crates/gpty-cli/skills/gpty/SKILL.md`.
- **Windows behavior is only proven in CI.** `ci-check`'s Windows step is a
  cross-compile; `windows-smoke` and the Windows GUT run are the runtime proof.
- **Screenshots need XWayland.** `scripts/screenshot-gpty` finds Godot's window
  through the X tree; on pure Wayland, report the failure and ask for the
  image. Its capture backend falls back from ffmpeg to ImageMagick;
  `SCREENSHOT_CAPTURE=import` skips a known-bad ffmpeg stall.
- **Docs mirrors are generated.** `docs/assets/repo/`, `docs/data/` and
  `docs/.cache/` are gitignored. `docs/setup.sh` copies the root docs into the
  site; a new root document needs its copy line and a `RELEASING.md`-style
  `readfile` page. Never commit the generated copies.
- **Hugo tarballs clobber the repo.** The Hugo release tarball contains
  `README.md` and `LICENSE`; extract only the `hugo` member or into a temp
  directory.
- **The docs versions dropdown is cached.** `docs/setup.sh` fetches release
  tags from the GitHub API with a one-hour cache; new releases appear after it
  expires, with no manual edit.
- **`gh run watch` can fail on a transient API error** while the run is still
  going. Confirm with `gh run view <id> --json status,conclusion` before
  calling a run failed.
- **No `dev/v*` branches.** The integration branch is long-lived; feature
  branches are short-lived and PR back to it, not to `main`. A line's branch
  outlives the line: the archive branch is not deleted, and it is not a second
  place to release from.

# Roadmap

The source of truth for all `gPTY` features; past, present, and planned.

- GitHub Issues will be used for user-reported bugs and discussions, not roadmap tracking.
- Boundary rules and non-goals live in AGENTS.md under "ADE Architecture Boundary".
- **The roadmap is a queue, not a diary.** It is split into one page per release chain, and within a release rows are ordered by priority - the first unchecked row (⬜) of the earliest unfinished release is the immediate next implementation. Ordering is: data-loss and correctness first, then security with a reachable path, then the release's own features, then robustness and tests, then low-reachability hardening, then polish, then work that can only happen at release time. Rows are never grouped by origin or by which release deferred them (the row text says that where it matters); completed rows stay under their release as the record, and the CHANGELOG carries the user-facing summary. A defect or follow-up found while working a row is added as its own row, in priority position, with enough detail to act on later. The Area column names the part of the project a row targets (TERM, GUI, IPC, CLI, SEC, PLUGIN, WIKI, CONCEPT, MEDIA, AGENT, CORE, BUILD, DOCS, PROJECT). Future holds ideas and evidence-gated work that is not scheduled.
