# Security Policy

This document states what the project defends against, what it deliberately does not, 
and how to report a problem.

Implementation rules for contributors live in [the security rules](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/security.md). This file is the
policy: the (currently limited) threat model, the limits, and the reporting process.

## Supported versions

| Version | Support |
| ------- | --------- |
| > 0.5   | :white_check_mark: Security and correctness fixes |
| < 0.5   | :x: |

Generally, fixes will land on `main` and ship in the immediate next release. There is no plan to 
have maintenance branches and/or backports to older minor versions - if a fix matters to you, 
please upgrade.

That said, if there is an issue with a significant severity and implications, the fix will be 
backported to prior releases as feasible.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting**: [open a private advisory](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty/security/advisories/new) (repository **Security** tab → **Report a
vulnerability**). It opens a private advisory thread visible only to the maintainers. Please do not
open a public issue, pull request, or discussion for a suspected vulnerability - that exposes every
user before a fix exists.

If private reporting is unavailable to you, open an issue titled `Security Request` with
**no technical details** and a maintainer will establish a private channel. In this channel,
be prepared to privately share:

- The affected version(s), commit(s), and platform(s);
- What an attacker could potentially control (a file the user opens, a program running inside a pane, 
 a remote response, another local user, etc.);
- A minimal set of reproduction steps, and the impact you believe it has.

### What to expect

This is a single-maintainer project, so these are best-effort targets, definitely not a contract or 
a guarantee:

| Stage | Target |
| ----- | ------ |
| Acknowledgement of the report | ~7 days |
| First assessment (in scope / not, severity, planned fix) | ~30 days |
| Fix for confirmed issues | On the immediate next release |
| Public disclosure | A GitHub security advisory published with the fix |

We credit reporters in the advisory unless you prefer otherwise. If a reported behaviour turns out
to be intentional and documented, we will explain the reasoning in the thread and record it here.

## Threat model

**Trusted: Your own user account.** `gPTY` trusts same-UID processes by design. A process running as
**you** can already read your files, attach to your terminals, and drive the control socket, so "another
program running as me can control the workspace" shouldn't be a vulnerability on its own (please open a 
discussion post if you think otherwise). Setting `GPTY_SECRET` raises the bar for *other users* of the
machine, and on Linux and Windows it also keeps the secret out of reach of code running in your
panes: the GUI and the CLI harden themselves at startup (a non-dumpable process on Linux, a process
DACL without memory access on Windows), so a pane program cannot read `GPTY_SECRET` from their
environment and therefore cannot authenticate to the control socket. That is a credential barrier, not
pane isolation, and it only exists when a secret is set (the default install sets none). The trust
above is for processes *outside* gPTY; code running *inside* a pane is not separated from the control
surface by a permission model yet, which is a known, tracked gap (see "A program in a pane can read and
drive every other pane" under Known limitations).

**Untrusted - must never gain authority:**

- **Terminal output.** Every byte a program prints, including escape sequences, is attacker-controlled
  if any program you run can be induced to print attacker-chosen text.
- **Files.** Saved layouts, profiles, workspaces, concept definitions, markdown, scrollback: files
  can arrive from a repository, a chat message, or a shared dotfiles setup. A file cannot turn that
  into code by naming a resource: pane settings go through a closed per-type allowlist
  (`PaneTypes.settings_schema`), and a data-supplied font path is read as bytes by `TerminalFonts`,
  never through `load()` - a `.tres` with an embedded script runs during `load()`, and Workspace
  Trust does not examine a font. A colour scheme is the same class of input: it is read as capped
  text, parsed by `gpty_core::scheme` under a closed native key set (or a narrow Alacritty, iTerm2,
  Base16 or CSV reader), copied to `user://schemes/` as data, and never loaded as a resource; a
  layout or profile cannot name one.
- **Remote responses.** Release metadata, documentation, anything fetched over the network.
- **Other users** on a shared machine, and any file or socket they could have written.

**In scope:**

- All untrusted data reaching a privileged action: Executing a process, writing a file outside the
  app's own `user://` store, gaining the control socket, or delivering input to a pane the user did
  not target;
- Cross-user attacks on shared hosts: socket squatting, world-writable paths, `PATH`/env manipulation;
- remote content driving a local action;
- A lower-trust pane influencing a higher-trust one (an ordinary shell pane feeding a root shell or
  an SSH session). This is in scope as a goal and has **no per-pane permission model yet**: with the
  default install (no `GPTY_SECRET`) a program in any pane can drive every other pane. Setting a
  secret closes the environment path that used to leak it on Linux and Windows (see Hardening in
  place), so the socket gate becomes real for pane programs - but that is a credential, not a
  boundary, and it is a documented known limitation rather than an unreported bug. Enforcement is on
  the roadmap (see Known limitations);
- Denial of service that locks the GUI thread or grows memory without a bound.

**Out of scope (by design, or accepted):**

- Processes *outside* gPTY that run as the same user controlling it (see above). A process *inside* a
  pane is the in-scope case listed earlier, not this one;
- Spoofable display state: the `gpty_state=<value>` OSC declaration and the heuristic agent-state
  tiers may be set by anything that can print; they are labelled display-only and are never an input
  to a decision. `gpty state` declares the same (display-only) state over the event socket, where the
  per-PTY event capability a pane injects into its children is the gate rather than the output
  stream; it is the declaration path on Windows, where ConPTY consumes the OSC before gpty sees it;
- What happens after a user approves a **Workspace Trust** prompt, activates a downloaded profile,
  or installs a third-party extension. Those prompts exist so the decision is explicit; after
  consent, gPTY runs what the file asks for;
- Unsigned release artifacts and the absence of code signing (see Known limitations);
- Third-party CLIs, editors, agents, and plugins the user runs inside a pane, and the files they
  write;
- A user pasting content into a shell, or running a command they typed.

## What gPTY deliberately does not do

- **No sandboxing.** A pane is a shell running as you, with your permissions. gPTY never claims
  otherwise.
- **No OSC 52 clipboard access.** Terminal escape sequences cannot read or write your clipboard;
  `parser.rs` interprets exactly one OSC sequence (`gpty_state=`) and it changes a badge.
- **No command execution from concept definitions.** A concept is data: a regex trigger, a stop
  condition, and a routing target. It can capture terminal output and hand it to a pane that
  displays it. It cannot write to a PTY. (This capability existed in earlier builds; see
  [CHANGELOG.md](gpty-doc:CHANGELOG.md).)
- **No scraping of agent TUIs.** Pane output is presentation, not a structured event source.
  Observability comes only from documented hooks (the OMP event extension) and the control API.
- **Configured "commands" are a program and an argv array, or one explicitly shell-evaluated launch
  line.** A saved tile or profile names a program and an argv array, which reaches the child without
  a shell; it may also name one `launch` line, which is the only shell string in the spawn path and
  is run verbatim through *your* configured shell (`-c`, or `/c` for `cmd.exe`). Nothing in it is
  expanded or templated, there is no profile-global command, and a launch tile always raises the
  Workspace Trust prompt. A saved file cannot supply environment at all: a tile's `shell_env` is
  dropped on restore with a notice, and the environment a pane gets - the inherited one plus your
  own global and per-pane settings - passes through one blocklist before it reaches a child.

## Hardening in place

These are load-bearing guards. Reports that require removing one of them should say so explicitly.

- **Control socket**: per-user path, `0600`, cross-UID peers rejected (fail-closed on Linux and
  macOS), 64 KiB request cap, 16 concurrent connections, optional shared secret compared in constant
  time, and `params` must be a JSON object (or absent): a positional/non-object value is answered
  with JSON-RPC `-32602` before it is dispatched or queued, because one reaching the GUI's drain
  raised a call error that aborted the rest of the batch; clients validate the socket path and the
  GUI binary before trusting either. The MCP server in front of it translates a tool call's
  arguments from the ids the tool advertises to the wire names the handler reads, and answers
  `-32602` for an unknown key (naming the nearest valid one) or a value of the wrong JSON type:
  forwarding the object verbatim dropped every name that differed, so a call silently performed a
  different action than the one requested.
- **Pane count**: a window holds at most 96 live panes, counted across every workspace because a
  hidden workspace's pane keeps its PTY, child process and grid. The one ceiling
  (`Workspace.MAX_LIVE_PANES`) is enforced where panes are created, so `new-pane`, `pane-run`, the
  palette, a profile activation and a layout or workspace file all stop at it and say so: a caller
  gets an error naming the limit, the user gets a toast, and a restore creates what fits and reports
  the rest. Measured at 96 panes: about 0.9 GB (GUI 295 MB plus shells 596 MB) and 3.9 s for a full
  restore, still inside a caller's 5 s timeout; before the ceiling a file with 300 tiles restored 300
  shells and left the GUI answering `list-panes` in seconds.
- **Event socket**: separate listener; *submitting* an event requires a per-PTY capability that is
  never reused and is compared in constant time. Reading the fan-out is open to same-UID processes -
  treat the event channel as non-confidential from your own user.
- **Child processes**: `LD_*`/`DYLD_*`, event-channel, pane-marker, and control-credential variables
  are stripped from every child, and startup-evaluation variables (`PROMPT_COMMAND`, `BASH_ENV`,
  `ENV`, `SHELLOPTS`, `PS4`, `ZDOTDIR`, `PERL5OPT`, `PYTHONSTARTUP`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `RUBYOPT`,
  `LESSOPEN`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF`, `GIT_PAGER`, `PAGER`) are refused from
  configuration. Absolute programs restored from files must be regular files that are not
  group/other-writable, with no group/other-writable directory above them (a sticky directory such
  as `/tmp` is allowed), and must be owned by you or by root - or, inside a user namespace that
  leaves host root unmapped (rootless containers, `--userns=keep-id`, Flatpak), by the kernel's
  overflow UID, which is accepted only while that UID is outside the process's own UID map. The same
  owner rule gates the `GPTY_GUI` and `GPTY_OMP` overrides, which name your own paths and so skip the
  parent-directory walk.
- **The GUI's and the CLI's own environment**: both harden themselves at startup
  (`gpty_core::hardening::harden_process`, called from the GDExtension's init and the CLI's `main`).
  A pane's shell is a child of the GUI and runs as you, so without this it can recover `GPTY_SECRET`
  from the parent's environment. On Linux the call clears the dumpable bit (`PR_SET_DUMPABLE 0`), so
  `/proc/<gui pid>/environ` and `/proc/<gui pid>/maps` are root-owned and a pane program gets
  `EACCES` (measured 2026-10-29), while the pane's own `exec`ed shell - and the programs it starts -
  returns to dumpable and stays debuggable. On Windows it installs a process DACL that withholds
  `PROCESS_VM_READ`, `PROCESS_VM_WRITE`, `PROCESS_VM_OPERATION` and `PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD` from the
  user (the rights a memory read or code injection needs) while keeping
  `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` (the socket's peer check opens a client with it),
  `PROCESS_TERMINATE` (a hung GUI stays endable), `SYNCHRONIZE` and `READ_CONTROL`, in one ACE for
  the process owner. There is no blanket `SYSTEM` ACE: `SYSTEM` holds `SeDebugPrivilege`, and a full
  grant would re-grant everything whenever gPTY itself runs as `SYSTEM` (the owner then matches it).
  A process that *enables* `SeDebugPrivilege` can open any process regardless of its DACL - that is
  an elevated debugger, not a normal pane, and the Windows test and smoke drop the privilege before
  probing. The cost is deliberate: a non-dumpable process on Linux produces no core dump and
  cannot be attached to by a same-user debugger or profiler, and a hardened Windows process cannot
  be opened for memory reads by the same user, so `GPTY_ALLOW_DEBUG=1` opts out for a developer who
  needs one. The Windows DACL is verified by the Windows CI jobs: a dedicated integration test (which
  also reads the installed DACL back and asserts one owner ACE without memory rights) and the
  smoke's `process hardening` step against the GUI and a client. macOS has no mechanism wired up;
  see Known
  limitations.
- **Restored layouts and profiles**: tile types, settings, and grid geometry are validated; a tile
  that starts a different program, passes extra arguments, or carries a `launch` line raises the
  Workspace Trust prompt before it runs, and `profileLoad` over the control socket refuses such a
  profile (a caller cannot answer a
  dialog, so naming the profile is not consent to what the file asks for) - unless the consent memory
  covers it: a pre-seed built-in's name and app version plus the spawn plans (program and argv, a
  launch line, and the workspace directory) recorded with it, a plugin's id and pinned revision plus
  the plans its install review listed, or a user profile whose every untrusted tile's exact
  program+argv at that directory was approved - because the record is proof the user approved that
  content in the GUI. A launch plan is the line itself and never names the shell runner, which is the
  user's own setting rather than the file's. A new
  app version, a new plugin revision, or different tiles under the same name or revision re-prompts.
  Provenance is gPTY's: fields inside a user profile file cannot make it a plugin profile, and the
  legacy built-in claim is stripped on load too. Environment is not a file
  decision: a tile's `shell_env` is dropped on restore with a notice naming what was dropped, and
  per-pane environment is the user's own - `user://pane_env.json`, written only by the pane settings
  UI and keyed by the pane's id, applied at spawn over the user's global environment. A pane's own
  working directory is the same class of state, in `user://pane_cwd.json`: keyed by the pane's id
  *and* a workspace id this build generates (`ws-` plus 12 hex, minted on the first load of a store
  that predates it), written only by the pane settings UI, and deliberately outside the trust plan
  key - like the pane's own environment - because no file can name an entry and a path that has gone
  missing falls back to the workspace's directory, then the user's home, at spawn with one
  warning. The Inspector's
  prompt and its two switches are the same kind of user-owned state, in `user://pane_inspector.json`:
  the settings table refuses them from files, the pane settings UI is the only writer, and the pane
  reads its own record at attach - so a profile cannot aim an Inspector, while a prompt and switches
  the user set survive a restart for the pane that carries that id. Saved commands
  (`user://commands.json`) are that class with no spawn reach at all: the Commands tab is their only
  writer, choosing one types its text into the *active* terminal pane (Enter only when the entry's
  `run` flag is set), no IPC method, CLI verb or plugin can add one, and nothing in a saved command
  is expanded - it is the user's own words for the shell they are looking at.
- **Workspace directories (v0.7.1)**: a workspace's working directory comes from
  `workspaces.json` and is handed to every terminal that workspace starts; an empty or unusable
  value resolves to the user's home (`PaneCwdStore.resolve`), the same directory a pane with no
  override gets. A directory is not
  executable on its own, so a plain shell in a file-supplied directory restores without a prompt
  (asking at every launch would train the user to dismiss the one dialog that matters), and a
  tile, profile or plugin cannot carry a directory of its own - the workspace owns it. A pane may
  point somewhere else through its Pane Settings **Directory**, which is that pane's own user-owned
  record (`PaneCwdStore`, above) and not an input to this gate: the plan key keeps naming the
  workspace directory the file supplied, and the override exists only because the user set it on
  that pane in that workspace. Where the spawn is already untrusted, the directory joins the trust
  decision: an untrusted tile's approval
  is keyed on program + argv + the directory the spawn will actually use, the Workspace Trust dialog
  names that directory, and changing a workspace's directory through the folder picker re-asks when
  the workspace holds an untrusted tile, cancelling the change otherwise. Editing a workspace file to
  point an approved program at another directory therefore re-prompts instead of restoring silently.
  The accepted exposure is the plain-shell case: a crafted or synced `workspaces.json` can start an
  ordinary shell in a directory the user did not choose, which matters only through a program that
  later trusts its working directory (a tool reading repository instructions, `git` running hooks).
  Reaching it needs the ability to write the user's `workspaces.json` or to have a copy synced to
  this machine - that is same-UID file access, which gPTY trusts by design (see the threat model),
  and a program already running in a pane could write the file itself.
- **Concepts**: the standard Rust `regex` crate only (no backtracking engine), bounded counts and
  lengths, a 16 KiB line cap before matching, and 4 MiB capture buffers.
- **Terminal parsing**: a program's output is untrusted, and `vte` keeps an OSC string's payload in
  a `Vec` that grows until the string terminates (its 1 KiB cap exists only in the `no_std` build),
  so one `EscapeStringGuard` (`crates/gpty-core/src/escstring.rs`) sits in front of *both* parsers -
  the terminal grid and the plain-text line parser - and closes a string that passes 64 KiB with a
  BEL. Measured 2026-10-30: `ESC ] 0 ;` followed by 256 MiB of payload held the grid flat at 6.2 MB,
  where it reached 267 MB before the guard. DCS, APC, PM and SOS payloads are read and discarded by
  `alacritty_terminal` and are not counted; the bound test feeds all five kinds, so a dependency
  that starts buffering one of them fails the test instead of growing. On Windows the guard cannot
  see a pane's OSC: ConPTY's host parses the child's output before gPTY does and buffers an
  unterminated string itself (measured 2026-10-30 - a 92 KiB unterminated flood from a pane produced
  zero bytes at the grid, and the smoke now says so instead of asserting a bound it cannot reach),
  so there the guard is unit-tested coverage while the claim above is conhost's to keep.
- **Markdown**: rendered from Markdown to escaped BBCode - never raw HTML or unescaped tags; links
  are scheme-checked and opened only after an explicit confirmation.

- **Media decoding**: the media backend links a pinned FFmpeg (LGPLv3, dynamically linked) built
  with `--disable-everything --disable-network`, so only the containers and codecs in
  `crates/gpty-media/components.txt` exist in the shipped libraries. A media path must be an absolute
  local **regular file**, and the bytes FFmpeg reads come from a descriptor this process opened:
  `O_NONBLOCK | O_NOFOLLOW`, verified with `fstat`, and handed over through a custom AVIO context, so
  FFmpeg never opens the path itself. A name swapped for a FIFO or device between the check and the
  open therefore cannot block the session - a blocked `open(2)` cannot be interrupted - and cannot
  redirect what is played. The demuxer's alias
  list is checked after opening, and the selected stream's codec id is checked against the same
  list before a decoder runs. Caps: 16 streams, 4096 px per side, 34 MiB per decoded frame, 8 audio
  channels, bounded queues, a 10 s open/probe budget and a 2 s close budget (`CLOSE_TIMEOUT_MS`). The size caps are re-checked on the
  *decoded* frame, not only on the probe - a frame wider or taller than 4096 px, or carrying more
  than 8 channels, is refused - and a resampled audio frame is bounded at one second per channel
  (`MAX_AUDIO_FRAME_SAMPLES`) *before* allocation, because a file claiming a tiny sample rate
  otherwise amplifies a 4 KiB packet into hundreds of megabytes. Decode runs on its own thread; a
  panic there fails the session instead of leaving it on "opening". The close budget is what
  keeps that thread from holding the GUI: a worker inside a decoder call cannot see the stop flag,
  so past the budget it is detached rather than joined (a pane close, and the window quit that
  drops every session). Nothing frees FFmpeg contexts under a running decoder - the abandoned
  thread frees its own if the call returns, and it is the one cost if it does not, ending with
  the process. No hardware decoder and no
  network protocol is compiled in.
- **Vault verbs answer only inside a registered root (v0.7.1)**: `vaultSearch`, `vaultRead` and
  `vaultWeight` take a `vault_path` from the caller, so without a list the control socket's
  knowledge base would be a file-read primitive over any directory a client names. They answer only
  for a root in the user's own `user://vaults.json`, written solely by the pane settings UI - a
  layout, profile, plugin or IPC call cannot add one, and neither can a Wiki pane merely being
  pointed at a directory. The shipped knowledge base is the exception, because it comes from gPTY's
  own bundle and a Wiki pane registers it itself. A refusal is `-32000` with
  `data.code = "not_registered"`. The same list gates `vaultWeight` before it writes the user's
  `link_weights.json`: an unregistered root could otherwise fill that store and, at its vault cap,
  evict the user's own entries. The native handlers read an in-process mirror of the list, and a GUT
  test asserts the mirror and the store agree.
- **Agent backends are bounded readers (v0.7.1)**: both process backends (`omp`, `cli`) read their
  child's stdout through one bounded line reader (`gpty_ai::frame`), so a backend that streams bytes
  without a newline cannot grow the GUI for the turn timeout, and a single OMP answer is capped at
  8 MiB before it is assembled. Backends are user-chosen programs with the user's own authority, so
  this is a memory bound, not a trust boundary. The prompt reaches the child on stdin (never argv),
  and the child's environment is stripped of `GPTY_SECRET`, `GPTY_SOCKET`, the event capability and
  the pane markers.

## Secrets and credentials

- **Nothing secret is required to build or run gPTY from source.** The app's own configuration lives under the Godot user directory; `.env`/`.env.*`, private keys, keystores and common credential files are gitignored as a precaution against a developer's local shell environment.
- **Commits are scanned locally and in CI.** `scripts/check-secrets` refuses high-confidence credential formats in the git index and runs in `ci-check --fast`, so the `pre-commit` hook runs it when `scripts/install-hooks` has been run. `.github/workflows/secret-scan.yml` runs gitleaks over the full history on every push, every pull request and weekly. GitHub's native secret scanning and push protection are also enabled.
- **A committed secret is rotated, not just deleted.** Revoke or rotate the credential first, then remove it from the current tree; a secret that was live is treated as disclosed even if history is rewritten. Open a private advisory when the exposure reaches a release artifact.
- **Release and CI credentials are short-lived or repository-scoped.** GitHub Actions uses its own token and OIDC attestations. A publishing token that predates this policy is tracked by the crates.io trusted-publishing row in the v0.9.3 roadmap and is rotated until that migration lands.
- **The `gpty-bot` app private key is a local credential.** It is stored outside the repository (mode 0600) and rotated from the app settings; it is never committed.

## Known limitations

Each is either accepted for the current scope or tracked as a roadmap item.

- **Media decoding is in-process C code.** FFmpeg is a large memory-unsafe decoder stack and is a
  deliberate exception to the memory-safety preference the rest of the untrusted-input path follows.
  The minimal build and the allowlists reduce the surface; they are not a sandbox. A decoder bug
  would be a same-process memory-safety bug, and media files should be treated as untrusted input.
- **Peer verification by platform.** The control socket checks that the connecting process runs as
  the same user, and fails closed on a lookup error, on Linux and Android (`SO_PEERCRED`), macOS and
  the BSDs (`getpeereid`), illumos and Solaris (`getpeerucred`), and Windows (the client process id
  the pipe reports, then its token's user SID compared with gPTY's own). Windows named pipes also
  reject remote clients and carry a default ACL for the creating user, SYSTEM and Administrators,
  but that ACL is inherited rather than verified - the explicit check is what makes it a gate.
  Remaining Unix targets (AIX, Haiku, QNX) have no peer-credential API wired up and still fail
  *open*, so file permissions are the only gate there. Windows environment keys are
  case-insensitive (and the PTY layer normalises them), so the `GPTY_*` credential and marker
  namespace is not case-sensitive there. On Windows the check is compile-verified locally and
  exercised by the `windows-smoke` CI job (a same-user client must be accepted); the rejection case
  needs a second user account and is not covered.
- **Shared-`/tmp` fallback.** The control socket's directory is chosen in order: `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`,
  `/run/user/<uid>` (Linux) or `$TMPDIR` (macOS), then a private state directory of your own
  (`$XDG_STATE_HOME/gpty` or `$HOME/.local/state/gpty`, created 0700), and only then
  `/tmp/gpty-<uid>.sock`. That last path is predictable in a world-writable directory: socket
  ownership and mode are validated before use, so nobody can read or spoof traffic, but another user
  can pre-create the path and deny service. It is reached only when no private directory exists or
  can be created.
- **A program in a pane can read and drive every other pane.** Every pane's shell is a child of the
  GUI and runs as you, so it passes the control socket's one gate (same user). The PTY layer strips
  `GPTY_SOCKET` and `GPTY_SECRET` from a pane's environment, but the default socket path is derived
  from `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, which is inherited, so the `gpty` CLI inside a pane finds the socket anyway.
  The secret closes that path on Linux and Windows: the GUI and the CLI harden themselves at
  startup, so on Linux a pane program's read of `/proc/<pid>/environ` fails with `EACCES` (measured
  2026-10-29; see Hardening in place), and on Windows the process DACL refuses the `PROCESS_VM_READ`
  a memory read needs, so with a secret set on the GUI the program cannot authenticate and is
  refused. That barrier is narrow: the default install sets no secret; on macOS the environment is
  readable by same-user processes through `KERN_PROCARGS2` (`ps -E`, `pgrep`); on both Linux and
  Windows the marking lands a moment after `exec`, so a process polling the platform's access check
  while a client starts can still catch that client's secret (the GUI outlives that window, and its
  panes do not exist while it opens); and an rc file that exports `GPTY_SECRET` puts it back into
  every pane's own shell, because
  the PTY strip happens before that shell starts. The reach is the whole control surface - `inject`, `pane-run`,
  `broadcast`, `new-pane`, `kill-pane`, `pane-read` and `pane-set` - so another pane's input *and* its output, and
  the settings that decide what it shows or, at its next restart, what it runs. `pane-set` cannot touch the
  user-owned stores (per-pane env, the Inspector's aim, the vault root registry) or a pane's identity: those keys
  are refused over the socket, so the reach is the pane's own configuration, not the user's consent records. Any
  process that can run in a pane (an install script, a `curl | sh`, a compromised dependency, an agent
  following an injected prompt) can type into your other panes, including a root shell or an SSH
  session, and read what they print. gPTY does not separate panes from each other and makes no such
  claim today. Workspaces do not help: all of a window's workspaces share one control socket, and
  every pane in every workspace is addressable by its id, which is matched across all of them. A
  label that two workspaces share (`T1`) is refused with an error naming every candidate rather than
  guessed from the active workspace, so an accidentally misdirected command fails loudly - that is a
  correctness rule, not a boundary, since any process can read `list-panes`' ids or guess them.
  Until enforcement lands, keep untrusted code and root shells or authenticated sessions apart by
  running one of them outside gPTY: without a secret set, the control surface is open to every program
  you run. A secret is not the fix either - it locks out the agents running in panes. The control
  surface is the intended agent workflow (an agent in a pane calling `gpty inject` or `gpty mcp`), so
  the planned fix is a per-pane permission the user grants, not removing the surface.
  Even then it will be a speed bump against opportunistic scripts and injected agents, not a boundary
  against a determined local attacker. Real isolation from code you do not trust has to come from the
  operating system - run it as another user, in a container or VM, or under a sandbox such as
  bubblewrap, away from the terminal that holds your root and SSH sessions. gPTY may one day offer an
  opt-in isolated pane (a shell started where the control socket is not visible); that is an idea, not
  a plan or a promise, and it would not change the "No sandboxing" statement above until it exists.
  A *sensitive workspace* flag is planned (see the roadmap) with one fixed rule: the panes of a workspace
  the user marks sensitive are not reachable over the control socket by any client - pane or outside, with
  no exception - and are not written to the history store. It is not implemented yet, so today no
  workspace has this property.
  Tracked in [ROADMAP.md](gpty-doc:ROADMAP.md).
- **A pane inherits your environment.** The PTY layer snapshots the GUI process's environment and
  strips only the `GPTY_*` keys, so everything else reaches every pane: `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, cloud
  credential pointers, proxy variables, `DISPLAY`. Launch gPTY from a shell that holds credentials
  you would not hand to a pane (or from inside a pane, or over SSH) and those panes inherit them.
  The same applies to the GUI the CLI auto-spawns: it is a child of the CLI and inherits *its*
  environment, so a `gpty` run from a credential-holding shell hands that context to every pane
  opened afterwards. On top of that inherited environment a pane gets your global `shell_env`
  overlaid by the pane's own entry from the user-owned `pane_env.json` store; saved files cannot
  supply environment. This is the user's own context, not a file's - but it bounds what any
  per-pane environment model can claim, and it is why environment is treated as authority rather
  than configuration.
- **Scrollback is plaintext** in `user://`. The store, its WAL siblings and the JSON stores beside
  it are created owner-only (0600) rather than with your umask, a store written by an older build is
  repaired to that mode when it is next read, and the directory that holds them is kept at 0700 -
  but the content is not encrypted: anything printed in a pane - tokens included - is stored on
  disk the same way a shell history file would be.
- **Logs do not carry program text by default.** gPTY ships with Godot's file logging off
  (`project.godot` leaves `debug/file_logging` unset). The log calls that do run name ids, paths,
  counts and error discriminants; pane output, a captured buffer, injected or pasted text, an
  environment value and an agent backend's stderr are `debug`-level, stripped of terminal control
  sequences and bounded, because those programs can print a prompt or a credential in an error. If
  you opt into file logging (`--log-file`), a log directory inside the user directory is repaired to
  0700 and its files to 0600 at the next launch; a path you choose elsewhere is yours to protect.
  The rule is stated in AGENTS.md and enforced for Rust log calls by `scripts/check-log-hygiene` in
  CI, so a new call that formats program text fails the build rather than leaking at runtime.
- **The update check is notify-only.** It fetches release metadata over TLS and shows a toast; it
  never downloads or executes anything, and the response is treated as display data.
- **Release artifacts are not code-signed, but carry build provenance.** There is no Authenticode or
  notarization. Each release publishes a `SHA256SUMS` listing every asset, and every asset is attested
  with GitHub's build-provenance attestation (SLSA v1), signed by the release workflow's OIDC identity -
  verify with `gh attestation verify <asset> --repo godot-pty/gpty`. That binds a download to the
  workflow, commit and runner that produced it; checksums without the attestation only catch corruption
  in transit. Verify the source or build locally if provenance is not enough for you. The release workflow also requires a signed annotated tag reachable from `main`, checks the crate and `server.json` versions against the tag, and runs its write/OIDC `publish` job only on staged artifacts after the `release` environment's required reviewer approves; no project code runs in that job.
- **Resource bounds are per-path, not global.** A program that floods a pane can still make that
  pane expensive: the output queue is bounded per pane (256 × 4 KiB, enforced by blocking the
  reader, so the child waits on the PTY buffer rather than the process growing - v0.5.4), and the
  render loop repaints less often when a pane's own grid work exceeds its per-frame budget instead
  of spending every frame on it (v0.5.3), and scrollback is committed by a per-pane writer thread
  whose pending queue is bounded by the store's retention window (v0.5.4) instead of one blocking
  insert per line under the grid lock. Concept matching still costs lines × enabled concepts per
  burst, which remains an open DoS item in [ROADMAP.md](gpty-doc:ROADMAP.md).
- **Parallel test runs are wall-clock sensitive.** The Inspector backend tests spawn real child
  processes and wait on them; the budgets are generous enough for a loaded parallel CI run, but a
  machine that is oversubscribed far beyond CI's shape can still time a turn out.

## Safe harbor

We will not pursue or support legal action against researcher(s) who, in good faith:

- Test against their own installation and their own data;
- Avoid accessing, modifying, or exfiltrating data that is not theirs;
- Report a discovered issue privately and give us a reasonable window to fix it before disclosing;
- Do not degrade the service for anyone else.

Security research that follows this policy is welcome. Please contribute via Issues and Discussions.

# Subprojects

gPTY is one project with several public repositories. This page records each
codebase's status and intent, so an OSPS review and a contributor can see what
ships in a release and what is installed separately. The machine-readable copy
is `project.repositories` in [security-insights.yml](security-insights.yml).

## Shipped in a release

| Repository | Status | Intent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [gpty](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty) | Active; GPL-3.0-or-later | The core application: the Rust crates, the Godot frontend, the CLI and the MCP server. Every release archive is built here. |

The core release also bundles the in-tree `extensions/gpty-omp-events` (MIT,
the OMP event bridge) and the vendored `godot/addons/gut` (MIT, test-only).
Neither is a separate project repository. Third-party components and their
licences are in [LICENSE-EXCEPTIONS.md](gpty-doc:LICENSE-EXCEPTIONS.md).

## Published separately (plugin catalog and data)

These repositories ship plugin profiles or data. A plugin profile is installed
by the user with `gpty plugin install <owner>/<repo>`; the inventory is read by
the plugin catalog. None is compiled into the core release.

| Repository | Status | Intent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [gpty-omp](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty-omp) | Active; Apache-2.0 | An OMP profile: a full-grid terminal running `omp`. |
| [gpty-herdr](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty-herdr) | Active; Apache-2.0 | A Herdr profile: a full-grid terminal running `herdr`. |
| [gpty-lazygit](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty-lazygit) | Active; Apache-2.0 | A lazygit profile: a full-grid terminal running `lazygit`. |
| [gpty-neovim](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty-neovim) | Active; Apache-2.0 | A Neovim profile: a full-grid terminal running `nvim`. |
| [gpty-claude](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty-claude) | Active; Apache-2.0 | A Claude profile: a full-grid terminal running `claude`. |
| [gpty-agent-workspace](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty-agent-workspace) | Active; Apache-2.0 | The published twin of the built-in Agent Workspace profile. |
| [gpty-knowledge-base](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty-knowledge-base) | Active; Apache-2.0 | The published twin of the built-in Knowledge Base profile. |
| [gpty-plugins](https://github.com/godot-pty/gpty-plugins) | Active; Apache-2.0 | The plugin inventory (`registry.json`) and its validator (`validate.py`). Not compiled into the core release. |

## Adding a repository

A new repository joins the list above and `project.repositories` in
[security-insights.yml](security-insights.yml) in the same change that creates
it. A repository that stops shipping is marked archived in both places rather
than removed from the history.

# Support

## Where to ask

- **Bug reports and feature requests**: open an issue with the matching form.
- **Security vulnerabilities**: do not open a public issue; follow [SECURITY.md](gpty-doc:SECURITY.md).
- **Usage questions and design discussions**: use GitHub Discussions.

## What is supported

- The latest release and `main` receive correctness and security fixes; see the supported-versions table in [SECURITY.md](gpty-doc:SECURITY.md).
- Linux is the primary target. macOS and Windows 11 builds are shipped, but are less exercised than Linux.
- Third-party CLIs, editors, agents and plugins that run inside a pane are supported by their own projects.

## What is not supported

- Backports to older minor versions, except a critical fix where feasible.
- Sandboxing: a pane runs as your user with your permissions. See the threat model in [SECURITY.md](gpty-doc:SECURITY.md).
- Platform code signing; releases ship `SHA256SUMS` and build-provenance attestations instead.

- Two modes: `UntilStop { stop_timeout_ms, stop_on_input }` (buffer output until timeout or user input, then route it to a pane) and `SingleLine` (notify-only: publish the match on the event socket, capture nothing, route nothing, leave the output in the terminal). A missing or unknown `capture_mode` is `UntilStop`; a legacy `cmd` key is ignored on parse.
- Matching: `concept::match_line` tests PTY output lines. Precedence is explicit - **a capture outranks a notify**: it returns the first `UntilStop` match, or the first `SingleLine` match when nothing captures, first-wins within each class. (First-match-only plus "notify starts nothing" let a broad notify-only concept consume every line and silently starve the capture behind it.) Within a class the order is the one `ConceptManager` merged the concepts in - the visual editor's canvas order when the store has one (see the Visual Concept Graph bullet). On `UntilStop` the engine enters capture mode - subsequent PTY output is buffered, not fed to the grid; on timeout or user input, `finalize_capture()` queues a `CapturedOutput` event. On `SingleLine` the match goes to the notice queue and nothing else happens.
- Capture lifecycle:
  - PTY output feeds `LineParser` → lines flow to the compiled `ConceptMatcher` in the engine's PTY-output handler (one read lock per batch, not per line), which answers "could anything match" with a single combined `RegexSet` pass before running `concept::match_line`'s ordered per-concept loop. The gate is derived from the same triggers and conditions are still evaluated by the loop, so it can only skip work, never change a verdict (`matcher_agrees_with_match_line_on_every_pair`).
  - On an `UntilStop` match → engine enters capture state, buffers raw bytes, suppresses grid feed. A typed line that matches is handled on the stdin path the same way. On a `SingleLine` match → the concept name is queued (`ConceptNotice`, bounded at 64, drop-oldest) and nothing else happens; `workspace.gd` drains it and emits `{type: concept, event: matched, mode: single_line, name, source}` on the event socket. Metadata only - never the matched line.
  - Timeout or user input → `finalize_capture()` queues `CapturedOutput` with plain-text lines and target label.
  - GDScript polls via `drain_concept_events()` each frame, routes to receiver pane by `target_pane_type`.
  - Receiver found → `acknowledge_capture` (bytes discarded). No receiver → `flush_capture` (bytes replayed to grid) + toast.
- Prompt restoration: Shell prompts lack trailing `\n` so `LineParser` never emits them. On acknowledge, raw bytes after last `\n` are extracted and fed to grid with `\r\n` prefix for correct cursor positioning.
- Default concepts: Shipped in `godot/concepts.default.json`. `ConceptManager._merge_concepts()` deep-merges defaults + user concepts (user keys overlay default keys). Trigger migration updates old regex patterns to new ones.
- Conditions (v0.5.4): a concept may carry `conditions: [regex, …]` - extra predicates over the same line the trigger matched; every one must match before the concept fires. They can only narrow a match: a concept whose conditions fail falls through to the next concept (precedence is unchanged) and never starts a capture on its own. Parsing rejects the **whole concept** when a condition is not a string, is empty/oversized, does not compile, or the list exceeds `MAX_CONDITIONS` (8) - dropping a single condition would widen matching, the dangerous direction. `GptyTerminal.validate_regex()` exposes the same engine-dialect check to GDScript.
- Visual Concept Graph (v0.5.4): `godot/scenes/ui/concept_graph_editor.gd` is a GraphEdit overlay opened from Settings → Concepts → "Open Visual Editor". Each rule is one chain - trigger → condition* → action (capture & route, or notify only); ports hold one wire, so chains cannot fork or merge. The canvas is **not** a second content store: `concepts` remains the single store. The `graph` sibling key in `user://concepts.json` holds only the canvas's own state - `positions` (keyed by `<name>#t` / `<name>#c<i>` / `<name>#a` and draft ids), `drafts` (nodes outside a complete rule, so unfinished work survives a close), and `order` (rule names, top-to-bottom as the canvas shows them) - never content. `ConceptGraphModel` (pure, unit-tested) builds the canvas from merged concepts, validates + compiles it back, writes a rule equal to its shipped default as *no* user entry (defaults keep tracking updates), tombstones a deleted shipped rule exactly like the manual dialog, and keeps content-invalid rules as drafts with an error instead of compiling them. The compiled entry's key set is closed by `entry_for_path` - a node can never smuggle another key into the file. **Rule order is precedence (v0.5.4):** `ConceptManager._merge_concepts` puts the rules `order` names first, in that order, and everything the canvas does not name after them - so a newly shipped default can never quietly outrank an arrangement the user made (it appears unranked on the canvas next time), and a store with no `order` key keeps exactly the shipped merge order (defaults first, then user entries in file order). `ConceptGraphModel.rule_order` is the single derivation (it accepts the editor's `Vector2` and the file's `[x, y]` alike), each trigger's title shows the rank it produced, and the editor's "Fit" re-rows with `tidy_positions` rather than Godot's `arrange_nodes()`, which lays nodes out by connection shape and would silently reshuffle precedence. Positions stay the canvas's geometry: `order` is derived from them when the editor saves, and nothing derives positions from `order`.
- Routed-content contract: `PaneBody.can_receive_content(event)` advertises current capability and `receive_content(text, event)` returns whether delivery succeeded. Routers must continue past declines and acknowledge source bytes only after `true`; if all receivers decline, flush the capture back to the terminal.
- Concepts that target Inspector (`git_log`, `cargo_check`) ship **disabled**. Do not re-enable them in defaults: captured terminal output must not be sent to an AI backend without explicit user opt-in. Inspector additionally gates captures behind its own `accept_concept_captures` export (default `false`).
- Legacy observer-target **concepts** are NOT migrated to inspector: `ConceptManager._migrate_actions_target` sets `enabled = false` on any concept whose action targets `observer` (at merge and save time), so a stale capture can never start an Inspector job.
- Matching cost under flood (v0.5.4): the aggregate cost is lines × concepts × regex, and the per-concept loop paid each regex's own prologue per line (~20 ns per concept), so a 128-concept library cost 2.7 µs on a line matching nothing. `ConceptMatcher` puts one combined `RegexSet` pass in front of the loop, which cannot change a verdict (same triggers; conditions still evaluated by the loop) and took the measured pane flood from 5.8 → 73.3 MB/s at the parser's ceiling and 8.6 → 44.9 MB/s for 128 typical triggers on short lines (`cargo run --release -p gpty-core --example concept_probe`). No rate cap on matches: the parse caps (count, trigger and condition length) bound the per-line work, the gate removes the per-concept multiplier, matching runs inside the pane's own task (one core, never the UI thread), and dropping matches under load would silently break the feature's contract. Re-measure with the probe before adding any cap.
- Alt-screen suppression: the engine skips `concept::match_line` while the grid is in alternate-screen mode (`TermGrid::is_alt_screen()`). Full-screen apps repaint themselves; their redraw lines are presentation, not shell output (an OMP TUI repaint re-emitting a transcript line containing `cat` must not fire the cat concept).
- Resize is not user input: only `StdinInput::Line` and `StdinInput::Raw` may stop an active `UntilStop` capture. `Resize`/`FlushCapture`/`AcknowledgeCapture` share the stdin channel but are internal plumbing; letting them finalize a capture replays old bytes into the grid and fires spurious "no receiver" toasts. There is also a 750 ms post-resize concept-match suppression window (`POST_RESIZE_CONCEPT_SUPPRESS_MS`) for the shell's SIGWINCH redraw.
- Concept event routing: `workspace.gd._process()` polls all terminal panes, drains events, and tries matching receivers by `_pane_type()` until one accepts. No accepting receiver → toast + flush. The same drain may fire a display-only reactive cue on the source pane (`UiEffects.reactive_for` → `PaneEffects.flash`): it never acknowledges, flushes or publishes, a hidden pane is skipped, and the per-pane 334 ms ceiling lives in `PaneEffects`, not here.
- **Concepts capture and display; they never execute.** A concept definition is untrusted data (a JSON file a user may have downloaded): `Concept` carries a trigger, a stop condition, and a routing target - no command, no label, no PTY write. The engine's only writes to a PTY are user input and resize. The visual editor keeps the same vocabulary: a node carries a regex, a capture mode + stop condition, or a routing target, and `ConceptGraphModel.entry_for_path` compiles the closed key set (no command field exists to add). Terminal ids stay unique process-wide (`start_shell` draws from a global counter) because they key capture state, status, and logs.
- Layout migration: `PaneTypes.migrate_pane_settings()` runs **before** type validation. Legacy `type: observer` + `stream: thinking` becomes `reasoning`; other observer tiles become `inspector`. Removing `observer` from `PaneTypes.ALL` without this step silently drops saved layouts.
- Pane-type vocabulary, one definition: the wire spelling is `PaneType::as_str()` (`gpty-core`), and everything else derives from it - serde's `Serialize`/`Deserialize` delegate to it (so a struct cannot emit `code-viewer` while the GUI registers `code_viewer`, which is what `#[serde(rename_all = "kebab-case")]` did), `PaneType::ALL` enumerates it, and `new-pane`'s accepted names, the plugin-manifest validator's closed set and the did-you-mean suggestions are built from that enumeration rather than re-listed. The GUI side is `PaneTypes.ALL` in `pane_types.gd`, read key-for-key by `pane_types_match_the_gui_registry_key_for_key` (`crates/gpty-cli/src/plugin_manifest.rs`, `include_str!` of the GDScript) - so a rename on either side fails a test instead of shipping, and the two count-only checks that used to guard it (`test_pane_types_all_has_six_entries` here, the literal list there) no longer carry that job alone. `observer` stays accepted (legacy layouts) in exactly two places: `PaneType::from_str` and `new-pane`'s translation.

A class is a mechanism that produced more than one defect, not a component and
not a symptom. The class decides the control, and the control decides whether
the next instance is caught by a gate or by somebody remembering a sentence.

## Review loop

- At each release cut, `./scripts/fix-forensics --check --since <previous tag>`
  must exit 0, and the class mix goes into the release's chain-page section as
  one line beside the closed rows.
- A class with a third member and no mechanical control gets a roadmap row for
  one: `PROJECT` for a repository-wide check, `CORE` or `BUILD` otherwise.
- A class whose share rises across two releases means the rule that owns it is
  not landing. Rewrite that bullet or skill step, **or** add the check - never
  add a fourth prose bullet.
- An inferred count is a hypothesis. It becomes a number only after the audit
  described in `scripts/fix-forensics`'s docstring, and the report labels it.
- A new check has the house shape: a docstring naming the defect it was born
  from, an `...-ok: <why>` marker for reviewed exceptions, and a registration
  in `scripts/ci-check` so editing it runs it.

## The corpus

Measured 2026-11-15:

```bash
git log --all --format='%s' | grep -cE '^fix'   # 402
git log --all --oneline | wc -l                 # 1440
./scripts/fix-forensics --all                   # 401 of 1255 on main (32.0%)
```

The difference is branches: `git log --all` sees the whole repository, while
the report walks the current branch's history. Use `--all` for context and the
release range for a gate. `git log --grep='^fix'` over-counts (409) because `^`
anchors every line of a message and seven bodies begin a line with "fix"; the
script filters the subject instead.

At the same measurement, 261 of 401 fixes (65%) touched no test path, and the
files fixes return to were `godot/scenes/terminal/workspace.gd` (78),
`godot/scenes/terminal/terminal_pane.gd` (43), `crates/gpty-gdext/src/lib.rs`
(32) and `crates/gpty-core/src/engine.rs` (21). A hotspot is a design smell, not
a target: read its last three fixes and ask whether one rule would have caught
all three.

GDScript is an interpreter in front of a C++ engine. The expensive work is not usually the
`draw_*` call - it is the per-element loop that builds the arguments, the node construction around
it, the allocation per cell, and the cross-FFI call per item. This page is the method for finding
and proving one of those costs, and the rule for deciding whether the work belongs in Rust.

## The sweep

Two committed tools, run by hand:

- `scripts/gdscript-audit` - a **report**, not a gate. It parses every `godot/scenes/**/*.gd` file
  into functions (indentation, inner classes included), tags loop context, and ranks literal cost
  atoms: a typed `String` indexed per element, a String append in a loop, an eager Dictionary
  default, a NodePath lookup, a group scan, `Image.create_from_data`, node construction,
  `get_string_size`, JSON in a loop, `range`, a theme read, a container write in a loop, a fresh
  `RegEx`, `await` on `_process`/`_draw`, and `duplicate`. `--top N` (default 40; `0` = all)
  bounds the output, `--hot` keeps functions named for frame/event work, `--json` is
  machine-readable. It exits 0 with findings; it is deliberately not in `ci-check` and has no
  allow-marker convention, because a heuristic gate goes stale or noisy.
- `godot/tests/bench/gdscript_probe.gd` - the idiom probe, headless:

  ```
  godot --headless --path godot -s res://tests/bench/gdscript_probe.gd
  ```

  Median of five runs per case, no assertions. It measures the shapes the audit finds: String
  indexing plus append vs a native slice, an eager `{}` Dictionary default vs a plain get,
  `range()` vs integer iteration, font measurement, the palette read, Image creation vs reuse with
  the copy forced, the audio interleave, and a NodePath lookup vs a cached reference.

The audit is a floor, not a source of truth. It misses costs that are prose (a settings broadcast)
or cross-file (a per-frame caller of a cold-looking helper), and it reports cold setup as loudly as
a hot loop. Read the function it names, then prove the cost with a probe before changing anything.

## What costs, with the 4.7.2 numbers

Measured with the probe on the 4.7.2 `arch_linux` build, 2026-11-15:

| Shape | Measurement | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| String index + append | 87 ns per character (34,857 us for 2000 x 200 `line[c]` + `text += ch`) | A 12,000-cell terminal repaint pays ~1.0 ms in this loop; one slice per row was ~500x cheaper. Do not build a run one character at a time. |
| Node construction | A Phosphor glyph `Label` costs 3.3-3.5 ms to enter the tree; re-assigning `text` on an attached Label costs ~0 | Free-and-recreate row UIs cost milliseconds per row. Pool rows and update in place. |
| Per-pane FFI drains | 192 grid-mutex calls + 96 NodePath walks per frame at 96 panes (call chain) | A per-frame loop over every pane is the cost, not the individual call. Batch in Rust, or gate the scan on a change. |
| Audio interleave | 84.8 us per 2048-frame stereo chunk | 8 chunks in one frame is ~678 us. Return a `PackedVector2Array` from Rust instead. |
| Palette read | 0.314 us per `UiPalette.active()` vs 0.032 us for a local | Reading it once per draw is correct; reading it inside a per-match loop is not (10k matches would be ~3 ms). |
| Font measurement | 175 ns per `get_string_size` | 2000 labels on a graph open is ~0.35 ms; it is not a frame stall by itself. The per-redraw scans around it are. |
| NodePath lookup | 65 ns vs 27 ns for a cached reference | 96 per frame is ~6 us. Cache the body on the wrapper, but do not mistake this for the FFI cost. |
| `range()` | 13.3 ms vs 13.5 ms per 1M iterations | **Flat on 4.7.2.** The `range` atom is a candidate only; never optimize it without a profile. |
| `Dictionary.get(k, {})` | 0.133 us vs 0.095 us per get | The eager default is ~40% more per call; real in a loop, invisible once per frame. |
| `Image` creation | 0.13 us per 1280x720 image; 0.07 us for `Image.set_data`; 0.2 us with `get_data()` forced | The data is copy-on-write. The remaining per-frame cost is the texture upload (`ImageTexture.update`), not the `Image` object; reuse alone is not a measured win. |

The other shapes that show up in this tree:

- **Whole-buffer copies.** `String +` / `String +=` on a streamed turn, `_editor.text` on a large
  note, `replace("[", "[lb]")` on a rendered body: O(n) per event, and the event is per token or
  per keystroke. Keep pieces and join once at the display boundary.
- **Rebuild instead of diff.** A model change that tears down rows and rebuilds them pays node
  construction even when the row identity is unchanged. The pane list was fixed this way; check a
  new list for the same shape.
- **Repeated invariant reads.** `_cell_cache.get("cols")`, `_grid_offset()`, `get_ascent`, the
  active palette and the default font are cheap once and repeated per row, per label or per match.
  Hoist them out of the per-element loop; a palette read at the top of `_draw` is correct.

## Move it to Rust

Move work when it is a **pure data transform over bytes, strings or arrays**, scales with the data
rather than with the UI tree, and needs no Godot engine type. The boundary should be a batch: one
call per frame or per build, flat arrays in, flat arrays out. A new FFI call per item is worse than
the GDScript loop it replaces.

The accepted shapes in this tree:

- the vault graph's parse, pair aggregation, layout, hit-test and label cull over the index's own
  answer (`PackedVector2Array` positions, one call per build);
- the media audio interleave over the decoded sample buffer (`PackedVector2Array`, one call per
  chunk batch);
- the per-pane concept/agent drains, which are already Rust queues behind a per-pane FFI accessor -
  one registry drain per frame with session-tagged envelopes.

What stays in GDScript:

- **All drawing** (`draw_rect`/`draw_string`/`draw_line`, the row layers, repaint granularity);
- **node wiring and layout** (panels, sidebars, dialogs, tile geometry, font metrics, theme
  resolution);
- **bounded configuration work** (settings sanitizers, pane-type validation) that runs per spawn or
  per save.

Rejected examples, so they are not re-proposed without new evidence: the text reader's UTF-8 cut
(the read/slice/decode is native; the GDScript part walks at most three continuation bytes),
mouse-report and paste-payload formatting (human-rate), the file tree (`DirAccess`/`TreeItem` is
UI-bound), and per-frame `Image` reuse for video (copy-on-write; the upload is the copy).

## How to measure

- Time the call with `Time.get_ticks_usec()` marks around each step, and the frame after it with
  `await get_tree().process_frame`; repeat at least three times and attribute every step before
  theorising (`testing.md`'s recipe, and the `gpty-live-gui-smoke` skill's "Timing an interaction").
- A perf claim about an interaction needs a **windowed** run. Draw numbers need a real display
  driver and `--disable-vsync`; under `--headless` every draw timing reads zero. Pure compute (the
  probe, a parser, a sort) may be headless.
- Use the committed end-to-end harnesses: `draw_bench.gd` (full/row/overlay repaint and the stream
  cadence), `graph_bench.gd` (query/parse/layout, request-to-canvas, and the 3D
  build/step/link cost), `reasoning_bench.gd` (burst/catchup), `switch_bench.gd`
  (workspace switch, cold/warm), `spawn_bench.gd` (pane creation). The probe is the
  micro-number; the harness is the user-visible one.
- Record **measured** (with the build/source) and **expected** (with the probe that will confirm
  it) separately in the roadmap row. A row lands only with a number and a test; if its gate
  misses, revert the code and close the row with the number. A micro-number is never presented as
  the user-visible gain; quote the end-to-end number with the probe that produced it.

## What is not a defect

- Native built-ins: packed-array indexing, `Rect2.intersects`, `String.substr`,
  `PackedByteArray.slice` - they are C++ already.
- One-off setup: building a panel's controls, connecting signals, loading a font.
- A palette read at draw time (the light/dark switch requires it) once per draw.
- `range()` on 4.7.2: measured flat; the atom is a candidate, not a finding.
- An `Image` object per frame: copy-on-write, measured sub-microsecond; the texture upload is the
  separate cost.

When the audit and the probe disagree, the probe wins; when the probe and the windowed harness
disagree, the harness wins.

- Indentation: tabs

That is why the button's exposed name is the words alone: the engine composes `"<accessibility_name>: <button text>"` (measured on 4.7.2), and a codepoint left in `text` trailed the words into the tree. `name` is a required argument because a `Button` is named from its `text` before its `tooltip` (`grep -rn "Icons.style_button" godot/scenes` must print nothing). `Icons.glyph(btn)` reads the codepoint back (`""` for a text button); a glyph that changes at runtime calls `Icons.set_glyph(btn, glyph)` after setting `accessibility_name`, which it mirrors onto the Label (`WindowChrome._sync_max_button`, `TerminalManager._toggle_minimize`).
