FFmpeg's `COPYING.LGPLv3`/`COPYING.LGPLv2.1` and `components.txt` ride in `licenses/`; the AUR recipe installs the libs and licenses under `/usr/lib/gpty` and `/usr/share/licenses/gpty`. When real macOS signing lands, sign **after** the injection. Never copy a distro FFmpeg into the bundle: the pinned soname is the point.

- Release bundles name the GUI `gpty-gui`, never `gpty`: the CLI owns `gpty` (its crate bin name, `mcp.json`'s `command`, the plugin API's `GPTY_BIN_PATH`) and `find_gui_binary()` auto-spawns a **sibling** called `gpty-gui` or `gpty-editor`. Renaming the export back to `gpty` shadows the CLI on PATH and breaks auto-spawn. Linux bundles also carry Godot's generated `gpty-gui.sh` launcher (clears the screen, sets the title, execs the sibling export). On macOS the `.app` name is preset-owned (`gPTY.app`), so discovery looks inside the bundle next to the CLI and under `/Applications` as well.

- Godot resolves both the data pack and the GDExtension library against the **real** executable path (`/proc/self/exe`), so a bundle binary may be symlinked but not renamed behind a wrapper: renaming `gpty-gui` without renaming `gpty-gui.pck` yields `Couldn't load project data ... Is the .pck file missing?`. `godot/export_presets.cfg` keeps `binary_format/embed_pck=false` for Linux (true for Windows), so the pack sits beside the binary.

- App icon and bundle version are project settings, not packaging details: `godot/project.godot`'s `config/icon` (`godot/icon.png`, cropped square from `assets/icon-source.jpg`) is what macOS turns into `Contents/Resources/icon.icns` and what Linux uses as the window icon, while the Windows preset needs the explicit `application/icon="res://icon.ico"` (Godot 4.7 embeds the PE resources itself - no rcedit). `config/version` feeds macOS `CFBundleShortVersionString`/`CFBundleVersion`; the release workflow overwrites it from the tag, while the committed value tracks the crate version (`ci-check`'s crate-versions step fails a stale one). Keep `application/app_category` single-word: Godot lowercases it verbatim, so a multi-word name becomes an invalid UTI (`public.app-category.developer tools`).

- `libc::mode_t` is `u16` on the BSDs and `u32` on Linux, so a raw `fchmod(fd, want: u32)` compiles here and fails the cross-check. `ci-check`'s BSD step compiles `gpty-core` through `gpty-ipc`, which is how the un-cast version was caught; cast with `want as libc::mode_t` and keep the modes small enough that the cast cannot lose a bit.

- A CI cache is a compiled artifact, so it may be shared between workflows only when the producer and consumer run on the **same runner image**: the release build links FFmpeg on `ubuntu-22.04` (the bundle's glibc floor) while `ci.yml` builds the same prefix on `ubuntu-24.04`, and a 24.04 `libav*.so` needs `GLIBC_2.38` (`__isoc23_*`) that a 22.04 link cannot take - the restored prefix ships in the archive, so the mistake would raise the product's floor rather than fail loudly. `media-deps`'s `.stamp` checks the version, components, platform, assembler and its own checksum but not the image, so it would have skipped the rebuild. `release-build.yml` therefore keys Linux as `Linux-ubuntu22-ffmpeg-*` and shares `ci.yml`'s key only on Windows, where both run `windows-2025`. Check who writes a cache key and on which image, not just that the key matches.

- The headless GUI has **no window geometry**: `godot --headless` leaves the root viewport at 0×0, so `Workspace._apply_layout` gives every tile a 0×0 rect, a pane body falls back to its `custom_minimum_size` (~38×38 px, 8×2 cells) and a terminal pane's fitted grid is therefore `_grid_for_size`'s zero - it starts its child at the configured fallback size (24×80), exactly as it did before pane sizes were fitted. Measured 2026-11-08 while verifying the v0.8.1 birth-size row: the headless `new-pane` still answered `stty size` with `24 80` after the fix, while the same build in a real window answered `60 205`. Headless is valid for IPC, PTY and output claims that do not depend on layout; any claim about a pane's size, `_apply_layout`, capture or UI needs a window (`scripts/ui-capture`, or a plain `godot --path godot` launch).

### wrong-constant

- vte `Perform::execute` CR/LF: PTY output uses CRLF pairs. The vte parser calls `execute` per byte. If you commit on both `\r` and `\n`, every line produces a spurious empty string. Track `last_was_cr` and skip the `\n` commit when preceded by `\r`.

- `alacritty_terminal` display_iter: returns negative line numbers for scrollback history rows. Never cast directly to `usize` - it wraps to a huge value. Always add the grid's `display_offset()` to normalize: `let line = (indexed.point.line.0 + offset) as usize`.

- GDScript `\UXXXXXXXX` escape: GDScript only supports `\uXXXX` (4-hex-digit BMP). `\UXXXXXXXX` (8-digit) does not exist - the parser mangles it. For non-BMP codepoints, use `char(0x10XXXX)` in `static var` initializers. Prefer BMP alternatives; this project's icons use Phosphor PUA codepoints (U+E000–U+F8FF), all expressible as `const` with `\uXXXX`.

- Multi-line `for` array colon: `for x in [...]` with a multi-line array literal requires `]:` at the end. Forgetting the colon produces a parse error at an unrelated line. Double-check after replacing inline array content.

- `tokio::time::Instant::now() + Duration::MAX` panics: The addition overflows. Use a safe large constant like `Duration::from_secs(86400 * 365)` (1 year) for inactive timeout sleeps.

- Bare CR must never commit a parser line: `LineParser` commits only on `\n` (LF); a bare `\r` stashes the pending text - an LF after it commits the CRLF line, a printable after it discards the stash (reprint/overwrite). Shells reprint the prompt on SIGWINCH as `\r` + clear-to-EOL + `\r` + prompt; committing on bare CR stamps a history row per resize, and restarting restores a growing pile of old prompts. Progress bars (bare-CR updates) likewise only commit their final state once a real line end arrives.

- Terminal pane cadence: `TerminalPane`'s flood back-off compares `_fetch_ms + _draw_ms` once per sync against `PANE_WORK_BUDGET_MS * cadence / _sync_interval` - a constant share of wall time (a quarter of a 60 Hz frame, ~24 %), not a fixed 4 ms. A fixed budget re-armed the back-off on every sync even after the cadence had stretched to 100 ms, so a streaming pane parked at the `MAX_SYNC_INTERVAL` ceiling (measured 2026-11-13 with `BENCH_FLOOD=1 draw_bench --max-fps 60` at 102x78: 10.5-13.3 syncs/s for 4.7 ms of work per sync). A sync over its share stretches the cadence, one under it calls `_relax_sync_backoff()`, and only user input resets it (`_note_view_input`, called by both send helpers since 2026-11-11) - a pane being typed into must never keep the stretched cadence, because a keystroke's echo is painted at the next sync (measured: 93.9 ms of back-off, 2-3 refreshes per 300 ms, against 14-19 once exempt). `test_flood_cadence.gd` owns the rule and pins both directions at the same 9 ms cost; the damaged-row paint half is the next bullet (closed in v0.8.3: a one-line update fell from ~2.3 ms to ~0.1-0.2 ms per sync at 102x78/120x60).

- Printable keys and the evdev keymap: `GptyTerminal.key_to_bytes` MUST early-return empty for printable ASCII keycodes (0x21–0x7E). Routing them through `godot_key_to_evdev` fabricates scancodes that collide with special keys (`z`→55=KP_MULTIPLY, `;`→59=F1, `` ` ``→96=KP_ENTER) and silently swallows the characters. Only Space (→57, for Ctrl+Space→NUL) and true special keys may reach the keymap.

- PTY Enter key: The Enter key MUST send `\r` (CR) to the PTY, not `\n`. `pty.rs:write_line` appends `\r`. The PTY terminal driver translates `\r` → `\n` in canonical mode; raw-mode programs read `\r` directly.

- Resize anchoring surgery: `TermGrid::resize` deletes the rows alacritty pulls in on row-growth and restores the cursor (xterm behavior). Run it ONLY when `display_offset == 0 && rows grew && !is_alt_screen() && history_size > 0`. That `history_size` test is read from the POST-resize grid and `grow_lines` ends with `decrease_scroll_limit(lines_added)`, so it passes only when scrollback was longer than the growth - the case where every new row came from history and no visible row was pushed off. The deletion therefore removes recovered scrollback rows and can never eat on-screen content; scrollback shorter than the growth is zeroed by that same call, failing the guard and skipping the surgery. It is NOT a "this is a TUI" test: a primary-screen app that paints without smcup (the OMP TUI) is guarded only on a fresh pane - launched after the pane had more scrollback than the row growth, it passes every condition and the injected `CUP`/`DL` escapes land in its screen. Only the alternate-screen check catches real full-screen apps.

- Bottom-edge overlays need BOTH anchors: a Control with `anchor_bottom = 1.0` but default `anchor_top = 0.0` stretches to FULL parent height - the offsets only shift it, they don't shrink it (the terminal search bar briefly covered the whole pane). Bottom strips must set `anchor_top = 1.0; anchor_bottom = 1.0` with a negative `offset_top`.

- Mouse reports are cells, 1-based, mapped through the same `_grid_offset()`/cell metrics as selection. The legacy X10 form offsets by 32 and cannot address past cell 223: drop such an event rather than clamping, or the app receives a click on a cell the user never touched. The report has no trailing newline, so a child that has mouse tracking on but left the PTY in canonical mode never sees it (that is the app's bug, not the pane's - the automated check drives a raw-mode child).

- Divider-drag arithmetic (the state machine is `tile_drag.gd`; `TerminalManager` keeps `drag_active`/`begin_line_drag`/`divider_limits`/`drive_edge_drag`/`end_edge_drag` as thin delegators) moves the divider in whole grid units, and the release commits the unit it showed. `drive_edge_drag` passes the distance from the **press** (mouse motion arrives in 1-3 px steps, so a per-event delta would round to zero) and `_preview_edge_drag` rounds it to units before moving anything: a pixel-continuous preview looked smoother and then hopped up to half a unit (~16 px on a 1920 px window) on release. The motion moves the line's wrappers (`before` tiles grow their far edge, `after` tiles move their near edge) without touching the tile model and without emitting `tiles_resized` (that signal drives `_apply_layout`, and emitting it per motion relayouted the grid and reflowed every terminal on every motion event). `begin_line_drag` snapshots everything the preview needs from the press: the tiles on the line, their committed offsets, one unit in pixels, and the unit travel limits - the same clamps `line_limits` reports, so the preview can never show a position the release refuses. `end_edge_drag` rewinds every tile to the press-time spans first (normally a no-op; it is what makes the commit idempotent if a spawn or kill moved a tile mid-drag), applies the step, and emits `tiles_resized` exactly once and then `divider_drag_finished` - the panes' `set_drag_resizing` turns their quiet-period `RESIZE_DEBOUNCE` into a ~10 Hz reflow while the drag runs and asks for the final reflow when it clears. The preview is absolute from the press, so backtracking is safe, and a line with no tile on its far side (the window border) never starts a drag. `_tiles_on_divider` reads the press-time snapshot when there is one and the live model otherwise, which is what lets `divider_limits` answer before any press. **The release must not be consumed**: a viewport that never sees the release of the press the handle took keeps its stale mouse focus and updates the cursor shape only after another press/release pair. Tiles are addressed by wrapper (`_tile_index_for_wrapper`), not by body (`_tile_index_of` resolves bodies and never matches a wrapper).

- GDScript `///` comments: GDScript uses `#` or `##` for comments. Rust-style `///` causes a parse error. Always use `##` for doc comments in GDScript.

- Edit tool on structured formats (YAML, TOML, Markdown frontmatter): the line-based `edit` tool can corrupt delimiter-sensitive files (YAML `---` blocks, TOML `[sections]`, frontmatter bounds). When editing config files, workflow YAML, or Hugo content, prefer `eval` with Python (`yaml.safe_load`, `tomllib`) to parse → modify → serialize. Reserve `edit` for Rust, GDScript, and plain Markdown where line semantics hold.

- GDScript has no octal literal. `0o600` is a parse error; file modes are hex (`0600` = `0x180`, `0644` = `0x1A4`, `0700` = `0x1C0`, `0755` = `0x1ED`), which is why `BasePersistenceManager.STORE_UNIX_MODE` is `0x180`. Tests that assert a mode must use the same spelling.

- `DirAccess.create_link(source, link_path)` creates the link at the **second** argument, and it is an instance method (`DirAccess.open(dir).create_link(...)`), as are `is_link` and `read_link` - calling them on the class is a parse error. Measured on 4.7.2: `create_link(victim, store)` leaves `store` a link to `victim`; passing an existing path as `link_path` fails outright, which reads as an unrelated setup failure if the order is reversed.

- A runtime-selected value cannot be a `const`, and a `static var` initialiser cannot name its own class - measured on 4.7.2 while splitting the chrome palette into `UiPalette`: `const A := SomeClass.static_fn()` fails to compile ("Assigned value for constant ... isn't a constant expression") and `static var _inst: T = T.new()` inside `T` fails with "Identifier not found: T". That is why `UiPalette` exposes the sets through `static func dark()`/`light()` with lazy caching and `use(mode)` switching them, and why `SettingsManager`'s seven colour vars read `UiPalette.active()` in their initialisers while `terminal_pane.gd` fills its overlay colours in `_init`.

### external

- `PopupMenu.set_item_submenu(index, name)` is a silent no-op on 4.7.2 (measured 2026-11-13 while adding the pane menu's Move to workspace submenu): the call succeeds, the child is parented, `get_item_submenu` still answers `""`, and the item never opens a submenu. `add_submenu_item(label, name)` binds it. The cost of the working form is that the item cannot go through `MenuItems` (which needs the index the setter takes), so it carries no icon - there is no move glyph, so the plain item is what shipped.

`gpty-plugin.toml` - the schema lives in `crates/gpty-cli/src/plugin_manifest.rs` (`parse_manifest`). Top-level keys: `id` (`owner/name`, `[a-z0-9-]` parts 1–63 chars), `name` (1–64 chars), `version` + `min_gpty_version` (semver `X.Y.Z`, no pre-release), `platforms` (subset of `linux|macos|windows`, default all), `build`/`startup` (argv arrays), and five array-of-table sections: `[[actions]]` (≤64: `name`, `command`, optional `args`), `[[events]]` (≤64: `name`, `type`), `[[link_handlers]]` (≤16: `scheme`, `command` argv), `[[concepts]]` (≤128), `[[profiles]]` (≤64, ≤64 tiles each, optional `grid_unit`). The first-party tool-layout plugins are one repo per tool under the `godot-pty` org - `gpty-omp`, `gpty-herdr`, `gpty-lazygit`, `gpty-neovim`, `gpty-claude` - each a single manifest with that tool's `[[profiles]]`; a repo is the install/review/consent unit (see the profiles-migration item).

Install & lifecycle (same release): `gpty plugin install <owner>/<repo>[@ref]` - `@ref` accepts any advertised git ref (tag, branch, or commit SHA); a bare install means the default branch's latest, and the review dialog shows the requested ref beside the resolved revision while the store pins the SHA (a moved tag = new revision = re-review) - clones `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>` into a staging dir under the data dir (`data_dir()/staging`, git driven by argv, never a shell), parses the manifest (64 KiB cap), gates it (the manifest's `id` must equal the install target; the current platform must be declared; `min_gpty_version` must not exceed the CLI), and - because a plugin's actions run as the user with the workspace API - sends a summary over the `pluginInstall` IPC method for a human to review in the GUI (`workspace.gd:_show_plugin_review`, the Workspace Trust pattern with the paneWait deferred response; the Rust fallback deadline for this method is 300 s, not 5 s, and that deadline travels with the request - `drain_ipc_requests` hands GDScript the remaining milliseconds, so the review dialog closes itself when the request dies and a late click cannot answer a dead channel while the user believes the install happened). No GUI answers (declined, disconnected, `--no-daemon`) => nothing installs. On acceptance the content moves to `data_dir()/plugins/<id>` (rename on one filesystem, old revision swapped with rollback), the per-plugin runtime dirs `state_dir()/plugins/<id>/{config,state,logs}` are created, and the record lands in the store: `state_dir()/plugins.json` (`crates/gpty-plugin/src/store.rs` - `{id, revision, enabled, installed_at}`, ≤256 records, atomic random-suffix temp + rename 0600, strict on corrupt files; the crate is the store the CLI and the GDExtension share, and `schema.rs` holds the caps both sides enforce). `list` / `enable` / `disable` / `uninstall` / `logs` manage the store and dirs; `run <id> <action>` spawns `GPTY_BIN_PATH` (or the current exe) with the action's `command` + `--key value` args - argv only, output captured to the log dir and printed on exit. A manifest's `build`/`startup` commands are **declared, not executed** - displayed in the review, run by no current item (executing them is its own trust decision). The plugin subcommand is excluded from the MCP tool list (like `state`): installing waits on a human, the admin actions touch local state, and `pluginInstall` is deliberately not a tool; the contract test names it in `NON_TOOL_ROUTED`. Every `plugin` action runs the stale-binary check first (`daemon::warn_on_version_mismatch`, the same bounded best-effort probe `mcp` and `main`'s generic dispatch run) - the plugin arm sits above that dispatch, so without it a CLI and GUI from different releases stayed silent while the older side called the newer side's store `plugins.json is corrupt` (v0.7.1 report); the probe is silent without a GUI, so the offline validator is unaffected, and the warning is stderr-only so `--json` output stays parseable.

Rules that must not weaken:
- **Nothing executes at parse/validation time**, and a manifest's own command arrays are never a shell string (`build`/`startup`/link-handler commands are argv arrays, ≤32 entries, ≤4096 chars total, no U+FFFD). A profile tile may carry one `launch` line, the same shell-string field a saved tile has: the validator holds it to one line of ≤1024 characters with no control characters, the install review lists it, and activating the profile runs it through the user's configured shell behind the Workspace Trust gate.
- **Every concept is engine-accepted**: the validator round-trips each `[[concepts]]` entry through the real `gpty_core::concept::concepts_from_json`; an entry the engine would silently drop (a trigger/condition outside the Rust `regex` dialect - e.g. a PCRE2 lookbehind) rejects the manifest. Entries hold to the closed key set the visual editor compiles (`name`, `trigger`, `enabled`, `conditions`, `capture_mode`, `stop_timeout_ms`, `stop_on_input`, `actions`; `capture_mode` ∈ {absent, `single_line`}), so a plugin concept cannot smuggle a key into the engine.
- **Tiles mirror `PaneTypes.sanitize_tile`** - pane type ∈ the eight `PaneTypes.ALL` entries (legacy `observer` refused with guidance), grid geometry within the profile's `grid_unit` (`60` when it declares none; `12` is the coarser authoring grid, and `cspan`/`rspan` default to that unit), `rows`/`cols` ≤ 500/2000, `attachment_id` pattern - with one deliberate difference: the sanitizer clamps legacy files, the validator rejects (a manifest is authored content; an out-of-range value is an authoring error). A profile that declares `grid_unit` must also set `min_gpty_version` to the first release that honours it (`0.8.4`): an older GUI ignores the field and infers the unit, which mis-sizes a layout that does not touch the grid's far edge. Never relax these to "clamp" and never duplicate the grid constants in the GUI.
- **`[[actions]].command` is the published API surface** - the same derivation `schema::mcp_tool_names()` produces (the 27 MCP tools); a manifest cannot name anything else. **`[[events]].type`** must be one of the event socket's names: gpty's own `pane.spawned`, `pane.killed`, `concept.matched`, plus the generic vocabulary (`gpty_core::events::GENERIC_EVENT_NAMES`) `session.bound`, `session.shutdown`, `agent.started`, `agent.settled`, `turn.started`, `turn.finished`, `tool.call`, `tool.finished`, `thinking.delta`, `state.declared`. The validator derives that list (`plugin_manifest::event_types`) and the extension's translation table is pinned against the same array, so the two cannot drift; a new socket event adds one name in `gpty_core::events`, and a native one adds a name to `NATIVE_EVENT_TYPES`.
- Unknown keys are rejected in manifest sections (closed schema - the manifest is untrusted input gated before approval, unlike the store's reader, which tolerates additive keys from another release); a profile's *tile settings* go through the pane type's closed table instead (`PaneTypes.sanitize_settings`), so an unknown key or a value outside a rule's set is dropped from that tile and named once by the restore notice rather than carried into the app.
- **Install and the sidebar's uninstall are the two content writers of the GUI's plugin view.** At acceptance the CLI stores the validated manifest's profiles in the record (`{id, revision, enabled, installed_at, profiles: [{name, grid_unit, tiles}]}` - caps 64 profiles × 64 tiles, an absent `profiles` key reading as empty so records written before this stay valid, and a reader whose rule is the same at every level: an unknown sibling key is ignored (another release may add one) while a required field, a type, a shape and the caps are refused - a renamed field still fails through its required-field check, and that failure names the version skew (`this store may have been written by a different gpty release; run the CLI and the GUI from the same release`) instead of calling the file corrupt. The write path keeps the manifest's closed concept key set in `validate_concepts`, so the store never emits a vocabulary the validator would refuse), and `GptyTerminal.installed_plugin_profiles()` returns the *enabled* records' profiles as JSON for `ProfileManager` (see the Profiles bullet). The GUI never parses TOML: the validator stays the single gate, and a hand-broken store degrades one entry at a time (the FFI logs the reason and answers `[]`, the GUI's refresh skips malformed entries). The file is read bounded: a store over 16 MiB (`MAX_STORE_BYTES`, `MAX_PLUGINS` × the 64 KiB manifest cap a record's content came from) is refused before it is parsed, on every reader (`store::read_store_text`), so a planted tile array is never loaded. The same record carries the manifest's **concepts** (`concepts: [...]`, cap 128 entries, the closed `CONCEPT_KEYS` set the validator enforces on the way in - the reader keeps an additive key and the engine ignores it - an absent key reading as empty exactly like `profiles`), and `GptyTerminal.installed_plugin_concepts()` shapes the *enabled* records into `{plugin_id, revision, name, concept}` for `ConceptManager.refresh_plugin_concepts()`. The sidebar's profile-row trash calls `GptyTerminal.uninstall_plugin()`, which shares the `gpty-plugin` crate's store removal with `gpty plugin uninstall`: the record is removed first, then the content and runtime directories are removed best-effort, and the GUI refreshes profiles and concepts from the same store. The concept merge puts plugin rules **between the shipped defaults and the user's own** - the builtins/plugin/user order concepts use (profiles now list user profiles before plugin profiles, with a user name always winning): names are derived on every merge, a plugin name yielding to a shipped default and to an earlier plugin with ` (n)` (`add_profile`'s convention, so an uninstall/re-install gives the bare name back), while a *user* entry naming a rule is that rule's **overlay** (a toggle writes a thin `{name, enabled}`, an edit a full entry) applied by name exactly as on a default - that is what makes the Settings toggle/edit/delete work on installed content. The Settings row carries provenance in a tooltip, and the visual canvas deliberately excludes plugin rules (its no-entry/tombstone save semantics are defined for the shipped defaults and the user's rules only; plugin rules are managed from Settings). Refreshes fire at init, after an accepted install review (the same deferred re-read as profiles), and on the `pluginsChanged` notice. **`[[events]]` and `[[link_handlers]]` are declarations, and the 2026-10 decision is that gpty never dispatches them.** Events: core ships the primitives - the event socket, open to same-UID subscribers, whose path a plugin program launched in a pane already receives as `GPTY_EVENT_SOCKET` - while an event→plugin-action dispatcher is out of core by the ADE boundary (observe/display, never orchestrate) and would be a new execution path driven by signals terminal output or a Tier-2 declaration can provoke; a plugin that wants events reads the socket itself. Link handlers: the Markdown view opens only `http`/`https`/`mailto` through `OS.shell_open` after a confirmation and ignores any other scheme, so nothing consults these entries - a click path would need an env-stripped argv spawn surface (Godot's own process spawn cannot drop `GPTY_SECRET` or a pane's event capability), a reserved-scheme policy and per-click consent, and no consumer exists. Both sections stay in the accepted vocabulary as reviewed declarations (the review text says "declared"; `build`/`startup` say "not run by gpty"), and pruning them would be a deliberate schema-break decision, never an oversight - revisit only with an ecosystem consumer plus that trust design. **The store's other writer is announced, not polled:** `gpty plugin uninstall|enable|disable` fires `pluginsChanged {"action", "id"}` over the control socket after the record is written, and the GUI's `ipc_handlers.gd` arm answers it by re-reading the store *synchronously* - so the CLI's reply means the profile list has caught up (the install review is the opposite case and keeps its deferred re-read, because the clone lands only after the answer). The notice is best-effort in the one direction that matters: no GUI, a refused connect or a timeout is dropped, and an admin action never starts a GUI (`daemon::ensure_running` is deliberately absent here, unlike `install`). It is routed but never an MCP tool (`NON_TOOL_ROUTED`), like `pluginInstall`: an MCP client has no reason to poke a GUI's profile list. Both fields are validated even though only `action` has a consumer today - `id` is inert (nothing stores or looks anything up with it) and the CLI cannot deliver a malformed one, since it notifies only after `PluginStore` accepted the id; it is checked because validation is a boundary property rather than a property of the fields that happen to be read, and the *shape* is not re-declared: the GUI's one mirror is `TrustedStore.valid_plugin_id` (public precisely because it now has two consumers - the consent records keyed on the same id, and this notice), with `plugin_manifest.rs::valid_plugin_id` still authoritative.
- **`gpty plugin validate <path>`** runs the shipped parser on a plugin directory (or its `gpty-plugin.toml`): offline, `--json`-capable, exit 1 on rejection - the authoring loop, and what the five first-party plugin repos' CI now runs: each installs the CLI from the v0.5.5 commit (`cargo install --git … --rev 2f17459… --locked`; the SHA is the pin, a tag is mutable) and validates its checkout with it. Each repo also keeps its own one-line `id`-equals-repo assertion, because that is the *install gate's* contract (`check_gates`) - the validator cannot know which repo a manifest lives in.
- **The install review shows what a profile would run, and records it**: each summary `profiles` entry carries `programs` (the distinct launch lines, then `settings.command`/`settings.shell`/legacy `shell` programs its tiles name, capped) and the dialog prints them, so accepting a plugin is informed consent for the profiles `_profile_consented` later honors at the revision the install pinned. The same entries carry `plans` - the exact spawn-plan keys `PaneTypes.tile_plan_key` derives (a launch line keyed by itself behind U+FFFD; otherwise program precedence, then `shell_args`, joined with U+001F), computed by `plugin.rs::profile_plan_keys` from the same tiles the store will hold. `approve_plugin` records the union in `user://trusted.json` as `{revision, plans}`, and a profile whose tiles change under the same revision no longer matches its approved plans, so it re-prompts instead of inheriting the approval. A record written before plans existed (the bare `id -> revision` string) still loads as an approval that covers no plans, so such a plugin's profiles ask once more.
- **Registry (2026-09):** `godot-pty/gpty-plugins` is the canonical index - `registry.json` plus `validate.py` - and the docs site's `/plugins/` page renders it: fetched live at build time, with the snapshot committed at `docs/assets/registry.json` as the offline fallback (the shortcode warns in the build log when it falls back, so a silently-stale page is visible to a maintainer; `docs/data/` is generated by `setup.sh`, which is why the snapshot is an asset). An entry is a closed key set - `id` (`owner/repo`), `repo`, `name`, `description`, `category`, `min_gpty_version`, `platforms` - validated structurally and, with `--check-repos`, against every listed repo's `gpty-plugin.toml` at HEAD (the repo's workflow runs that on push, on PRs, and weekly, so a vanished or renamed repo is noticed). Policies live in that repo's README and must not weaken: an id is owned by its repo and immutable while the repo exists; `min_gpty_version` is a floor the registry *states*, never an install gate (the CLI's own check is the gate); removing an entry stops new installs only, because every install is pinned to a commit SHA. The registry is display data - nothing in it executes, and `gpty plugin install` never consults it.

Top invariable rules and invariants across the project. Read this card for fast lookup; detailed rationale and edge cases live in the dedicated topic guides.

## Architecture & Boundaries

- **L0–L2 Owned, L3/L4 Open Market:** gPTY owns the PTY foundation (L1) and public control surface (L2: JSON-RPC socket, CLI, MCP, events). Orchestration (L3) and agents (L4) are guests; core never absorbs orchestrator state machines or background runners.
- **Observe and Display, Never Orchestrate:** Core displays agent state (badges, status); it does not manage agent lifecycles or background blocks. Primitives only: `paneStatus`, `waitForOutput`, events.
- **Public API Boundary:** The MCP tool list is auto-generated from clap commands in `crates/gpty-cli/src/commands/schema.rs`. All agent verbs travel through documented tools and methods.
- **Display Name vs. Identifier:** UI and prose use `gPTY`. Machine identifiers stay lowercase: `gpty` binary, crate names, repo, socket paths, env vars (`GPTY_*`).

## Godot & GDScript Invariants

- **Single-Threaded SceneTree:** Godot's SceneTree is strictly single-threaded. Background Rust threads must NEVER call Godot methods or mutate nodes directly. Queue updates for GDScript polling or use `call_deferred()`.
- **No NUL in Strings:** Godot strings cannot hold `\u0000` (NUL is decoded as `\uFFFD` and triggers parser warnings at load). Never use NUL checks in GDScript; validate path and string terminators in Rust.
- **`TextEdit` Deferred Signals:** Programmatic assignment `text = ...` emits `text_set`, not `text_changed`. `text_changed` is emitted only by edits and is deferred by one frame (`call_deferred`). In tests, use simulated typing drivers rather than direct assignment.
- **Untyped Arrays Across FFI:** gdext `Array<Variant>` parameters reject typed GDScript arrays like `Array[Dictionary]` at runtime. Always pass untyped `Array` across the GDExtension boundary.
- **Geometry & Custom Minimum Size:** In Godot 4.7+, a container layout requires `custom_minimum_size`. A stylebox's content margins define its minimum dimensions; an empty track or all-zero box collapses sizing.
- **Escape Key & GUI Input:** In Godot 4.7.2, `_gui_input` is delivered exclusively to the focused control and does not bubble to ancestors. Intercept Escape at an input stage with focus checks rather than in container `_gui_input`.

## Rust & GDExtension Invariants

- **Short-Lived Grid Lock:** `TermGrid` is wrapped in `Arc<Mutex<TermGrid>>`. Acquire the lock briefly, extract or clone needed damage/cells, and drop the guard immediately. Never hold locks across blocking I/O or tokio yields.
- **Clean Teardown via `Drop`:** When a `GptyTerminal` is freed (`queue_free()`), Rust teardown must terminate spawned shells and cancel tokio tasks in `Drop` to prevent orphaned processes and zombie threads.
- **Tokio Runtime:** One process-wide `LazyLock` tokio runtime in `gpty-gdext` is shared across all terminal instances. Never instantiate ad-hoc tokio runtimes.
- **Blocking Operations on Worker Pools:** SQLite operations, vault index passes, and file reads must run on `spawn_blocking` or dedicated threads, never on the main GUI thread polling IPC.
- **No Unwinding Panics Across FFI:** Panics crossing the C/FFI boundary cause undefined behavior or process aborts. Catch errors in Rust and return structured error JSON or default values.

## Security, Logging & Ownership

- **Output Is Never Log Material:** Pane output, captured terminal buffers, injected/pasted text, environment values, and backend stderr are never logged above `debug`, and never written to disk by default. Enforced by `scripts/check-log-hygiene`.
- **Owner-Only Files (0700 / 0600):** Runtime directories and state files (`user://`, SQLite databases, sockets, scratch files) must be created and repaired to 0700 (directories) and 0600 (files). Enforced via `owner_only` helpers.
- **Regular File & Path Gates:** Any path read by the GUI or backend must be validated as an absolute, local, regular file (`fstat`/`is_file`, `O_NONBLOCK | O_NOFOLLOW`). FIFOs, special devices, and directory traversals are rejected before open.
- **Timing Invariance:** Authentication token checks (`GPTY_SECRET`) must compare bytes in constant time without early-exit branch leaks.

## Testing & CI Gates

- **Safe Fixture Paths:** Fixtures go through `TestPaths` only - `fresh_dir("name")` for a fixed-name directory (it clears the previous run's leftover first), `remove_tree(path)` for cleanup, and `is_safe_path_under(path, root, windows)` when a comparison is needed, because a raw prefix compare cannot agree on `C:\` from the environment and `C:/` after `path_join`. Never call `DirAccess.open("")` (which opens the project root).
- **Assertions Do Not Guard:** `assert_eq`/`assert_not_null` return void, so the next line runs even when they failed. Index or dereference only behind an explicit `return` (`if dialogs.is_empty(): return`, then `dialogs[0]`); never index a call's result in place - `scripts/check-test-guards` fails that shape (`_list_meta(pane)[0]`) and `gut-check` reports it as the test's failure rather than aborting the run.
- **Fast Local Gate:** Run `./scripts/ci-check --fast` before staging. It checks formatting (`cargo fmt`), workflow lint, docs validity (`scripts/docs-check`), clippy, GDExtension surface, log hygiene, theme tokens, and test guards.
- **Windowed vs. Headless:** Headless Godot runs have a 0×0 or 64×64 root viewport, no display driver, no hover states, and no tooltips. Layout, pixel-diff, and pointer tests must run headed or set viewport sizes explicitly.
- **No `--no-verify`:** Never bypass commit hooks (`git commit -n`) or push hooks without documenting an emergency justification in the commit body.

The roadmap is a prioritized queue split into one page per release chain under `docs/content/docs/roadmap/` (`v0.1.md` … `v1.0.md`, then `future.md`). `ROADMAP.md` is the root index, and `docs/content/docs/roadmap/_index.md` renders it on the site.

Detailed execution of roadmap tasks is guided by `skill://gpty-roadmap-task` (body at `.omp/skills/gpty-roadmap-task/SKILL.md`).

## Core Principles

- **The queue is the priority:** Within a release, row order *is* the priority, and the first unchecked row (⬜) in the earliest unfinished release is the answer to "what's next".
- **Release chain order:** Open chain pages in version order, take the first chain that still has a ⬜, and take the first ⬜ on that page. An earlier release with a leftover ⬜ always precedes a later one. Future is never picked from.
- **No separate grouping:** No grouping by origin or carry-over headings. Finished rows stay in place with evidence, and the changelog carries the user-facing release notes.

## Row Format

Every row is exactly one line in the release table:

```markdown
| ✅ or ⬜ | AREA | **Title** - evidence, fix, tests |
```

- **Status:** `⬜` for open, `✅` for completed.
- **Area:** Exactly one of `TERM`, `GUI`, `IPC`, `CLI`, `SEC`, `PLUGIN`, `WIKI`, `CONCEPT`, `MEDIA`, `AGENT`, `CORE`, `BUILD`, `DOCS`, `PROJECT`.
- **Title:** Unique across all release chains in bold (`**Title**`), followed by ` - ` and the actionable description.
- **Escapes:** Escape literal pipes in cells as `\|`, and enclose `<` inside backticks to prevent raw HTML stripping.

## Priority Ordering Rules

When adding or re-prioritizing rows, follow this strict precedence:

1. **Data-loss and correctness:** Bugs causing data corruption, accidental deletion, or broken core behavior.
2. **Security with reachable path:** Exploitable or exposed security defects.
3. **Release headline features:** The primary differentiating features scoped for the release.
4. **Robustness and automated tests:** Flake fixes, test coverage, race elimination.
5. **Low-reachability hardening:** Defense-in-depth and static verifications.
6. **Polish and aesthetics:** Visual consistency, theme alignment, copy improvements.
7. **Release-time tasks:** Packaging, tagging, and deployment verification.

Ties break toward the smaller item.

## Defect and Follow-up Tracking

- **No silent fixes:** A defect or follow-up discovered while working on a task is never fixed silently, queued in a comment, or folded into an unrelated commit.
- **Add to queue:** Add it as its own row in the appropriate release in priority position, with the evidence that makes it actionable (failure observation, code location, proposed fix).
- **Folded details:** If a triage note, correction, or clarification exists for a row, update that row's text directly rather than adding a separate "corrections" row.

## Evidence Screenshots

Images in `docs/static/images/` follow specific naming conventions:

- **Release screenshots:** Named `v<version>_<n>.png` (generated by `scripts/screenshot-gpty`).
- **Roadmap evidence:** Named `issue-v<build>-<slug>.png` (`<build>` is the build version where the capture was made).
- **Placement:** Never embed an image inside a table row. Place screenshots under a `## Screenshots` section at the bottom of the chain page with a bold caption explaining numbered callouts, and reference the caption from the row.

## Closing a Row

1. Flip `⬜` to `✅` in place.
2. Update the row text to describe what shipped, concrete measured metrics, and passing regression test names.
3. If the row closed a bug, ensure the commit carries a `Cause: <class>` trailer matching [Defect classes](gpty-doc:docs/content/docs/agents/defect-classes.md).
4. Run `python3 scripts/docs-check` and `./scripts/build-docs` to ensure synchronization.

## Adding a Release Chain

1. Create `docs/content/docs/roadmap/<slug>.md` with front matter (`title`, `weight` incremented from previous chain).
2. Add a brief paragraph summarizing what the release chain achieves.
3. Add `## vX.Y.Z - Name` sections with three-column tables.
4. Link the new chain page from `ROADMAP.md` as `docs/content/docs/roadmap/<slug>.md`.

- Edition: 2024 (requires Rust ≥ 1.85)
- Format: standard `rustfmt`
- Async runtime: `tokio` (one global `LazyLock` runtime in gdext, initialised once and shared by every `GptyTerminal`)
- Grid sharing: `Arc<Mutex<TermGrid>>` - lock briefly, clone the grid, release
- Thread Safety: Godot's SceneTree is strictly single-threaded. NEVER call Godot methods, mutate nodes, or emit signals directly from background `tokio` threads. Instead, queue the state changes for GDScript to poll, or use Godot's thread-safe `call_deferred()`.
- Lifecycle & Teardown: When a `GptyTerminal` is destroyed (e.g., `queue_free()` in Godot), the Rust side MUST ensure the spawned shell and background `tokio` tasks are cleanly terminated (via the `Drop` trait) to prevent zombie processes or memory leaks.
- State directory creation: `gpty_ipc::transport::state_dir()` creates its directory on both arms. The Unix `private_state_dir` always did; the Windows `local_app_data()` now creates `%LOCALAPPDATA%\gpty` on first use too. This is the contract stores rely on - `vaults.db` (`VaultStore::open`), the recovery copies and the plugin store open files inside it without creating the parent - and a fresh Windows profile used to fail the wiki index with `unable to open database file` until the smoke's seeded plugin record happened to create the directory. Do not move the creation into individual stores, and keep the Windows arm equal to the Unix one (a test pins `local_app_dir`'s creation on every platform).
- Vault index: `gpty_core::vault` is the wiki pane's note store - one SQLite FTS5 file at `state_dir()/vaults.db`, reached from GDScript only through the *static* `GptyTerminal.vault_index`/`vault_search` (they answer about a directory, not a terminal, so a pane needs no grid). Its walk (`scan_vault`) is the single definition of what a note is, and `MAX_NOTES` (2000) / `MAX_DEPTH` (16) / `MAX_NOTE_BYTES` (1 MiB) live there so the pane's list and the index cannot disagree - the pane must not grow a second copy of those rules. It reuses the scrollback store's skeleton deliberately: the same pragmas, the same `user_version` gate pattern (its own counter, now at 2 - the bump rebuilds the derived tables rather than migrating them), external-content FTS5 with the three triggers, `store::restrict_to_owner` on the db and its `-wal`/`-shm` siblings, and the process-wide `store::write_guard` held innermost across one transaction - with a `(vault_id, rel_path)` key and `porter unicode61`, because notes are prose ("running" matching "run") where terminal lines are not. A pass re-reads only notes whose mtime (nanoseconds; seconds would miss a same-second same-size edit) or size changed, drops rows for vanished notes, prunes rows whose vault root is no longer a directory, and **never prunes from a truncated walk** - the notes it did not reach would be deleted. Bodies are cut at `MAX_NOTE_BYTES` with the torn UTF-8 tail dropped, the same cut `TextRead` makes on the display path, so a hit can never name text the view does not show. Both FFI functions return JSON with `error` present only when the query could not run, so "no match" stays distinguishable from "not indexed". `VaultStore::open` is `store::open_with_recovery`, so an index SQLite cannot read moves to `vaults.db.corrupt` and the next pass rebuilds it.

- A note's **label** - the `title` a `vault_search` hit shows and `notes_fts` ranks by (`title, body`) - is `note_title`: the first heading *past* a leading, closed YAML frontmatter block (`---`…`---`/`...`, the shape Obsidian writes its properties as), else the file stem. The block never becomes the label (without the skip its opening `---` was the body's first non-empty line and every such note was named by its stem), an unterminated `---` is not frontmatter so the scan behaves exactly as before, and **no `title:` key is read** - that is a properties-UI decision, not a label rule. The block's text stays in the indexed body: it is ordinary visible Markdown (the renderer shows it), so a property value remains searchable.
- Wikilinks (`gpty_core::links`, the `links` table, `GptyTerminal.vault_links`): `[[target]]` occurrences are parsed **in the index pass** - the pass already reads every changed body, so the parse is free, sits in the same transaction as the note row, and cannot drift from the text the FTS index holds. One row per **occurrence** (`links(vault_id, src, seq, line, target, resolved)`, primary key `(vault_id, src, seq)`, indexed on `(vault_id, resolved)`), because a backlink is not syntax: it is the same edge read in reverse (`WHERE resolved = …`), so nothing is authored twice and the per-mention line is what the panel lists. A fenced block, an inline code span or a backslash-escaped opener is literal text (a note documenting the syntax must not create edges); the caps are 512 occurrences per note and 1024 bytes per target; and `alias`/`fragment` are parsed but **never stored** - the edge is to the note, and a fragment is navigation: `links_for` re-parses the note body it already holds and attaches each occurrence's fragment by `seq` (the pane half below follows it). Resolution (settled - do not re-derive it elsewhere): a target containing `/` names a path (`note` matches `note.md`), a bare target names a file stem; exact case first, then a *unique* case-insensitive match; more than one match at either stage is **ambiguous** and is never silently picked. `resolved` is a *derived* column, maintained in exactly two places: `upsert_batch` rewrites a row's edges (resolving against the note set *after* its own inserts, so a batch that adds a stub and its linker settles both ways), and `reresolve_links` re-derives the whole vault when the note set actually moved (`added`/`removed`) - a stub that appears resolves its linkers, a vanished target loses its resolution, a stem that is now shared stops resolving; an ordinary pass writes nothing. A removed note's rows are deleted with it, and `clear_vault`/`prune_dead_vaults` drop a vault's links. The `user_version=2` bump **rebuilds** the derived tables instead of migrating them (a v1 store's notes were never link-parsed; the next pass re-reads the vault), and ambiguous *candidates* are derived at query time from the same rules rather than stored - no column for a list, and the answer cannot disagree with `resolved` because both come from one note set. Nothing here executes: a link is an edge, never an action.

  **The pane half (2026-10):** `Link` carries the occurrence's byte span (`start`/`end`), and the Markdown renderer's mention pass is the *same* parser, so what the preview links and what the index stores cannot disagree - a fenced block, a code span and an escaped opener are literal in both. `GptyMarkdown.render(text, wikilinks)` replaces each accepted occurrence with an opaque sentinel before Markdown parsing (emphasis, headings and tables around it are untouched, and the label is never re-parsed), then substitutes `[url=gpty-note:<percent-encoded target>[#<percent-encoded fragment>]]label[/url]` in the finished BBCode; the target and the fragment are each encoded so a space or `]` cannot end the tag, and the one literal `#` is the only separator (a `#` inside either part is percent-encoded). A mention written inside a Markdown link's label (or an image's alt text) **yields to its container** and renders as plain label text: nested `[url]` tags leave the click target undefined, and the outer link is what the author explicitly wrote. The flag is off for every non-wiki caller (`MarkdownView.wikilinks_enabled`; Inspector, Reasoning and code previews keep literal `[[…]]`), and only this renderer can emit the scheme (`safe_url` still admits just http/https/mailto, so a document's own Markdown link cannot impersonate a mention). The About page's `gpty-doc:` scheme is the second opt-in mode: `scripts/build-docs` rewrites a link between two bundled documents to `gpty-doc:<repo path>#<heading text>`, the renderer percent-encodes the path and fragment halves separately under `MarkdownView.doc_links_enabled` (a 1024-byte cap on the payload), and `DocsViewer` resolves the decoded path against `DocsBundle`'s key map - a path is never joined to the filesystem, and a document the build did not bundle is refused. `MarkdownView` never opens it: it emits `note_link_clicked(target, fragment)` (both percent-decoded) and the owning pane decides. Following resolves through `GptyTerminal.vault_link_resolve` → `VaultStore::resolve_target`, which runs the index's own `NoteIndex` over the index's note set (`note_paths`, now shared with `links_for`/`reresolve_links`) rather than a second GDScript rule - so an ambiguous stem answers with its candidates and is never picked, and a mention typed but not yet saved resolves too, because resolution needs the note set rather than the source note's stored rows. The wiki pane's link panel (`Links to` / `Linked from`) shows one row per occurrence with its line, an unresolved row names the target (with the candidates when ambiguous) and is not clickable, and a resolved/backlink row follows **in place** through `_request_leave` (Save/Discard/Cancel; no history stack in v1 - the notes list is the escape). A resolved outgoing row lands on the heading its mention named (`fragment`, re-derived by `links_for` from the stored body - the table still stores no fragment) and a backlink row opens the linking note at the mention's line; a mention into the note already open replaces nothing and only moves the view, so it asks nothing. The landing is derived in two steps: `MarkdownAnchors` scans the **source** for ATX headings (leading frontmatter and fenced blocks skipped) to answer which heading a fragment - exact text first, then case-insensitive - or a source line (its nearest heading above) means, and `MarkdownView.scroll_to_heading` finds that heading line in the *rendered* parsed text, because `RichTextLabel.scroll_to_line` counts rendered lines while the index counts source lines. The preview scroll is queued for one frame (the label has no visual lines before its layout pass; `get_character_line` is -1, measured on 4.7.2), and the view skips an identical re-render - the editor's settled render 0.4 s after a note opens would otherwise reset the scroll - while an actual render cancels a pending scroll. Edit mode scrolls the source by line directly. A fragment the note does not contain still opens the note and is reported; a line with no heading above it lands at the top, which is its nearest derived position. The panel is rebuilt when a note opens and again after a save's re-index, and is capped at `MAX_LINK_ROWS` (50) per section with the remainder counted, because the parser admits 512 occurrences and backlinks are unbounded. A click is a read: resolution answers a vault-relative note and `_open_note` loads it through `vault_note_read`, with the editor's containment, cap and regular-file gates unchanged.

- Link graph canvas (`GptyTerminal.vault_graph` → `VaultStore::graph` → `VaultGraphModel` → `VaultGraphView`): the wiki pane's **Graph** view draws the vault's own link structure - no new file type, no second store, and nothing written. The store answers `{"nodes", "edges", "truncated"}` from `vaults.db`: every indexed note (labelled by `title`), a `ghost:<target>` node per distinct unresolved target, and one aggregated row per ordered `(src, resolved)` pair with its `COUNT(*)` of mentions (then the unresolved `(src, target)` rows), deterministically ordered (count DESC, then src/dst; notes by path, ghosts by target). `MAX_GRAPH_EDGES` (10k per class) and `MAX_GRAPH_GHOSTS` (2k) set `truncated` instead of drawing part of a vault as if it were all of it, and `graph_limited` is the test seam for the caps (the `scan_vault_limited` pattern). The pane queries it when the Graph button is pressed - every mutation (save/create/rename/delete/link rewrite) already re-indexes - and `VaultGraphModel` (pure, unit-tested) normalizes the answer: self-references are dropped (the panel lists them), the two directions of a pair become one edge carrying `ab`/`ba`/`mutual`, stroke width and layout springs are *logarithmic and clamped* (`EDGE_MIN_WIDTH`..`EDGE_MAX_WIDTH`, `MAX_SPRING`) so one hub cannot drown the drawing or collapse the graph, and the layout is deterministic (sunflower seed + FNV-1a jitter, never `hash()`; a size-bounded Fruchterman–Reingold relaxation with grid-approximated repulsion, because the walk's 2000 notes make all-pairs repulsion 4M pairs per sweep). `VaultGraphView` is one custom-drawn `Control`, not a `GraphEdit` of node controls (the 2000-note ceiling is where that renderer stops being right): pan/zoom/drag are session geometry that a re-query preserves (only unseen ids are placed, near a neighbour; **Relayout** discards every drag for the deterministic arrangement), off-screen nodes/edges are culled, labels appear for all nodes only above `LABEL_ZOOM` (hovered/selected always), arrows are an optional toggle with mutual pairs drawn double-headed, and ghosts are outline circles. A node click opens the note through the same leave guard as the list; a ghost click runs the preview's own `_follow_target` (missing → create-from-link, ambiguous → report - never a guess). Display-only: nothing in the canvas reads a path the index did not name or writes anything.
- Declared edge weights (`LinkWeights`, `LinkWeightsStore`, `vaultWeight`): the link graph's authored layer. Measured weight is `COUNT(*)` mentions, a crude proxy - two notes can be deeply related and mention each other once, or name-drop ten times and share nothing - so the user (a right-click **Set/Clear declared weight** control on an edge) or an agent (`gpty vault weight <vault> <src> <target> --weight N` / `--clear`; MCP `vault-weight`) may state one number that overrides it **for display**. Rules, settled 2026-10: (1) **never in `vaults.db`** - that store is a derived cache a schema bump rebuilds, and authored work must survive a rebuild; the map is user-owned (`user://link_weights.json`, `{"vaults": {<absolute root>: {src: {target: weight}}}}`, the `PaneEnvStore`/`TrustedStore` shape: typed reads, capped at `MAX_VAULTS` 32 / `MAX_ENTRIES` 1024 per vault and weight 1–100, atomic temp+rename 0600). (2) **Display-only, absolutely**: `VaultGraphModel.apply_weights` sets `declared` and `weight` on the parsed edge and never touches `count`; thickness, the layout spring and link-panel order read `weight`, while the drawn edge set, navigation, writes and every trust decision read only the index - an authored weight can never hide an edge, create one, gate a click, trigger a write or count as consent (the Tier 2 declaration rule). (3) **Pair-shaped write, directed keys**: the canvas draws one edge per note pair, so its control writes both directions of `(src, target)` (`set_pair`/`clear_pair`); the IPC verb writes exactly one directed pair; the model takes the larger of a pair's two declarations. (4) **Pruned lazily, never on a truncated answer**: showing an untruncated graph drops declarations whose endpoint is no longer an indexed note; a truncated answer must not, because the notes it does not name are still real. An **in-app rename re-keys both endpoints** (`LinkWeightsStore.rekey_note`, one write, run by the pane immediately after the verb succeeds and independent of the optional mention rewrite) before any complete graph can prune the old name, so the curation follows the file; a stale destination row (a rename requires that note to be absent) merges with the moved row, and the moved declaration wins the shared targets. An *outside* move is indistinguishable from a delete to the index and still prunes (queued in Future) - the prune is the only thing that bounds the file. (5) The GUI answers `vaultWeight` (the store is `user://`, which the CLI cannot resolve), so the agent verb needs a running GUI and never auto-spawns one.
- Note editing (`vault_note_read` / `vault_note_write`): the wiki pane's editor reads and writes one note through the same module, so the vocabulary keeps one owner. `read_vault_note` reuses the index's cut (`read_file_capped`), refuses any path the walk could not have produced (relative, no hidden component at any level, `.md` last), and requires a regular file - a FIFO planted in a vault must not reach `File::open`, which would block the GUI thread the FFI runs on. It answers the file's CRLF shape and a **note stamp** - mtime in **microseconds**, not the index's nanoseconds, because the stamp round-trips through JSON, whose numbers are doubles (1.7e18 ns loses its low bits there; 1.8e15 µs is exact) - plus size. `write_vault_note` edits an *existing* note and never creates one: the path goes through the same vocabulary, the canonicalized result must stay under the canonical vault root (so a note symlinked inside the vault is written through and one pointing outside is refused), the content is capped at `MAX_NOTE_BYTES`, and a stamp that differs from the one the caller loaded is refused with `NoteError::ChangedOnDisk` (`code: changed_on_disk`) unless the caller forces it. The replacement is a hidden sibling temp file (random name via `temp_suffix`, never a fixed one) renamed over the target, which keeps the note's own mode - the temp file is created with the process umask, and a vault may be shared - and cannot truncate a file it fails to rewrite. `vault_note_write` re-indexes the vault before answering (`indexed: false` when the save landed but the index could not), because the file is the index's source of truth and a caller must not have to remember a second call. Only `Outside` and `Io` failures are logged: a bad path or a stale stamp is a refusal the caller asked about, and the pane reports it through its toast or overwrite dialog.

  **Creating, renaming, and deleting (2026-10):** the editor's other file verbs live in the same module and are held to the same vocabulary - a vault-relative `.md` path with no hidden component - with three distinctions that matter. (1) They act on the vault **entry**, never through it: a symlinked note is unlinked (delete) or moved as a link (rename), and its target stays where it is, because deleting must not reach a file the vault does not contain; reads and writes keep following links, with the `Outside` refusal. (2) Creation and the rename destination must have a directory that already exists **and canonicalizes inside the vault** - creating through a directory symlinked out of the vault would write outside - and never make directories. (3) A create or rename **claims** the destination with `create_new` before anything else (`rename` then replaces only its own claim, and removes it if the rename fails), so an existing note, symlink or directory answers `NoteError::Exists` (`code: exists`): there is no overwrite path and no check-then-write race. A rename preserves the file's mtime/size (the caller's stamp stays valid) and re-indexes like a save, so `removed`+`added` re-derive the link table - links by the old stem stop resolving, links by path follow it. The pane wires these to the list/toolbar: New note (default `Untitled.md`, a bare name gains `.md`, a collision re-opens the same question with the typed text), Rename and Delete on the open note (delete is a confirmation that also says unsaved work will be lost), and **create-from-link** for an unresolved mention or panel row - missing only, never an ambiguous stem, which stays a report. A dirty buffer's recovery copy is re-keyed on rename and dropped on a confirmed delete; `_has_open_ask` counts only *visible* dialogs (an answered one is hidden before its action runs), because the create-from-link question's success may open the leave question for the note being edited. A rename also offers the reference update as **its own step** (`GptyTerminal.vault_link_rewrite_preview` then `vault_link_rewrite`; core `preview_link_rewrite`/`rewrite_links_after_rename`): the rename makes mentions of the old stem/path unresolved, so the pane asks - with the count - before any other note is written, and only the occurrences that resolved to the old name *before* the move are respelled (alias and `#` fragment preserved, CRLF kept, fenced code and code spans untouched because the parser defines what a link is). The note at its new path is a candidate only when its buffer is clean: the pane passes that state as `include_renamed` (the preview and the apply take the same flag, so the question's counts are what can land), a dirty buffer passes false and is never written under, and the apply answers `renamed_note` - the text that landed plus its fresh stamp - so the editor adopts both in place rather than re-reading (a save right after therefore does not see a stale stamp). A new name a link cannot spell (`[`, `]`, `|`, `#` or a control character would be re-read as syntax, and a control character breaks the line-oriented parse) refuses the whole pass rather than writing a broken mention; a note over the read cap is skipped rather than written back as a prefix. The write goes through `write_vault_note` and the apply re-plans in the same call, so an edit made while the question was open is read fresh and only a note that changes between that plan and its write answers `changed_on_disk` (counted as skipped); the apply re-indexes, so the new backlinks appear at once.
- Note recovery copies (`vault_scratch_read` / `vault_scratch_write` / `vault_scratch_clear`, `gpty_core::vault::write_scratch`/`read_scratch`/`clear_scratch`): the buffer lives in RAM and `write_vault_note` runs only on explicit save, so a crash or an outside kill takes every unsaved edit - these three statics are the other half, a snapshot of the dirty buffer kept **outside the vault** and offered back when the same note is reopened. The layout is `state_dir()/scratch/<fnv1a64(canonical root, NUL, rel path)>.json`, written atomically (hidden random temp + rename) with the directory at 0700 and the file at 0600, FNV-1a spelled out locally rather than `DefaultHasher` (whose algorithm Rust does not promise across releases - a toolchain bump would orphan every copy). The record repeats the identity it was written for (`vault`, `path`, `mtime`, `size`, `text`), and a read that does not match answers *absent* - a stale file, a collision, or an unparseable record can never restore the wrong text - as does an unreadable one, since an absent copy is the normal state and no scratch failure is toasted (the pane cannot offer a copy that was never written, the buffer is on screen, and its own save reports what a full disk means). `scratch_error` logs under the rule `note_failure_is_diagnostic` already defines - only the failures nobody asked for - because a refusal a caller requested on purpose must stay quiet: GUT counts an engine error as a failure, and the wire test asks for `bad_path` deliberately. The copy's `text` is the editor's **LF buffer space** - the same space `_saved_text` is normalized into, or a CRLF note would open already dirty, write a copy of its own file, and offer it back as an edit nobody made - and its `mtime`/`size` are the stamp the buffer was *loaded* from, so a restore after the file moved on still hits `changed_on_disk` and the pane's overwrite dialog instead of silently overwriting. The pane's write is a **throttle** (`SCRATCH_DEBOUNCE`, armed by the first dirty edit and not restarted per keystroke: a restarted debounce never fires during a long typing run, which is exactly when the most work is at risk), and every *deliberate* end drops the copy - a save, the Discard answer of the close ask, and the vault change the settings panel performs without a dialog (keyed to the vault the buffer belonged to). A restore is never automatic (a `RestoreConfirm` dialog: Restore / Discard / Escape = not now), is refused while the note is read-only (a restored buffer could not be saved and the close guard would not see it as unsaved work, so the offer would be a promise the pane cannot keep - the copy is kept instead), and joins `_has_open_ask` so it cannot stack on another ask. Nothing on this recovery path touches a vault: a save or a file verb (`_create_note`/`_rename_note`/`_delete_open_note`) is the pane's only note write, and a copy is never one. The copy shares `MAX_NOTE_BYTES` with the note it copies, so a buffer past that cap gets no copy - `write_vault_note` refuses its save by the same limit, and the two must not disagree about what can be written back. **A prune rides every write** (`prune_scratch`, the first thing `write_scratch` does - the 1.5 s throttle is the only writer, so it is a few short directory listings a minute at most, and running it before the copy is located means even a write refused for a vault that is no longer a directory tidies the directory): a copy is dropped only when its own record names a vault that is **definitively** gone - the path is absent, or exists as something that is not a directory - because anything else (a permission error, an unmounted network path, an I/O error) cannot say the vault is gone and a vault that is merely hard to reach must keep its copies. A copy whose *note* is missing is kept too: nothing on this path walks a vault, so a note that merely was not listed (a truncated walk) can never cost the work this feature exists to keep, and a deletion needs a record that says "unreachable" - never one the code could not read, parse, or find a vault in, and never a name the module did not build. Stale `.gpty-scratch-*.tmp` remains of a write that died mid-rename are reclaimed on the same pass once older than an hour (a live temp lives microseconds, so no writer can lose one to the age check). Every prune failure is a diagnostic - housekeeping never fails the write it rides on.

- **The vault's public API is native IPC, not a pane** (`vaultSearch` / `vaultRead`, `crates/gpty-gdext/src/vault_ipc.rs`): `gpty vault search <vault> <pattern>` and `gpty vault read <vault> <path>` (MCP `vault-search` / `vault-read`) expose the knowledge base to agents through the same control socket as every other primitive. Both are answered in Rust, registered in `ipc.rs` beside `version`/`shutdown`, because a vault is a directory rather than workspace state - there is nothing for `WorkspaceIpcHandlers` to consult - and the walk plus SQLite must run on the blocking pool (`spawn_blocking`), not on the GUI thread that polls `drain_ipc_requests`. **Search re-indexes before it queries** (`index_vault`: changed notes only, bounded by `MAX_NOTES`/`MAX_DEPTH`; its `truncated` flag rides in the answer), so a note edited outside gPTY - by Obsidian, an editor, another agent - is searchable without any pane reopening the vault; the cost is one stat walk per query, not a write. **Read is a read**: `read_vault_note` supplies the path vocabulary, the regular-file gate and the 1 MiB cut, and neither method writes to the vault. Errors are JSON-RPC: `-32602` for a malformed request (missing param, non-absolute or non-directory vault) and `-32000` with `NoteError::code()` in `data.code` for a refusal, so a client can tell `not_found` from `bad_path` without parsing prose. No vault command auto-spawns a GUI (`may_autospawn` returns false, the v0.5.6 rule): search and read are queries, and the weight write needs the GUI's store but still refuses to create one. `vaultWeight` is the one vault method that is **not** native: its store is the user's `user://link_weights.json`, which only the GUI can resolve, so it is registered in `gdscript_methods` and answered by `WorkspaceIpcHandlers` (display-only; it writes that store and nothing else). The two handlers answer only for a root in the user's registered list: `VaultRegistry` (`user://vaults.json`, written only by the pane settings UI) pushes its canonical roots into `vault_api.rs`'s mirror, and `vault_root()` refuses anything else with `-32000` plus `data.code = "not_registered"` before a walk starts - the root is the caller's choice, and the file-read reach it would grant is the user's to make. `vaultWeight` (GDScript) consults the same store before writing.

- Media backend (`gpty-media`, v0.7.0): the only crate that links FFmpeg. `scripts/media-deps` downloads the SHA256-pinned FFmpeg 9.0.2 tarball and builds the LGPLv3 **shared** library set from `crates/gpty-media/components.txt` (`--disable-everything --disable-network`, decoders/demuxers/parsers only); Windows uses vcpkg. `components.txt` is the single component policy, and `tests/build_recipe.rs` checks it against the runtime `ALLOWED_*` lists in both directions - adding a format means editing that file, not a second list. Every job that compiles or loads the GDExtension needs the prefix (`./scripts/media-deps` appends the env in Actions); local `ci-check` sources `dist/ffmpeg/<platform>-<arch>/env.sh`.
  - Trust boundary: `validate_path` is applied in Rust as well as GDScript (absolute, local, **regular file**), and the file FFmpeg reads is one `source::MediaFile` opened: `O_NONBLOCK | O_NOFOLLOW`, verified by `fstat` on that descriptor, then wrapped in a custom `AVIOContext` (read + seek callbacks, `AVFMT_FLAG_CUSTOM_IO`) so FFmpeg never opens a path. A name swapped for a FIFO/device between the stat and the open would otherwise block `open(2)` - which no interrupt callback can break - and redirect the session. A symlink to a regular file is still playable: the link is resolved once and its target opened under the same flags. The open/probe deadline closure is owned by that module and freed with the context, never leaked; the demuxer allowlist is checked after open (`input.format().name()` reports an alias list, e.g. `mov,mp4,m4a,3gp,3g2,mj2`, so any alias must match), and the selected stream's codec is checked by *codec id* (`Id::name()`, stable) rather than the implementation name (`libdav1d` for `av1`). Attached-picture video streams (cover art) are skipped, not treated as video tracks. Caps: `MAX_STREAMS` 16, `MAX_VIDEO_DIMENSION` 4096, `MAX_FRAME_BYTES` 34 MiB, `MAX_CHANNELS` 8, `OPEN_TIMEOUT_MS` 10 000 (an interrupt callback, cleared once open succeeds), `CLOSE_TIMEOUT_MS` 2 000 (the join bound: a worker still inside a decoder call past it cannot read `stop`, so it is detached with its FFmpeg contexts and frees them itself if the call returns).
  - Decode model: one `std::thread` per session - never the Godot thread and never the two-worker tokio runtime. Bounded queues (`VIDEO_QUEUE_FRAMES` 2, `AUDIO_QUEUE_CHUNKS` 16) provide backpressure; `send_bounded` waits on a full queue while checking `stop`, so a pane that stops polling cannot deadlock close. `poll_video`/`poll_audio` are non-blocking. `seek` does **not** wait for the worker: it claims a serial, queues the command and returns, because a decoder stuck inside a libavcodec call would otherwise hold the Godot thread for the whole deadline (5 s, once per slider step). The worker publishes that serial as the applied epoch, and `poll_*` delivers nothing while the caller's serial is ahead of it - it still *drains*, since the worker blocks on a full output queue and only reaches its command check once there is room, so returning early would deadlock the two; frames carry the epoch they were queued under, and `poll_*` discards older ones. Per-stream cursors drop frames decoded from the keyframe *before* the target. The worker stays alive after EOF so a seek/replay can restart it (`Finished` is not a death).
  - Binding rules (asserted by `tests/binding_rules.rs`): never use `Input::packets()` (its iterator's `mem::transmute_copy` relies on `repr(Rust)` field order), container metadata (not necessarily UTF-8), frame dimension setters, `sample::Buffer`, filters or subtitles. Packets are read with `Packet::read` and resolved by stream index. `ffmpeg-the-third` is pinned; the facade keeps the binding replaceable.
  - Output: video is tightly packed RGBA8 (`width * height * 4`) from `swscale` with row-stride repacking; audio is interleaved f32 from `swresample` at the caller's rate/channels, accumulated into ~2048-frame chunks. PTS are microseconds. `GptyMedia` returns one frame/chunk per call as `Dictionary` + `PackedByteArray`/`PackedFloat32Array` (empty dictionary = nothing queued); `GString` inputs are JSON.
  - Licensing: the FFmpeg build is LGPLv3 (`--enable-version3`, **no** `--enable-gpl`) and dynamically linked; ship its license texts with release artifacts. The build is a media attack surface: no sandboxing claim, no hardware decode yet, no network protocols compiled in.

Policy (threat model, supported versions, reporting, what gpty does not defend against) lives in [SECURITY.md](gpty-doc:SECURITY.md). The rules below are implementation constraints for this repo.

- No concept execution path: a concept is data (trigger, stop condition, routing target). Never add a field, label match, or click handler that makes a concept write to a PTY - the trigger runs against untrusted terminal output, so that would be remote-triggered execution with no consent step. See the concept bullets above.
- Concept Engine ReDoS: The `gpty-core` crate MUST always use the standard Rust `regex` crate. PCRE or back-tracking engines are strictly prohibited to prevent ReDoS (Regex Denial of Service) attacks when parsing large amounts of terminal output.
- OSC 52 Clipboard Syncing: `parser.rs` implements no clipboard sequence - `osc_dispatch` reads only the whitelisted `gpty_state` declaration and strips every other OSC payload, a title included - which keeps copy/paste bound to Godot UI inputs. Do NOT implement OSC 52 clipboard injection/syncing without placing it behind an explicit Godot confirmation dialog to prevent drive-by clipboard hijacking.
- Pasted text (v0.7.1): the clipboard is untrusted - any web page can set it - so `TerminalPane.build_paste_payload` runs ONE filter (`_paste_text`) on both branches and wraps only what survives: C0 controls other than newline and tab, plus DEL, are dropped. Never send the text to the PTY untouched on the bracketed branch (DECSET 2004) either: `ESC[201~` inside the text closes the paste, and everything after it - a newline included - arrives as typed input, the "pastejacking" shape. Dropping ESC also keeps the sequences a bracketed application would interpret out of the paste. The v0.9.0 file-drop and link paths insert through this same function rather than writing to the PTY themselves. A second filter copy is how the two branches drift back apart - add cases to `godot/tests/unit/test_paste_payload.gd`, not a new helper.
- Restore vs. user intent: `PaneTypes.tile_spawns_untrusted(td, default_program)` is the Workspace Trust predicate - program (`command` > `shell`) and non-empty `shell_args` count as a new decision. Env is not a file decision: restore strips a tile's `shell_env` (with a toast naming what was dropped) before it can reach a spawn, and per-pane env comes only from `PaneEnvStore` (`user://pane_env.json`, keyed by `attachment_id`, written only by the pane settings UI), overlaid on the user's global env at spawn. The Inspector's `system_prompt`, `auto_run` and `accept_concept_captures` follow the same rule through a second user-owned store (`PaneInspectorStore`, `user://pane_inspector.json`, the same id-keyed lifecycle): the settings table refuses them from files, the pane panel is the only writer, and `PaneBody.apply_user_state` overlays the record at attach, after the id is final, for every pane-entry route. Every restore path must consult the predicate: the sidebar profile-activation and workspace-restore paths show the dialog, and `profileLoad` over IPC **refuses** an untrusted profile, because a caller cannot answer a dialog and naming a profile is not consent to what the file asks for. Never compare a different key than the spawn path consumes. The consent memory (`TrustedStore`, `user://trusted.json`) applies on top of the predicate and is the only thing that short-circuits it: a shipped builtin approved at this app version, or a tile whose exact spawn plan (`PaneTypes.tile_plan_key(td, cwd)` - the same program+argv derivation) an approval covers, skips the dialog; a plugin approval (id + pinned revision + the plans the review listed, written when the install review is accepted) is what covers that plugin's own profiles - `_profile_consented` decides by the loader's `_origin` stamp (see the provenance bullet below), so an approved revision whose recorded plans cover the tiles activates without re-asking, while a newer revision re-prompts and so do different tiles under the same revision; a new version/revision re-prompts, and content that arrived any other way (user-authored profiles, layout files) never records consent and keeps asking. Only the trust dialogs' confirm paths write the record (builtin approval from the profile dialog, plugin approval from the install review); nothing else may write it, and `_profile_consented`/`_tiles_untrusted_without_consent` must consult nothing but the predicate and the record. Do NOT exempt built-ins from the gate outright - first approval stays explicit; the record is what makes later activations smooth. A tile's `launch` line (v0.8.4) is the one shell text a profile may ship: one line, ≤1024 characters, no control characters, passed verbatim - no variable expansion, templating or profile-global command - and expanded through the user's *configured* shell (`PaneTypes.spawn_argv` -> `shell_run_args`, `/c` for `cmd.exe`) at `TerminalPane._start_child_if_ready`, the only `start_shell` call site. It is always untrusted, so a launch tile always asks; its plan key is U+FFFD + the line (U+FFFD is refused by every sanitizer, so no program or argv can forge a launch key) and deliberately carries no runner - the shell is the user's own setting, not the file's, and the install review runs before any shell could be known, so the GUI and the CLI must derive the same key without it.
- Workspace directory (v0.7.1): `workspaces.json` supplies each workspace's `cwd`, which every terminal in it receives, so the directory joins the trust decision exactly where the plan is already untrusted. `Workspace._spawn_cwd` returns the workspace's sanitized directory only when it is usable and `""` otherwise — no configured directory, so a relative or stale store value cannot alias an approval; both child backends then resolve `""` to the user's home in `PaneCwdStore.resolve`, one answer for the terminal and the `cli_view` — and the plan key appends it after U+001E (`sanitize_cwd` refuses control bytes, so the last U+001E always opens the directory and an argv ending in an absolute path cannot be read as one). Both restore gates pass it: `_init_workspaces` per entry, `_profile_consented` for the active workspace (a profile opened in a new workspace inherits that directory), while the plugin branch of `_profile_consented` stays program+argv because the install review runs before any workspace exists and a plugin is arbitrary code either way. `_remember_profile_consent` records the directory-qualified key the dialog showed. The folder picker (`_set_workspace_cwd`) asks when `_tiles_untrusted_without_consent(tiles, new_dir)` refuses — an untrusted workspace — and changes silently for one whose tiles all run the default shell. A tile, profile or plugin cannot carry a directory (`workspace_cwd`/`cwd`/`pane_cwd` are not file-settable pane settings; the workspace owns the default and the pane's own override is the user's).
