That override is `PaneCwdStore` (`user://pane_cwd.json`, key `ws-<12 hex>/<attachment id>`): written only by the pane settings UI, and unreachable from a file because the workspace id is generated locally (`PaneTypes.new_workspace_id`) and never authored. It is therefore outside `PaneTypes.tile_plan_key`, exactly as the pane's own env is — the same class of user-owned spawn state, never file authority — and a stored path that has gone missing warns once and falls back to the workspace directory in GDScript, before the PTY layer (which drops an unusable cwd silently) can see it. Accepted exposure, documented in SECURITY.md: a plain shell in a file-supplied directory restores without a prompt, because a directory is not executable and asking at every launch would train the user to dismiss this dialog.
- Profile provenance (v0.7.1): trust is derived from where a profile was loaded, never from fields inside it. `ProfileManager.get_all_profiles()` is the only place that knows, and it stamps `_origin` (`plugin`/`user`; the shipped defaults are seeded user profiles); `load_profiles()` strips `builtin`, `plugin`, `plugin_id`, `revision` and every `_`-prefixed key from user entries, because the loaders that own those fields re-stamp them after loading. `Workspace._profile_consented` branches on that stamp and treats an unstamped dict as user content, so a `profiles.json` entry claiming a plugin id + approved revision (or the legacy builtin claim) gets the plan walk, not the identity record. A pre-seed builtin or plugin approval must also cover every untrusted tile's plan key (`TrustedStore.approved_plan_keys` for the legacy builtin records/`plugin_plans`): a name or a revision alone is not consent to tiles. The install review carries the plans it lists (`plugin.rs::profile_plan_keys`, the Rust mirror of `PaneTypes.tile_plan_key`) and `approve_plugin` records them, so a profile whose tiles change under the same pin re-prompts; the profile dialog may extend an already-approved revision's plans, but never create one (only the install review approves a revision).
- Inspector/adapter children: `SessionOpenRequest::strip_env` carries `gpty_core::pty::STRIPPED_INHERITED_ENV_KEYS`, applied by both `gpty-ai` backends. The child is a third-party CLI - it must never inherit `GPTY_SECRET`, `GPTY_SOCKET`, the event capability, or the pane markers, because a GUI started from inside a pane carries all of them.
- Inspector prompt construction: `gpty-ai/src/prompt.rs` quotes untrusted capture behind a fence one backtick longer than the longest run inside it (capped at 32), and flattens `concept_name`/`source_pane` to a single line. A literal ``` fence was closable by any program that printed three backticks, which let the rest of the capture land as instructions rather than quoted data - keep the fence outgrowing its content.
- Environment reach: a pane inherits the GUI process's environment (portable-pty snapshots it; only `STRIPPED_INHERITED_ENV_KEYS` are removed), so launching gPTY from a credential-holding shell hands that context to every pane - and so does the GUI the CLI auto-spawns, which inherits the CLI's environment in turn - and `BLOCKED_ENV_KEYS` matching is byte-exact, which is correct on Unix but not on Windows, where the PTY layer normalises keys case-insensitively and the `GPTY_*` credential/marker namespace is therefore not case-sensitive. On top of the inherited environment a pane gets the user's global `shell_env` overlaid by its own entry from `PaneEnvStore` (`user://pane_env.json`, written by the pane settings UI); saved files cannot supply env.
- IPC hardening: the **control** socket defaults to `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/gpty.sock` (fallbacks `/run/user/<uid>/gpty.sock`, then a private state directory - `$XDG_STATE_HOME/gpty` or `$HOME/.local/state/gpty`, created 0700 and tightened if lax - and only then `/tmp/gpty-<uid>.sock`; macOS `$TMPDIR` first; `GPTY_SOCKET` overrides). The shared-`/tmp` path is predictable in a world-writable directory, so another user can squat it and deny the control surface - that is why the private directory is preferred and why a squatted path is a DoS, never a spoof (the socket's owner and mode are validated before use). **One instance owns the endpoint.** `serve()` probes an existing socket before replacing it and refuses when a server answers - a leftover file from a crash is still replaced, a live one never is (it used to be unlinked, which orphaned the running GUI while both windows stayed up); the event socket and the Windows pipe follow the same rule (a taken pipe name is refused, not retried forever); the pipe's `first_pipe_instance` claim is spent only once a create succeeds, so a transient failure cannot leave the name unclaimed for a racing process; and an instance that cannot bind sets the shutdown flag and says why in a toast, because a window with no pane API is worse than no window. The server chmods the socket 0600, rejects cross-UID peers on Linux/macOS (fail-closed), caps requests at 64 KiB (`-32600`), connections at 16, request reads and response writes at 30 s each, and dispatches each handler under its own budget - `register` defaults to 30 s, while a held answer declares a longer one with `register_with_timeout` (`paneWait` 75 s, `pluginInstall` 305 s, both its fallback + 5 s). A single connection-wide deadline must not come back: it cut `paneWait` at half its published 60 s and `pluginInstall` at a tenth of its review window, and the client saw a dropped socket instead of an answer. An overrun now answers `-32000 handler timed out`. When `GPTY_SECRET` is set on the GUI, clients MUST present it (mismatch → `-32001`); tests/scripts probing a secret-configured GUI must set the same env var. Do NOT weaken these gates when editing `server.rs`/`transport.rs`.
- OMP event socket: a **second** listener (`gpty-events.sock` / `default_event_socket_path()`, `\\.\pipe\gpty-events` on Windows) does not honor `GPTY_SOCKET` or `GPTY_SECRET`. It registers three methods: `ompEvent` (the authenticated submission path), `subscribe` and `eventsPoll` (read-only fan-out, bounded at 64 subscriptions, **not** capability-gated), and nothing else. Subscriptions are per-process and expire after `SUBSCRIPTION_IDLE` (120 s) without an `eventsPoll` - the next subscribe or emit releases the idle slot and its queued events, so abandoned clients (or reconnecting ones that never reuse their id) cannot exhaust the 64-slot cap. Read access is therefore open to any same-UID process, which is inside the documented threat model but is a wider surface than the single-method submission path; do not treat the event channel as confidential from same-UID peers. Each PTY gets an ephemeral `GPTY_TERMINAL_SESSION_ID` + `GPTY_EVENT_CAPABILITY` injected at spawn on every platform; **submitting** events requires the capability, and a leaked capability cannot inject text, create panes, or shut down gPTY. Do not register `ompEvent` on the control socket, and do not expose event submission as an MCP tool. The shipped `@gpty/omp-events` extension reaches the listener on either transport through one `net.connect(path)` call; on Windows the path must be a `\\.\pipe\` name (checked from the path alone, never `stat`ed), and on Unix the socket must be owned by this user and inaccessible to group/other.
- Accessibility tree (v0.8.0): when an accessibility driver is loaded, the engine publishes the app's Control names and the terminal's visible grid on the user's AT-SPI bus (a text node replaced per settled screen, `A11y.publish`, plus one-line announcements). That is another same-UID read surface for pane text, like the event socket's unauthenticated `subscribe`/`eventsPoll` - it is gated on the engine finding a driver (the export carries one, the Arch editor build does not) and on nothing else, so with accessibility on, any process running as the user can read what a pane currently shows. Element values and roles never reach AT-SPI on this adapter (queued in the roadmap), so only the published text node and the control names leave the process; do not widen that set (e.g. publishing scrollback) without deciding the read surface deliberately.
- IPC trust model: the IPC channel is local-only and trusts same-UID processes - a process running as the user can already control that user's session, so this is the accepted threat model for a single-user dev machine. On multi-user/shared hosts, set `GPTY_SECRET` on the GUI and every client. That trust covers processes *outside* gPTY: a program running in a pane also passes the gate (the inherited `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` lets the CLI derive the socket path), so with no secret set panes are not separated from the control surface - a known limitation recorded in SECURITY.md and queued in the roadmap. A secret does gate pane programs on Linux and Windows, because the GUI and the CLI harden themselves (see the process-hardening bullet) and the environment path that used to leak it is closed; that is a credential, not pane isolation. Never describe `GPTY_SECRET` or the `GPTY_*` env stripping as pane isolation, and do not claim the secret on macOS (it still exposes the environment to same-user processes through `KERN_PROCARGS2`). Anyone controlling a process's environment controls that process: env-var attacks are mitigated at the socket/binary boundary (`validate_socket_path`/`validate_gui_binary`), not by treating the environment itself as trusted.
- Process hardening (v0.7.1): `gpty_core::hardening::harden_process()` runs at every startup that can hold `GPTY_SECRET` - the GDExtension's `InitStage::Core` and the CLI's `main`. On Linux it sets `PR_SET_DUMPABLE 0`, which makes `/proc/<pid>/environ` and `/proc/<pid>/maps` root-owned; on Windows it installs a process DACL with a single ACE for the process owner: `PROCESS_TERMINATE | PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION | SYNCHRONIZE | READ_CONTROL`, withholding `PROCESS_VM_READ`/`PROCESS_VM_WRITE`/`PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD` (plus `PROCESS_VM_OPERATION`, implicitly). There is deliberately no `SYSTEM` ACE - `SYSTEM` holds `SeDebugPrivilege`, and a blanket grant would re-grant everything whenever gPTY itself runs as SYSTEM. Both stop a program in a pane from recovering the secret from the GUI or a client process. Do NOT remove the call, make it conditional on anything else, or re-exec either process after it. A failure is logged (GUI: `log::warn!`; CLI: stderr) and MUST never stop startup. `GPTY_ALLOW_DEBUG` (truthy values only - `1`/`true`/`yes`/`on`) is the documented developer opt-out, because a hardened process cannot be debugged or profiled (and a non-dumpable one has no core dumps); keep it truthy-only so an empty or `0` value cannot silently disable the marking. The Windows mask lives in `windows_policy` behind a compile-time assertion that no memory/thread-injection right is granted, with a unit test that runs on every platform - never add `PROCESS_VM_READ` back (it is what reads the PEB environment block), and keep `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION`, which is exactly the mask the socket's peer check opens a client with (without it every command is rejected). A pane's shell is a separate `exec`ed child and returns to dumpable on exec - never add a path that leaves pane processes non-dumpable, or the user cannot debug their own programs. The smoke's `process hardening` step asserts both halves on Linux (`SMOKE_ENV_READ`/`SMOKE_MAPS_READ` denied, `SMOKE_PANE_READ` allowed) and the DACL split on Windows (`SMOKE_WIN_VM_READ` denied, `SMOKE_WIN_QUERY`/`SMOKE_WIN_TERMINATE` allowed), against the GUI and a long-lived `gpty mcp` client; both Windows probes drop `SeDebugPrivilege` first (it overrides any process DACL) and print the token SID and the privilege state. `crates/gpty-core/tests/windows_hardening.rs` (a separate test binary because the DACL is process-wide, run by the `rust-windows` job) asserts the same split directly on its own process - including the before state and a `GetSecurityInfo` read-back that the installed DACL has one owner ACE without memory or thread-injection rights; macOS is skipped on purpose because `KERN_PROCARGS2` has no wired mechanism.
- Sensitive workspace invariant (planned, v0.9.5 - see ROADMAP): when a workspace is flagged sensitive, its panes are unreachable over the socket by **every** client, outside clients included, with no setting, grant or per-workspace exception; that is a permanent rule, not a default. A sensitive pane is treated as nonexistent by the one pane resolver, `list-panes`, `broadcast`, `pane-wait`/`pane-status`, the event stream, concept matching and the ambiguous-label error, and nothing about it is written to `HistoryStore`. The flag is user-owned (`WorkspaceStore`): no profile, layout, plugin or IPC call may set or clear it. Any new IPC verb that takes a pane id or label must go through the resolver and is covered by the enumerating test; never add a second lookup path, and never add a way to widen this rule. It is a speed bump against same-user code, not encryption or a sandbox - say so wherever it is described.
- Peer credentials (v0.5.4): `peer_uid_matches` in `gpty-ipc/src/server.rs` is the socket gate, and every arm fails closed - Linux/Android `SO_PEERCRED`, macOS + the BSDs `getpeereid`, illumos/Solaris `getpeerucred`, and Windows a raw-`extern` `win_peer` module (`GetNamedPipeClientProcessId` → `OpenProcess` → token user SID → `EqualSid`, no `windows-sys` dependency, the same pattern as `pin_library`). AIX/Haiku/QNX have no API wired up and still answer `true`; that is documented in SECURITY.md rather than implied. The BSD arm is compiled nowhere else - `ci-check` has a BSD cross-check step and CI's `rust-tests` job installs `x86_64-unknown-freebsd` for it. Adding a platform means adding its arm here, not a `cfg(unix)` shortcut.
- Store writes (v0.5.4): every `user://` store goes through `BasePersistenceManager._write_file`, which builds the file under a random sibling temp name (no `O_EXCL` in GDScript, so the *name* is the protection - 64 random bits cannot be pre-planted) and sets mode 0600 (`STORE_UNIX_MODE`) before renaming it over the target; the rename replaces the target itself, never writing through a symlink planted at the store path. The scrollback database is the same idea in Rust: `store::restrict_to_owner` chmods the SQLite file and its `-wal`/`-shm` siblings to 0600, because SQLite otherwise creates them with the process umask (measured 0644). Do not replace the random suffix with a fixed one and do not drop the explicit mode. The vault index (`state_dir()/vaults.db`, `gpty_core::vault`) is the same shape and the same rule, and it holds copies of vault note text outside the vault, so its mode matters exactly as much. **The repair half (v0.7.1):** The write path only fixes a store when something saves it, so a store written by an older build kept the umask's mode indefinitely - measured on a normal install: `layout.json` and `profiles.json` 0644 next to `concepts.json` 0600, and the engine-created `user://` root 0755. Both are now repaired at the one moment everything passes through: `BasePersistenceManager._read_file` tightens the store it is about to read, and `secure_user_root()` (once at start-up, from the base autoload's `_ready`) tightens the directory to 0700 before any store is loaded. The mechanism is one implementation, `gpty_core::owner_only`, reached from GDScript through the static `secure_store_path` and used as well by `store::restrict_to_owner` and `vault`'s recovery-copy directory. It opens the path with `O_NOFOLLOW` and `fchmod`s that descriptor, so a symlink at a store path is skipped rather than chmod'd through, and it only rewrites a *looser* mode of a file this user owns - another account's path is left silently alone, because it is not a mode this process can fix. Best effort by design: a mode that cannot be set is one warning per store per run (`_mode_failure_reported`) and the load proceeds. Do not add a second chmod call site: the two things this rule buys (no link followed, only our own loosened mode) are exactly what a bare `chmod` loses. **The corruption path (v0.8.1):** a store SQLite answers `NotADatabase`/`DatabaseCorrupt` for is *renamed*, never written - `<path>` and its `-wal`/`-shm` siblings move to `<path>.corrupt`, siblings first so a stale WAL cannot replay the damaged store's frames into its replacement, all under `store::write_guard` so two panes restoring at start-up cannot move each other's replacement. `rename` replaces a planted destination link instead of writing through it and moves a source entry as the entry it is, and only those two SQLite codes license the move: a busy, read-only or unopenable store stays put, because moving it would destroy evidence without making it work. Both SQLite stores — the scrollback database and the vault index — open through this one helper (`store::open_with_recovery`), so each recovers as `<name>.corrupt`.
- Vault containment (v0.7.1): a note is a file the vault contains, and `gpty_core::vault` enforces that in one place - `resolve_inside` canonicalizes a note path and requires the result under the canonical root. A read, a save and the index walk all use it, so a symlink pointing out of the vault answers `outside_vault` instead of another file's text and is not indexed at all (`vault::walk` skips it and counts it in `outside`, which the pane's footer shows). A link that stays inside is followed, and the walk catches a loop with a visited set of canonical directories rather than the depth cap. Do not go back to `std::fs::metadata` in the walk: it follows every link, and the index is what `vaultSearch` - a control-socket method - answers from, snippets included, so an outside file's text would come back in a search result. Tests: `symlinks_out_of_the_vault_are_not_listed_or_indexed`, `a_symlink_out_of_the_vault_is_neither_read_nor_written`, `a_symlink_loop_terminates_and_lists_each_note_once`.
- Vault root registry (v0.7.1): a root the control socket's vault verbs may look inside is the user's decision, not the caller's. `VaultRegistry` (`user://vaults.json`) is the one list; `Workspace`'s `settings_applied` handler is its only writer (the pane settings UI), so a layout, profile, plugin or IPC call cannot add one and a Wiki pane merely pointed at a directory registers nothing. The shipped knowledge base registers itself when a Wiki pane resolves `KnowledgeStore.TOKEN`, because it comes from the app's own bundle. `vault_api.rs` keeps an in-process mirror (the native handlers run on the blocking pool) and `vault_root()` in `vault_ipc.rs` refuses an unregistered root with `-32000` + `data.code = "not_registered"`; `vaultWeight` consults the same store before writing `link_weights.json`, so an unregistered root cannot fill that user-owned store. Never enforce this in one caller: a second gate is how the pane path and the socket path would drift apart.
- Parser memory is bounded (v0.7.1): every consumer of PTY bytes - the grid in `term.rs`, the line parser in `parser.rs` - MUST put the single `gpty_core::escstring::EscapeStringGuard` in front of its `vte` parser. `vte`'s `std` build keeps an OSC string's payload in an unbounded `Vec`, so an unclosed `ESC ]` grows memory at the writer's speed; the guard closes the string past `MAX_ESCAPE_STRING_BYTES` (64 KiB) with a BEL and parsing resumes. Do not add a second implementation or a per-consumer cap: two copies is exactly how the grid stayed unprotected while the line parser was capped. Only OSC is counted because only OSC buffers (DCS/APC/PM/SOS measured flat, their payloads are `Perform::put` and discarded); `crates/gpty-core/tests/escape_string_bound.rs` feeds all five kinds against a counting allocator, so a dependency that starts buffering another one fails there.
- IPC params contract (v0.7.1): `params` is named-only. `IpcServer` answers any frame whose `params` is not an object (absent and explicit `null` mean "no arguments") with `-32602` *before* dispatch, and `WorkspaceIpcHandlers.request_params` is the drain's second layer. Both layers answer `-32602` so a client sees one contract. Every refusal arm follows the same split, through `WorkspaceIpcHandlers.bad_param` (`-32602`, a value the request named and the handler cannot accept) and `refused` (`-32000`, a well-formed request naming app state it cannot satisfy) — `error()` takes no default code. GDScript has no try/catch, so a non-`Dictionary` value reaching a typed handler (`params: Dictionary`, `paneWait`'s `params.get(...)`) aborts the drain loop (`WorkspaceIpcHandlers.dispatch_request`, called from `_poll_ipc_requests`) - and every request already taken off the Rust queue is then neither handled nor answered, each caller waiting out its own timeout. Every new dispatch path must take params through that guard, and the typed handlers must not be widened to accept arrays. The MCP edge is the third layer (`commands/wire.rs`): it derives each tool argument's JSON shape from its clap definition, renames the ids whose wire key differs (`pane_type` -> `type`), and refuses an unknown key, a wrong JSON type or a contradictory pair with `-32602` *before* the socket is touched - a half-translated request is one that silently does something else, which is how `new-pane` created a terminal whatever type was asked for. The same rule covers helpers, not only handlers: a sanitizer with a typed parameter (`sanitize_tags(raw: Array)`) raised on caller data and aborted the batch exactly as a mistyped handler would, so a value taken from a request is untyped at the helper and the *edge* refuses the shape it cannot use.
- Concepts have no execution path (v0.5.3): `command_template`, `substitute_template`, `matching_commands`, and the click-to-run handler were removed. A trigger is a regex over untrusted output, so any action it could take would be an execution primitive governed by whatever a program printed - a downloaded `concepts.json` was arbitrary command execution with an attacker-chosen trigger, and it fired silently in whichever pane matched (including a root or ssh pane). Do NOT reintroduce a command/action field, a label-based PTY write, or a click handler that runs anything from a concept without a per-concept consent boundary (plugin trust lane). Concept parsing still caps count (128), trigger length (1024), actions (32), and clamps `stop_timeout_ms` to ≤ 600 000 ms (`concept::concepts_from_json`); a legacy `cmd` key is ignored, never parsed into the vocabulary. Lines over 16 KiB are never regex-matched; capture buffers are capped at 4 MiB. `LineParser::feed` additionally force-closes an OSC sequence past 64 KiB through the shared `EscapeStringGuard` (see the parser-memory bullet above): vte's `std` build keeps OSC bytes in an unbounded `Vec` (its 1 KiB cap is no_std-only, and alacritty forces `std` on), so an unterminated sequence grows memory and leaves the parser stuck inside the string, swallowing every later line. **Conditions (v0.5.4)** are regexes over untrusted output held to the same stance (`MAX_CONDITIONS` 8, 1024 bytes each, standard `regex` crate) and a malformed condition rejects the whole concept rather than being dropped (dropping narrows away a predicate and widens matching). **The visual editor's storage** is untrusted file input too: `ConceptManager._sanitize_graph` caps positions (512), drops out-of-range/non-finite coords, caps draft chains (32) and draft nodes (256), clamps the capture timeout, and drops unknown keys; `ConceptGraphModel.entry_for_path` compiles a closed key set, so a graph node can never introduce a `cmd` or any other key into `concepts.json`.
- PTY env sanitization: `pty::sanitize_envs` runs at spawn - the single choke point for settings, user-owned per-pane env, and the inherited environment. Keys must match `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`; dynamic-loader injection vectors (`LD_PRELOAD`, `LD_AUDIT`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `LD_ORIGIN_PATH`, `DYLD_*`), startup-evaluation keys the shell or the next tool runs (`PROMPT_COMMAND`, `BASH_ENV`, `ENV`, `SHELLOPTS`, `PS4`, `ZDOTDIR`, `PERL5OPT`, `PERL5LIB`, `PYTHONSTARTUP`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `RUBYOPT`, `LESSOPEN`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF`, `GIT_PAGER`, `PAGER`), event-channel keys (`GPTY_EVENT_SOCKET`, `GPTY_EVENT_PROTOCOL`, `GPTY_TERMINAL_SESSION_ID`, `GPTY_EVENT_CAPABILITY`), and pane-marker keys (`GPTY_ENV`, `GPTY_PANE_ID`) are dropped from untrusted env. Trusted runtime vars (`GPTY_ENV=1`, `GPTY_PANE_ID=<attachment_id>`, and the event-channel vars) are injected last by `GptyTerminal.start_shell()`, bypassing the blocklist. `GPTY_PANE_ID` is the pane's stable `attachment_id`; if unset at spawn it falls back to the per-PTY session id. Inherited control credentials (`GPTY_SECRET`, `GPTY_SOCKET`, `GPTY_GUI`) are stripped via `CommandBuilder::env_remove` so child shells cannot control the workspace. Do NOT remove entries from `BLOCKED_ENV_KEYS` without a security review.
- `cli_view` is a second spawn surface and is held to the same rules as a terminal tile: it runs argv (never a shell string) from the pane's `command` + `shell_args` - exactly the keys `PaneTypes.tile_spawns_untrusted`/`tile_plan_key` already gate, so a profile or manifest tile that names a program still asks for Workspace Trust - and `CliProcess::spawn` holds the program to `pty::validate_program` (a name resolving into the working directory is refused; an absolute path must be a file another user cannot swap). `STRIPPED_INHERITED_ENV_KEYS` is removed from the child: a plugin's status command is a third-party CLI and must not inherit `GPTY_SECRET`/`GPTY_SOCKET` or a pane's event capability. It has no PTY (that is the point - a view, not a terminal), no stdin, and renders bytes as text with no ANSI interpretation, so no sequence can move the cursor or change what is drawn. Do not give it a concept-receive, PTY-write, or command-execution path driven by terminal output - that would make a pane's output an execution primitive.
- Agent observability allowlist: the OMP extension may forward session/turn/tool **metadata** and bounded `thinking_delta` text. Never forward prompts, answer text, tool arguments/results, provider payloads, credentials, or session file paths. The translation boundary enforces that as a per-event **field allowlist** (`omp_events.rs::ALLOWED_FIELDS`): the downstream object is built field-by-field with caps (ids/names ≤ 128 B, `reason` ≤ 64 B, `text` ≤ 8 KiB, non-negative integers, bools), and any field not listed - including one a future extension version adds - is dropped rather than passed through. Adding a field to an event means adding it to that table, deliberately. A reasoning delta that would exceed the 8 KiB text cap is **split by the extension on code-point boundaries** (never truncated, and never capped by JavaScript string length - the server measures UTF-8 bytes); the server counts and rate-limit-warns a submission that still exceeds it instead of losing it silently. The queue between the socket and the frame's drain is 1024 events/session and 4 MiB globally (`EventQueue`), with `omp_event_stats()` exposing both drop counters. Never persist `GPTY_EVENT_*`, OMP session IDs, or thinking text in layout/profile JSON. Reasoning accordion records stay in RAM until a later `feat(history)` SQLite path exists.
- Third-party AI CLIs: do not read or reuse OAuth tokens, call backing services with harvested credentials, bundle proprietary CLIs, or scrape TUI output. Users launch agents in terminal panes; gPTY only consumes documented hooks/extensions.
- Env-var hijacking: `GPTY_SOCKET` must be an absolute path owned by the current UID with mode `0o600`-style privacy - `transport::validate_socket_path` runs client-side before connect and refuses insecure sockets (they would receive commands and `GPTY_SECRET`). `GPTY_GUI` binaries are validated by `transport::validate_gui_binary` before auto-spawn: an absolute, regular file, not group/other-writable, whose owner the one rule in `pty::validate_executable_file` trusts (this user, root, or the overflow UID of a user namespace that leaves host root unmapped). Do NOT weaken these checks when editing `client.rs`/`daemon.rs`/`transport.rs`, and do not add an overflow arm to the socket or peer-credential checks - those compare against this process exactly.
- IPC framing (v0.7.1): a connection carries newline-framed JSON-RPC requests and may carry more than one. `handle_connection` loops until EOF and answers each frame in order (`handle_frame`), so a pipelined client gets one response per request instead of losing its tail with the connection. Each frame is read under its own `MAX_REQUEST_LEN` (64 KiB) bound and its own `IO_TIMEOUT` read wait, so a frame cannot allocate past the bound and an idle connection cannot hold a slot forever; the handler still dispatches under its own registered budget. An over-bound frame is answered `-32600` and closes the connection, because the stream is no longer frame-aligned; a parse error answers `-32700` for that frame and the batch continues; a wrong `gpty_secret` answers `-32001` and closes. The connection cap is unchanged (16), so a peer that opens connections and says nothing holds a slot for at most one read timeout, exactly as before.
- User-owned saved commands (v0.8.1): `SavedCommandStore` (`user://commands.json`) is the same class of user-owned state with a narrower reach - the Commands tab (Settings) is its only writer, so no profile, layout, plugin or IPC call can add an entry, and `Workspace._deliver_saved_command` writes the **active** terminal pane only (`_send_line_to_term` when the entry's `run` flag is set, `_send_to_term` otherwise, then `_snap_to_bottom`). Nothing spawns from it, the text is never expanded, and the palette lists it as data (`PaletteModel.entries(saved)`) rather than reading the store itself.
- Colour-scheme import (v0.8.6): a scheme file is untrusted input - the picker can be pointed anywhere. `SettingsManager.import_scheme` reads it through `TextRead.read_prefix` under 16 KiB (a truncated read is refused, never parsed) and hands it to `gpty_core::scheme::parse_scheme`, whose native JSON has a closed key set with exactly 16 palette entries, whose YAML reader accepts a block-mapping subset only, and whose iTerm2 reader refuses a DOCTYPE internal subset, CDATA and any entity but the five predefined ones (eXternal entities are never fetched). The validated native copy is written through `_write_text` into `user://schemes/`, never `load()`ed as a resource, and that copy is what a pane reads. A layout, profile or IPC caller still cannot name a scheme (`color_scheme_path`/`pane_scheme` are `file: false`; `pane_scheme` is also `ipc: false`), and a pane's own scheme comes only from `PaneSchemeStore` (`user://pane_schemes.json`, the pane settings UI's write path).
- Layout restore trust: saved tiles from `workspaces.json`/`layout.json` (legacy)/profiles are untrusted input - `PaneTypes.sanitize_tile` validates the pane type and settings dict, clamps grid geometry (`PANE_MAX_ROWS`/`PANE_MAX_COLS`, mirrored by `MAX_ROWS`/`MAX_COLS` in the FFI - an unbounded stored `rows`/`cols` allocated the cells before the first frame); the settings themselves are a **closed per-type table** (`PaneTypes.settings_schema`: `text` — with an optional `values` closed set —/`backend`/`int`/`float`/`bool`/`color`/`id`/`tags`/`argv`/`shell program`/`font path`/`dir path` rules - a value outside a rule's `values` set is refused like an unknown key, and `kind: "backend"` folds an alias to its kind while keeping an unknown name - with `file: false` for keys only the app may set: the terminal's env/appearance paths, and the Inspector's `system_prompt`, `auto_run` and `accept_concept_captures` - a profile cannot aim a pane at a prompt or turn auto-send on, because a routing concept would then send captured output to a model with no gesture) - `sanitize_tile` filters with `SOURCE_FILE` (unknown and app-only keys dropped, reported once), and `PaneBody.apply_settings` filters again with `SOURCE_RUNTIME` and is the **only generic assignment path** (a pane's own override assigns its named keys explicitly): there is no "set any exported property" path, which is how a tile once chose `font_bold_path` and had the next reload `load()` it. The control surface's `paneSet` and `new-pane --setting` filter that same table with `SOURCE_IPC`, a third source that also honours an `ipc: false` marker on the values that are not a caller's: the pane's identity (`type`, `attachment_id`), its geometry (`rows`/`cols`), the user's own env (`shell_env`), the Inspector's aim (`system_prompt`, `auto_run`, `accept_concept_captures`) and the wiki's restore-only `graph`/`open_note`. Neither verb writes `PaneEnvStore`, `PaneInspectorStore` or `VaultRegistry` - those stores remain the pane settings UI's alone - so an IPC caller can point a pane at a vault without widening what the socket's vault verbs may read, and a live-only aim that would vanish at the next restart is refused rather than half-applied. **No path that came from a file may reach `load()`/`ResourceLoader`**: a font is built from bytes by `TerminalFonts` (absolute regular file, extension gate, 32 MiB cap, magic + face check; only the bundled `res://` constants use the loader, because an export carries their imported `.fontdata`, not the source `.ttf`), and a color scheme is a capped `TextRead` (16 KiB, regular file) whose text only feeds `set_palette`'s hex parser. A `.tres` whose sub-resource is a GDScript executes during `load()`, and Workspace Trust does not see it - a font is not a spawn plan. A new pane property that should survive a layout needs a row in that table, and `test_pane_settings.gd::test_every_pane_type_accepts_the_settings_it_saves` fails when one is missing; terminal `shell_args` are sanitized (`PaneTypes.sanitize_shell_args`: ≤32 args, ≤4096 chars, no U+FFFD); code_viewer/file_tree/wiki pane paths must be absolute; the code viewer caps a read at `TextRead.DEFAULT_MAX_BYTES` (1 MiB, the shared `TextRead.read_prefix` guard) and refuses anything `FileAccess.file_exists` reports false for (its regular-file check refuses directories/devices/FIFOs - a FIFO open would otherwise block the GUI thread); the wiki pane's note view reads through `GptyTerminal.vault_note_read`, which applies the same 1 MiB cut, the same regular-file gate and the same torn-tail drop in `gpty_core::vault`; and the file tree asks for confirmation before `ExternalLink` hands its `file://` URI to `OS.shell_open`, because a downloaded `.desktop` file is *run* by the mime handler - a handler that refuses the URI copies it and says so in a toast. The wiki pane's editor is this repo's one pane *write* surface and is held to the same rule: every write is an explicit user action - Save/Ctrl+S, New note, Rename, or a confirmed Delete - and never the pane's own idea, and every path follows the walk's vocabulary. A save must name an existing note, and its canonicalized path must stay inside the vault - a symlink out of the vault is refused, one pointing at a sibling note is written through - the write is atomic and keeps the note's own mode, and a file whose (mtime, size) stamp differs from the one the pane loaded is never overwritten without the user confirming it. Create/rename/delete act on the vault **entry** (a symlinked note is unlinked or moved as a link, its target untouched, so deletion cannot reach a file the vault does not contain), a create or rename destination is claimed with `create_new` so an existing note answers `exists` instead of being replaced, and it may only target a directory that already exists and canonicalizes inside the vault. Do NOT remove these guards when adding pane settings. Programs restored from those files are validated at spawn: `gpty_core::pty::validate_program` resolves a bare name through the `PATH` the child inherits (the tile's own `shell_env` when set, otherwise the user's - the value `execvp` searches) and holds the first match to `validate_executable`'s rule - a regular file, not group/other-writable, owned by this user or root, with no writable ancestor - while an absolute path is checked directly. `PATH` itself is not blocked: the shipped profiles launch `omp`, `lazygit` and `nvim` by name. A name that resolves nowhere is passed through (the spawn fails as it always did); a name resolving into the working directory is refused. The Inspector's adapter argv is held to the same rule at `session_open`. Wiki links are held to the same rule too: following a mention is a *read*, never an action. The renderer emits a `gpty-note:` URL from the note's own text (percent-encoded, label escaped, and gated by `MarkdownView.wikilinks_enabled`, which only the wiki pane sets), `MarkdownView` hands the decoded target to its owning pane instead of `OS.shell_open`, `vault_link_resolve` maps it to a note in the *index* (never a caller-supplied path), and the pane opens that note through `vault_note_read` - so the containment check, the 1 MiB cut and the regular-file gate are the note editor's, unchanged. A target that resolves nowhere, or to a shared stem, is reported rather than guessed; no vault text can become a path the pane reads directly or a URL the system opens. The About page's documentation viewer mirrors that shape with `gpty-doc:`: the renderer emits it only under `MarkdownView.doc_links_enabled` (only that viewer sets it), the decoded path is looked up in the generated bundle's own key map (`DocsBundle`) - never joined to a filesystem path or opened - and a document the build did not bundle is refused with a toast.
- Media decode (v0.7.0): media files are untrusted input and the backend links **FFmpeg** - a C decoder stack - as a deliberate exception to the memory-safe-decoder preference; SECURITY.md states the exception and what is not claimed. The shipped FFmpeg is pinned (9.0.2, SHA256), LGPLv3, dynamically linked, and built with `--disable-everything --disable-network` so only the components in `crates/gpty-media/components.txt` exist at all. On top of that the runtime validates the path (absolute local regular file), opens the descriptor itself (`O_NONBLOCK | O_NOFOLLOW`, `fstat`-verified) and hands FFmpeg a custom AVIO context over it, so a name swapped for a FIFO/device after the check cannot block the worker or redirect the session and FFmpeg never opens the path at all; the demuxer alias list after open, and the selected stream's codec **id** before a decoder runs; caps are 16 streams, 4096 px per side, 34 MiB per frame, 8 channels, bounded queues and a 10 s open budget. Decode runs on a dedicated OS thread, never the GUI thread and never the shared tokio runtime. There is **no sandboxing claim** - a decoder bug is a same-process memory-safety bug - and nothing in a media file can become a command or a write: the path is a read and the output is frames and samples. The caps are re-checked on the decoded frame, not only on the probe (a frame past 4096 px per side or 8 channels is refused), and a resampled audio frame is bounded at `MAX_AUDIO_FRAME_SAMPLES` (one second per channel) **before** `frame::Audio::new` - a file claiming a tiny source rate otherwise multiplies a 4 KiB packet into hundreds of megabytes at the target rate. A panic in the decode worker is caught and fails the session rather than leaving it on "opening". The close is bounded too (v0.7.1): `stop_and_join` waits `CLOSE_TIMEOUT_MS` (2 s) and then detaches the thread instead of joining it forever, because `Packet::read`, `send_packet` and `receive_frame` run inside C and consult no interrupt callback - without the bound, a bitstream that makes a decoder spin holds the Godot thread at pane close and at window quit, which drops every session. The abandoned thread frees its own FFmpeg contexts when the call returns (never from outside it), so it leaks only if the call never returns; that thread is the one cost, and it is bounded by the process.
- Agent backend streams are bounded (v0.7.1): `gpty_ai::frame::read_frame` is the ONE reader for a backend child's stdout (both `omp` and `cli`), because `Lines::next_line` buffers a whole line before any size check can see it - the CLI bridge had the bound and the OMP stream did not. It fails as soon as a frame's content passes the caller's limit, and a single OMP answer is capped at `MAX_ASSEMBLED_ANSWER_BYTES` (8 MiB) before it is assembled. Backends are user-chosen programs with the user's own authority: this is a memory bound, not a trust boundary.
- OSC agent-state declaration: the published `gpty_state=<value>` OSC sequence is the Tier 2 agent-state channel, implemented in `parser.rs` (`osc_dispatch`) - the FIRST interpreted sequence in a discard-only parser; do not expand the parser further without a security review. Strictly whitelist enum values (idle/working/needs-attention/completed/failed); single-shot per parse; rate-limited (≥500 ms between accepted declarations per terminal, `DECLARATION_MIN_INTERVAL_MS`). It is spoofable by design - pasted text and `cat`-ed files can emit it - so it may set UI display state ONLY and must never trigger actions, concepts, layouts, or IPC. The engine applies it only when not alt-screen, not capturing, and outside the post-resize suppression window (same guards as concept matching). Tier 1 (capability-authenticated event socket) remains authoritative; Tier 3 (regex/idle/exit heuristics in `agent_state.rs`) is display-only and never a decision input. States surface through `paneStatus` (`agent_state`, `agent_state_tier`) and the titlebar badge. **Windows has no Tier 2 OSC channel**: ConPTY re-renders its own model and consumes sequences its VT engine does not implement, so the declaration never reaches the parser - measured in CI, where a DECSET 2004 from the same PowerShell fixture arrives while every declaration test fails. The declaration path there, and the authenticated alternative everywhere, is `gpty state <value>`: it reads the pane's own injected credentials (`GPTY_EVENT_SOCKET`, `GPTY_TERMINAL_SESSION_ID`, `GPTY_EVENT_CAPABILITY` - the only credential a pane's child holds, because `GPTY_SOCKET`/`GPTY_SECRET` are stripped) and submits `gpty.state.declared` (`state.declared`, one whitelisted `state` field) over the event socket. Same display-only authority, capability-gated instead of spoofable; it is deliberately **not** an MCP tool (an MCP client is not inside a pane, and there is no IPC method behind it).
- `broadcast-input`: a fan-out of `inject` over the `GPTY_SECRET`-gated control socket. Text is written to each PTY verbatim, exactly as `inject` does (the target shell interprets it - no additional interpolation by gpty). Pane tags used for targeting must be sanitized like `attachment_id` (`[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}`). A pane that has no child yet holds that text instead of writing it (`TerminalPane._pending_input`, capped at the 64 KiB per-call limit; a call that would exceed it is refused whole rather than truncated) and flushes it at start, so the queue is bounded by the same number the API already accepts per call - 96 panes × 64 KiB is the hard ceiling, and only until the first layout pass.
- Release identity is not a code trust signal (v0.8.1): a job holding `id-token: write` authenticates as the project, so it must not check out or execute an event-derived ref - code scanning alert 13 was exactly that (the MCP registry job checked out the released tag on a `workflow_run` and ran the validator from it). The rule: a privileged job runs default-branch code only and reads a tagged tree as data (the contents API into `$RUNNER_TEMP`), and its `ref:` stays a literal, because every event-derived value is a taint source for the `actions/untrusted-checkout` queries. See the alert 13 row in the v0.8.1 roadmap. The release workflow follows the same split: `release-gate` and `export` are read-only; `publish` holds `contents: write` and the OIDC identity, downloads the staged `gpty-release-dist`, runs only pinned actions, and waits on the `release` environment's required reviewer. No project code runs there.
- Plugin trust model: plugins are arbitrary code running as the user - the same trust as any editor extension. Review-then-run (reuse the Workspace Trust confirmation dialog), pin revisions, per-plugin config/state/log dirs, manifest validation with size/count/path caps (reuse concept parse caps and `sanitize_tile` rules). The installed record store is read bounded (`store::read_store_text`, 16 MiB) and refused before parsing - a record's tiles and concepts are pass-through JSON, so the count caps alone cannot size the read. Never claim sandboxing.
- Update checker: the startup GitHub-release check is notify-only - it never downloads or executes anything, and a remote `tag_name` is validated by `_is_valid_semver` before it reaches the toast. The response body is integrity-untrusted (TLS transport only; GitHub release artifacts are unsigned): treat remote version strings as display data. If a future "Download update" action is added, it MUST verify artifact integrity (pinned checksums or equivalent) before installation - a MITM'd response could otherwise point at a malicious payload.

- **UI/UX assessment method** - used by the UI re-baselines (v0.8.0 and v0.8.5) and the terminal fidelity probes (v0.9.1 and v0.9.2). Run the real app (the actual main scene, autoloads and Rust extension) in a private sandbox with a fresh first-run state, so no existing settings or layouts influence it; drive it through the committed capture harness (`scripts/ui-capture <state> <out-dir>`, staging table `godot/tests/bench/ui_capture.gd`), which seeds a named state through the real autoloads with synthetic clicks and key events and saves the app's own rendered viewport as PNG - never a desktop capture; `scripts/ui-capture --list` prints the states - the table is the owner, so this page does not count or copy them, and a state added or renamed shows up there; a state may also carry `"tab": "<name>"` to open a Settings state on that tab rather than System (`light-settings` uses it for the Appearance tab, where the theme and UI-scale controls live), and a surface that needs auditing becomes a state in that table rather than another scratch driver. Keyboard reachability is part of the method: `scripts/ui-capture --audit-focus <state>` stages the same state and prints the focus owner, the visible dialog's own focus owner, whether Escape closes the surface, every visible `FOCUS_NONE` button, and the Tab order; a visible control with no keyboard path is a finding even when a shortcut or a mouse path exists, and a `FOCUS_NONE` control whose action is reached from somewhere else declares itself with `KeyboardFocus.declare_mouse_only(control, reason)` - the audit prints it as a `mouse-only button` with that reason and counts only the undeclared ones as `unaccounted=`. An open overlay's controls are snapshotted before the Escape that closes it, so its own rows are named instead of counted as zero. The Tab-order walk follows explicit `focus_next` rings and stops at the first one it enters, so on a surface whose first stop is inside a ring it prints that ring and not the rest - read `focusable=` and the mouse-only lines for the whole surface, and stage a state whose first focusable control is the surface you mean (the BUILD row *The focus audit stops inside the first keyboard ring* widens the walk). A capture needs a real display driver (`--headless` has no redraw pass), each launch is bounded (`CAPTURE_TIMEOUT`, default 120 s: a launch that never presents a frame is killed and fails its state instead of hanging the run or leaving a blank window behind), two runs of one state must be pixel-identical, and `scripts/ui-capture-check` asserts that plus that a perturbed control changes exactly one image (it needs a display, so it is not in `ci-check`) - a state that stages something animated must pin it for the same reason (`agent-badges` re-applies the badge and stops the pane's per-frame work: the spinner cycles at 8 fps and the attention pulse at 1.2 Hz, so a live one never repeats); small windows (800×500, 560×340) resize the root viewport, so the image is the layout at that size, not OS window behaviour; read the UI code to explain what the captures show and to count hard-coded styling; compute contrast as WCAG ratios from colour constants in the code or from sampled pixels. Mark each finding **verified** (reproduced in the running app, with a control where one mattered), **observed** (seen once or without a control) or **code** (read in the source, not exercised); roadmap rows use these words, plus *not tested* and *measured*. List what the assessment did not examine, and queue that list as a row instead of dropping it. Do not modify project files while assessing. `scripts/ui-capture-check`'s perturb target defaults to `settings` when the list has it, else the first named state (`--perturb` overrides); a state with neither overlay nor pane cannot be the target (exit 2, so `ui-capture-check empty-workspace` cannot run alone), and each state costs three launches. Synthetic input is WINDOW space: `Input.parse_input_event` does not apply the content scale while a Control's `get_global_rect()` is layout space, so `ui_capture.gd`'s `_click` maps through `root.get_final_transform()` (unscaled, the `settings-terminal-150` state could not open Settings; the transform is identity at 100 %, so 100 % captures are byte-identical). A small-window state cannot stage its empty workspace through `close_all` - the click lands on the clipped pane section at 560x340 - so `empty-workspace-560x340` seeds the zero-pane store state instead.
- **Tests own their temp artifacts.** Any test that binds a socket or writes a database, store directory or fake script creates a `tempfile::TempDir` in the test body and lets it drop (a helper that hands back a path must hand back the guard too — a bare `PathBuf` whose `TempDir` dropped at return is a leak with extra steps). Bind it to a name: `let _ = …` drops it immediately. `tempfile` is a dev-dependency of every crate that needs it, `std::env::temp_dir()` is where the guard lives, and `scripts/ci-check` runs both cargo test passes under an empty `TMPDIR` and fails the run if anything is still in it — so an unguarded test is caught by the first full gate, not by a full `/tmp` months later. Shared `static` state is the same class: a test that mutates a queue or map must clear it on every exit path - timeout, error and panic included - through one `clear_state()` helper, or a stale entry breaks the next test. The process environment is the other global: `gpty-ipc`'s transport tests guard `GPTY_SOCKET`/`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` through one `EnvVar` lock that restores the previous value on drop, and an unlocked `set_var`/`remove_var` pair failed a real `ci-check` parallel run.
- Tests live in `godot/tests/` - `unit/` for pure-logic classes, `integration/` for scene-tree tests. A test that needs a pane's shell sets `SettingsManager.cfg_shell_command = SettingsManager.default_shell_command()` (never a literal `/bin/sh`: on Windows that is refused by `validate_executable` and the spawn fails as an engine error, which GUT counts as a test failure), and a test that needs exact bytes from a *child* builds its command line with `ShellFixtures.print_text()` (`godot/tests/helpers/shell_fixtures.gd`) - and a test that needs a *mode* to come from the child rather than from its shell spawns its pane with `ShellFixtures.no_line_editing_args()` (`bash --noediting`; the default shell sets DECSET 2004 around every line its readline edits, which made `test_bracketed_paste.gd` pass 3/3 even with the fixture's command line replaced by a bare `sleep 30`) - spawning through `Workspace._spawn_pane`, not `TerminalManager.spawn_pane`, because only the former parents the wrapper so `_ready` runs the shell - and a transition (on, then off) in that file uses `ShellFixtures.print_text_pair()`, since a holding fixture cannot be typed into a second time - or, when its child is spawned as argv instead of typed into a shell (a `cli_view` pane), with `ShellFixtures.print_text_argv()`: `print_text()` returns a *cmd.exe* command line, and on Windows argv hands that line to `cmd.exe /c`, which re-parses it - `\"` is not cmd syntax, so PowerShell received the script as a quoted *string* and printed it rather than running it (measured on `windows-smoke`), which is why the argv form names PowerShell directly there and keeps the shell on POSIX - and, when it *waits* for those bytes, waits for the shell to be printing first (a nonzero `idle_ms` in `get_status()`: a line typed into a console app that has not attached yet is read by nothing), and a test that asserts a scroll *offset* waits for the child to stop printing first - a scrolled-back pane anchors its view to late output, so a line arriving between the scroll and the assertion moves the offset by that many lines (`windows-smoke` measured 44 → 88 while `cmd.exe` was still flushing, and the sentinel read as the defect under test) - and then gives the child's own startup a budget sized for a process launch rather than for the assertion. A cold `powershell.exe` on a Windows runner measured past the 10 s `test_bracketed_paste.gd` used to allow, which reported a cold start as "the mode never arrived" (`windows-smoke`).
- A test that compares a path **Rust produced** with a GDScript string must normalize separators: `std::fs::canonicalize` answers `\\?\C:\...` with backslashes on Windows while `user://`-globalized paths use `/`, so `ends_with("/name")` passes on Linux and fails on `windows-smoke` (measured 2026-11-01: `test_the_native_mirror_is_this_list`, one failing test of 902 while the mirror itself was correct). Compare the last component or replace `\` with `/` first - never the host's spelling. The same Windows-only class of failure is a multi-line string literal: the repo sets no `eol` attribute and the runner checks out with `core.autocrlf` on, so a `"""…"""` expectation carries CRLF while the code under test emits `"\n"`, and the two print identically in GUT's `[Failed]` block (`test_feedback_text.gd` failed `windows-smoke` this way while Linux passed). Build expectations by joining lines with `"\n".join(...)`. The third member of the class is a path a **child process printed**: Godot's own paths use `/` even on Windows (`path_join`, `OS.get_user_data_dir`) while `cmd` reports its cwd with `\`, so `get_text().contains(workspace_cwd)` compared two spellings of the same directory and failed `windows-smoke` while the payload proved the child had started in the right place (`test_the_child_starts_in_the_panes_directory`, 2026-11-15). Normalize both sides (`path.replace("\\", "/")`) and put the expected value plus the pane's `start_error()` in the assertion, so the message says which half was wrong.
- Mocking autoloads: Use `MockAutoloads.setup()` / `teardown()` in `before_each`/`after_each`. `setup()` also seeds the integration baseline the old first run produced: one `Workspace 1` holding one terminal. The app's own first run has no workspace and no pane (the first pane creates `Default`), so a test of that state overrides `WorkspaceStore.FILE` with `{"active": 0, "workspaces": []}`, and a test that clears the store adds a workspace before touching `_workspaces[0]` (see `test_layout_restore._make_workspace`). `MockAutoloads` hands out the live store, so a "the store did not change" assertion can compare an array against itself (`get_store` returns the stored Dictionary and a manager returns its array by reference); snapshot with `.duplicate(true)` in any test that claims a refused call left a store unchanged, and never hand a live member to a save (`_save_settings_file` passing `cfg_sidebar_folded` itself meant a later `.clear()` emptied the stored list).
- Persistence managers (`SettingsManager`, `ProfileManager`, `WorkspaceStore`) are mocked via `set_script()` on the existing autoload node, redirecting `_read_file`/`_write_file` to an in-memory Dictionary - avoids touching disk and preserves Godot 4 global name bindings. (`SettingsManager` etc. are static constants - never `free()` autoload nodes).
- Signal testing: GDScript lambdas cannot capture outer primitives. Use GUT's `watch_signals(node)` + `assert_signal_emitted(node, "signal_name")` instead of `node.signal.connect(func(): captured_var = true)`.
- Editor tests must *type*, not assign: a `TextEdit`/`CodeEdit` programmatic `text = …` goes through `_set_text(p_text, /*emit_signal=*/false)` and emits only `text_set` - `text_changed` is emitted for edits (`insert_text_at_caret`, `remove_text`, undo) and is **deferred, one frame later** (`call_deferred`; Godot 4.7.2, `scene/gui/text_edit.cpp`). So a test that assigned `text` and asserted a live preview or a dirty marker would assert nothing, and code that trusts the signal's timing would break on both counts - `wiki_pane.gd` recomputes its dirty state from the buffer instead, and `test_wiki_pane.gd`'s `_type_into()` driver (`select_all` + `insert_text_at_caret` + one process frame) is the way edits reach it in a test.
- A test that asserts a terminal pane's title or tooltip must set and read it in one call. A tile follows its child's OSC title while the child runs, and cmd.exe reports `Administrator: C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe` as soon as ConPTY starts, so a test that sets a name, awaits frames and then reads it can read the shell's title instead - `windows-smoke` run 43617896053 failed exactly that way, and `test_small_window.gd` now sets and reads synchronously (the assertions are the label's layout, not title precedence).
- Type checks: `body is SomeClass` requires a compile-time class name. For runtime type discrimination, use `body._pane_type()` string discriminators.
- A perf claim about an interaction needs a **windowed** run, and one repetition is not a number: the synchronous GDScript cost plus the frame it delays does not exist headless, and the first workspace switch after launch measured 551 ms against a 63-75 ms steady state (2026-11-09, five workspaces; that comparison is `switch_bench`'s `cold` sample now, and the one-shot turned out to be the arriving workspace's unstarted panes, not the switch path). Time the call with `Time.get_ticks_usec()` marks around each step and the frame after it with `await get_tree().process_frame`, repeat at least three times and attribute every step before theorising; the recipe is `skill://gpty-live-gui-smoke` (body at `.omp/skills/gpty-live-gui-smoke/SKILL.md`)'s "Timing an interaction", the pane's own `_fetch_ms`/`_draw_ms` (read them off the body; the status bar prints FPS only) cover the frame half, and `godot/tests/bench/draw_bench.gd` measures render cost alone - `forced_us` for a full repaint, `row_us` for one row's bands, `overlay_us` for the cursor layer, and `BENCH_FLOOD=1`/`BENCH_SPARSE=1` for a full-screen or one-line stream (`sync_us` = fetch + repaint per damage sync, `avg_rows` = rows repainted, `backoff_ms` = the pane's cadence back-off; the stream modes force no repaint, so the file also runs against a pre-split pane). The same shape is `godot/tests/bench/switch_bench.gd` for a workspace switch, with its two payloads behind `SWITCH_CMD_A`/`SWITCH_CMD_B` and the window behind `SWITCH_WINDOW`; it settles both panes (non-empty screen, quiet grid) before the measured loop and fails on a switch into an empty pane, which is how it read 37 ms for a switch whose real cost was 992 ms. A `-s` launch under `--headless` clamps the root to 64x64 and no pane starts its child, so the bench never exercises the path it means to time: a harness that needs real tiles runs windowed, as `godot/tests/bench/spawn_bench.gd` does (per-spawn `sync_us` and child-resolved `total_us` as the grid fills to 64 panes, the slope between them, RSS and `children` per milestone, and one attribution line per whole-window pass).
- A GPU shader effect's cost is a **frame time, not a delta**: under `--disable-vsync` a Godot run is bound by `max(CPU, GPU)`, so at 1080p the harness itself floors at ~215 µs and a cheaper shader cannot be isolated by subtracting a plain run - that subtraction understates the effect whenever only the plain run is CPU-bound. Drive the shader at 4K (or a larger offscreen `SubViewport`) so the GPU is the limiter and read the frame time as the GPU cost; measured 2026-11-15 on the RTX 5070 Ti (Vulkan, offscreen): the CC0 smoke/FBM tree at 8 octaves cost 0.29 ms at 1080p and 1.02 ms at 4K, a 4-octave sin-free variant 0.33 ms at 4K. `godot/tests/bench/effect_bench.gd` is that measurement for the shipped terminal effects (`BENCH_EFFECT=crt|grain|none`, `BENCH_SIZE`, `BENCH_FRAMES`): it prints the plain-rect baseline and the effect's median frame time on the same rect, and it must run on a real GPU - a session that falls back to llvmpipe measures software cost only and cannot replace a declared budget.
- **The README's cost table is a published claim with an owner.** `scripts/measure-cost` re-measures the five rows the README prints (idle one pane, zero panes, first launch, OpenGL3 warm, the 30,000-line scrollback delta) by launching the built app in a `scripts/ui-sandbox` sandbox and sampling `VmRSS` from its own `/proc/<pid>/status` at steady state - median of five readings after the control socket answers a `list-panes`, with the spread printed to stderr beside each row's pane count. `--check` fails past 10% on a row (`MEASURE_TOLERANCE`), past that run-to-run noise on the scrollback delta, and when the Forward+/OpenGL3 ratio drops below the "Nx lighter" ratio the prose claims, because a table that moves while the sentence does not leaves the README contradicting itself. It needs a Linux GPU session - under `--headless` there is no renderer, so the figures do not exist there - and a `./scripts/build` output, never a debug build. `--stamp` is the half `ci-check` and a docs-class push run: it compares the table's "measured on the shipped vX.Y.Z" line against the crate version and needs no GPU, so a release bump cannot leave the table naming the previous release. Taking the measurement is a release step (`skill://release`, body at `.omp/skills/release/SKILL.md`); the figures also appear on gpty.dev, because the docs build mirrors `README.md` (its `readfile` shortcode rewrites `docs/static/images/` to `/images/`, so a README image works on both surfaces). The README's chart is generated, not drawn: `docs/data/cost-history.json` is the ledger (`--record` appends one entry per release) and `scripts/render-cost-chart` renders it to `docs/static/images/cost-history.svg`, with `--check --require-current` failing in `ci-check` when the SVG is stale or the ledger lacks the version being released - no display needed, so the picture cannot drift from the table it sits under. **An attribution needs an A/B**: before calling a release-to-release delta a regression, build the previous tag and measure it on the same machine with the same harness - the v0.8.1-vs-v0.8.2 investigation (2026-11-13) traced the OpenGL3 row's apparent 25% growth and the scrollback row's 31% to a capture that did not reproduce on either build, and found the real change was 7 MB of startup cost (649 to 656). Inspect a chart edit with `rsvg-convert -o /tmp/chart.png docs/static/images/cost-history.svg`: the sandboxed image reader draws shapes but no text, so it cannot answer a layout question. `--release-dir` measures a shipped archive the same way, and `scripts/backfill-cost-history` walks a folder of them; two eras need handling there - v0.7.0+ ships `gpty-gui` beside a separate `gpty` CLI, earlier releases ship one GUI binary (`godopty` at v0.1.0) with no CLI, and v0.1.0/v0.2.0 predate the control socket entirely, so those measure the launch as it opens rather than a pane count. A pre-0.3.x socket is bound with the caller's umask and the current CLI refuses a 0644 socket on purpose; the harness tightens the file (the sandbox is 0700) rather than weakening the client.
- A headless run cannot answer a UI question whose truth is a pointer or a paint. Under `--headless` Godot has no display driver: `Viewport.gui_get_hovered_control()` is null even over a plainly visible `Button` (measured 4.7.2), no tooltip ever appears, and `frame_post_draw` never fires. So a test of a hover, a tooltip or a popup asserts the inputs the engine reads rather than the outcome - the control's `mouse_filter` (a `MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE` label is never a hover target), its `tooltip_text`/`get_tooltip()`, its `accessibility_name`, its `accessibility_live` - and the visible half is proven on a headed launch or by a `scripts/ui-capture` image of the state. The cursor shape itself is readable on a headed run without a human: a throwaway `-s` probe moves the pointer with `Input.parse_input_event` and reads `Input.get_current_cursor_shape()` after each step - that is how the v0.8.3 resize row was proven (HSIZE over the divider's band, still HSIZE immediately after a drag, ARROW over the pane body), and the probe is deleted afterwards. This is why the agent-state badge's tooltip is pinned by `mouse_filter` plus the string in `test_agent_badges.gd` and its rendering by the `agent-badges` capture, while the pointer landing on the badge was verified once on the headed build.
- A headless layout probe starts at a 64×64 viewport, and a headed launch's size is not `--resolution`: `godot --headless -s res://script.gd` instantiates the real `main.tscn` into a root viewport of `(64, 64)` (measured 4.7.2, 2026-11-08), so a probe of pane geometry measures a 38×38 tile and a terminal keeps its spawn grid rather than the fitted one - set `root.size = Vector2i(1920, 1080)` and `await process_frame` before adding the scene. The windowed app sizes itself from `SettingsManager.cfg_window_size`/the project setting instead of the flag: `--resolution 1600x900` still laid out a 1920×1080 workspace (the pane rects were 1738×1030, then 868×1030 after a split), so a probe that needs one window size sets it through the setting. That is the `-s` probe's viewport; the headless **app's own** root viewport is 0×0, so a size or layout claim made there is a claim about `_apply_layout`'s zero-rect fallback, not the real window (see the headless-GUI bullet in `pitfalls.md`).
- Accessibility is measured in two halves, because headless can prove neither the tree nor the reader: GUT asserts the metadata the app produces (`test_accessibility.gd`: `A11y.publish`'s node shape, pane identities, the terminal's `visible_text()`, and that no glyph-only button lacks an `accessibility_name`), `scripts/ui-capture --audit-accessibility <state>` prints a staged state's names/live modes/recorded values and the glyph buttons that have none (`unnamed=0` is the pass), and `scripts/accessibility-probe` walks the exposed AT-SPI tree of a rebuilt export (`./scripts/build` first; the Arch editor build has no AccessKit driver, and `A11y.screen_reader()` is false-unknown headless). The probe needs a display, a live at-spi bus and `org.a11y.Status.IsEnabled` (it sets and restores it), so it is not in `ci-check`. It also prints a report-only `a11y-values:` line (`text-interfaces`, `value-interfaces`, `marker-in-value`, `role-names`) that never gates the run: that line is how a later engine is graded on whether an element's value reaches AT at all. One thing in that log does gate it: the probe fails a run whose app output carries `Accessibility updates are only allowed` - the engine's refusal of a write made outside the control's own accessibility update. The `file-dialog` capture state walks the workspace row's **More → Set Directory**, so the picker's own frame is a captured surface; `--audit-focus file-dialog` covers its Escape and traversal. The probe's `REQUIRED` names are the current chrome's controls, and a menu item is only published while its popup is open - that is why the title bar contributes `More pane actions` and not the `Minimize pane` item inside that menu. The probe injects its marker through a `gpty` CLI (`GPTY_CLI`, else `gpty` on `PATH`, else `target/release/gpty`) and exits 3 without one - a run that cannot type the marker cannot assert the half it exists for - and it prints its first non-empty `Text` answers as `a11y-text:` lines. GUT reaches the gated push path through `A11y.force_enabled`, because headless has no accessibility driver.
- Headless resource leaks: GUT warnings about unfreed children and GDExtension `RID`/`ObjectDB` leaks are benign in headless mode - the dummy render server doesn't track GDExtension resources. Production renderer handles these correctly. The exception is a cycle the app itself owns: a `RefCounted`/`GDScript` entry in the list (not a `Node`, not a RID) survives a plain `godot --headless --quit-after N` run with no test harness at all, and that is a real defect, not headless noise - reproduce it there and read `pitfalls.md`'s owner/helper rule before dismissing it.
- A new `class_name` needs `godot --headless --path godot --import` before `gut-check` can see it: headless runs resolve global classes from `godot/.godot/global_script_class_cache.cfg`, which only the importer refreshes (that is why `ci-check` imports before GUT) - running `gut-check` alone right after adding a class fails with "Could not find type".
- The GUT gate is `./scripts/gut-check`, never the bare `godot -s addons/gut/gut_cmdln.gd` command (`ci-check` and `ci.yml` both call the script; CONTRIBUTING and the testing docs point at it). To run scoped tests while developing, pass a script filter directly (e.g. `./scripts/gut-check test_test_paths.gd`, `./scripts/gut-check -s <script> -t <test_name>`, or `./scripts/gut-check --dir unit`), which runs inside the full sandbox (`XDG_*` and `GPTY_TEST_USER_DIR` redirection) with stall and parse-error monitoring. If a bare invocation is unavoidable, pair `-gtest=` with `-gconfig=`: `.gutconfig.json`'s `dirs` still apply, so `-gtest=<one file>` alone runs the whole suite (measured 2026-11-08: 9 tests in 1.2 s with `-gconfig=`, 87 scripts / 1071 tests in 140 s without), while `gut-check`'s own stall message prints the `./scripts/gut-check --select <name>` recipe that narrows correctly. Use `-gdir=res://tests/unit -gselect=<filename substring>`: `-gselect` matches *script* names, so a test name there fails with "Could not find script matching" and runs nothing - narrow to one test with `-gunit_test_name=<test function>` beside it - and a bare invocation needs the same sandbox (the endpoint, user-root and secret variables below), or the run meets a developer's live GUI on the socket. GUT exits 0 after a parse error aborts the run - measured 4 of 40 scripts, 1.3 s instead of 57 s, no Run Summary - so the script owns the command and judges the output instead: Godot parse/script-error lines fail it, the Run Summary must be present and end in `All tests passed!`, the reported script count must equal the `test_*.gd` files the gdirs hold, and every script must contribute at least one test. The script also owns the clock: it ends a run the moment a script/parse error appears **before any test has started** (after that, a runtime error is GUT's to attribute and the run finishes so its failing-test list can be printed; measured 2 s from launch to a FAIL that prints the line, where a doomed run spent the whole timeout), and the deadline itself (default 600 s) escalates SIGTERM to SIGKILL, because Godot does not die on SIGTERM while a script waits - `timeout 300` was still alive with its Godot child after seven minutes (2026-11-02), which is how runs survived a 600 s cutoff. A run that produces no output for `GUT_STALL_TIMEOUT` (default 120 s) is a hang rather than a slow test - the suite starts a test every ~0.15 s and the longest single test waits 2.1 s - so it is killed well before the deadline and the failure names the last test started, its script, and the `-gselect` command that re-runs just that file (`GUT_STALL_TIMEOUT=0` disables the check). Adding a test directory means adding it to that script, not just to a command line: GUT does not recurse (`include_subdirectories` is off), and a `test_*.gd` nested below a gdir is reported as never-run rather than quietly skipped. The script also owns a **private endpoint and profile for the run**, which is not hygiene but the gate working at all: the suite spawns real panes, every instance binds the control *and* event endpoints, and one instance owns each - so a developer's open workspace used to make every pane-spawning test refuse its bind, set the test instance's shutdown flag and quit it mid-suite (measured 2026-10-14: 12 scripts, no Run Summary, which reads as a crash rather than as "close the app"). `GPTY_SOCKET` moves both listeners at once (the event path is derived from the control one; on Windows it is the pipe name), `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`/`XDG_DATA_HOME`/`XDG_STATE_HOME` point at one 0700 temp dir the trap removes, and `GPTY_SECRET` is cleared so a developer's shell cannot make the test instance demand a secret no test client has. The suite's **user root** is the same sandbox: `GPTY_TEST_USER_DIR` is set on every platform, and it is the one seam both halves read - `BasePersistenceManager.resolve_store_path` redirects every `user://` store through it and the gdext `history_db_path` redirects the scrollback database the same way. Setting it on Unix too is deliberate (the XDG dirs already cover Godot's `user://` there): the normal Linux gate exercises the seam, so a Windows-only path cannot drift unnoticed. On Windows, where the XDG variables do nothing because Godot resolves `user://` through the Known Folder API, `LOCALAPPDATA`/`APPDATA` are sandboxed as well (the Rust state/data directories read them directly). The GUT run does **not** use `--log-file`: Godot's file logging is off by default (`debug/file_logging` is unset), so there is no engine log to move, and the gate's own log capture already holds stdout for its judgment. The smoke does use it (it needs a failure-time engine log); adding it to the GUT command was the only difference from the known-good Windows run and the step hung with both the MSYS and `cygpath` spellings, so it stays out until a Windows run pins that down. `GUT_TIMEOUT` (600 s) caps the Godot process so a hung suite fails the gate instead of holding the runner to the six-hour job cap; the script enforces it itself (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL), so it no longer depends on a `timeout` binary and stock macOS is bounded too. `-d` is not passed: Godot parses it as `--debug`, and a runtime error in a test then breaks into the interactive debugger - measured on Windows as a 1.7 GB flood of the same `Debugger Break` that stalled the suite until the timeout; without it GUT records the failure and the gate's own checks fail the run. Tests that need a filesystem path use `TestPaths.user_path(...)`, never `ProjectSettings.globalize_path("user://...")`: a bare `user://` path bypasses the seam and on Windows writes the developer's real profile. Do not add a second rule - `BasePersistenceManager.resolve_store_path` is the store half, `history_db_path` the gdext half, and `TestPaths.user_dir()` asks the same `user_root_override()` for the directory. A fixture directory whose name is the same on two runs is created with `TestPaths.fresh_dir("name")`, never `user_path()` plus `make_dir_recursive_absolute`: it deletes the leftover first, so a teardown that was refused (or an interrupted run) cannot make a fixed name inherit another test's files. `TestPaths.is_safe_path_under(path, root, windows)` is the bounds rule the helper and `remove_tree` share, and `normalize_path` unifies the Windows drive separator before comparing: a `C:\` root from `GPTY_TEST_USER_DIR` and a `/`-joined child must normalise to the same spelling, because `String.simplify_path()` keeps the drive separator as written - `test_a_windows_drive_root_accepts_its_children` pins that on Linux, and a comparison must never edit a real path's bytes (a root that ends in a space is the same class).
- A harness that waits for work done off the frame must wait on wall time, never on a frame count: `scripts/ui-capture` runs Godot with `--disable-vsync`, where 120 frames can be ~0.2 s, so a capture state that waits for a `WorkerThreadPool` build polls `Time.get_ticks_msec()` against a deadline (~10 s) and the owner's own task id (`ui_capture.gd`'s `wiki-graph` state waits on `body._graph_task`) - a 120-frame loop failed while the build was still running. The same class of trap is script mode: `godot -s <script>` compiles that script's dependencies *before* the project's autoloads are registered, so a script that references another script naming an autoload (even through a typed field, e.g. `WikiPane` -> `KnowledgeStore`) fails to load with `Identifier not found: <Autoload>`; load it by path after `await process_frame` and keep the field untyped, as `godot/tests/bench/graph_bench.gd` does. Resolve an autoload through `root.get_node("SettingsManager")` - the nodes are present under `root.get_children()`, only their names as identifiers are missing - and never annotate a `-s` bench with an app class: `var tm: TerminalManager` or `body is TerminalPane` compiles that file into the load, where its autoload-dependent field fails and takes the whole script with it. `ui_capture.gd` duck-types (`"_terminal" in body`) and finds autoload-dependent nodes by script path for this reason; the v0.8.4 row **The capture harness compiles before autoloads, so pane-bearing states capture bare pane bodies** removed the last typed app class (`AgentBadge`) from it, and `scripts/ui-capture` now fails a capture whose log contains `SCRIPT ERROR` or `Failed to load script`, because such a run still writes a PNG.
- An engine error raised inside a test fails it: GUT reports it under `Unexpected Errors`, and passing assertions elsewhere do not save the test. A test that deliberately feeds invalid input must therefore avoid a logging API - `JSON.parse_string("")` logs `Condition "error != Error::OK"`, which failed `test_backend_choice.gd` on 2026-11-12 - and use the checked form instead (`JSON.parse` plus its error code, as `BackendChoice.roster` does). An assertion is not a guard: `assert_eq`/`assert_not_null` return void and the next line runs even when the assertion failed. Index or dereference only behind an explicit return - `var dialogs := _dialogs_of(pane)`, `assert_eq(dialogs.size(), 1, "…")`, `if dialogs.is_empty(): return`, then `dialogs[0]` - and guard a cast the same way (`if x == null: return`, as `test_inverse_paint.gd` does). `scripts/check-test-guards` fails a suite file that indexes a call's result directly (`_list_meta(pane)[0]`, `get_signal_parameters(...)[0]`): that shape cannot be guarded in place, and it is how three `dialogs[0]` reads raised `Out of bounds get index '0'` on `windows-smoke` run 44648884305. `gut-check` now lets an error GUT has attributed to a test finish the run and reports it as that test's failure with Godot's `at:` location and GUT's own per-test list; a run it cannot judge (collection-time parse error, no Run Summary, a stall) is reported separately as "not trustworthy". Comparing values of different types is the same class (`value == "@terminal"` on an `int` raises `Invalid operands`), and Godot 4 names `Range`'s bounds `min_value`/`max_value`. Rust's `godot_error!` **and** `godot_warn!` also arrive at GUT as engine errors (`PrintLevel::Warn` goes through `push_warning`'s logger arm), so a Rust-side refusal that is a handled outcome logs with `godot_print!`; warn/error is reserved for conditions the app does not handle.
